articles.title: Putin rejects mobilization rumors, many Russians unconvinced
articles.summary: Russia’s President Vladimir Putin has dismissed rumors about military mobilization. But many Russians, including many DW users, say they are preparing for the possibility.
articles.byline: Viktorija Terentjeva, Sergey Dik, Nickolai Linke, Evgeniy Dyuk

image.caption: Will Russia start conscribing more young men again to fight against Ukraine? (file photo from June 2022)Image: Donat Sorokin/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Twice within the first week of September, Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed rumors of a looming mobilization campaign in the country. On September 1, Putin called the rumors "complete nonsense" and described them as an "information attack" against Russia.
Two days later, on September 3, at the Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin said that "there is no scenario today that would require mobilization."
Summons are cause for unease among Russian DW users

DW's Russian service asked readers in Russia, on condition of anonymity, whether they see signs of an impending mobilization. The most common response from DW readers concerned receiving summonses from military enlistments offices.
"My nephew received a summons for data verification," wrote a reader from the industrial city of Naberezhnye Chelny.
"I received a summons ordering me to appear for data verification. I'm self-employed. What should I do?" wrote a user named Maxim.
"One of my friends, a school teacher, received a summons through the government services portal [Gosuslugi] on July 9 to update his records," said another reader, Sergei.

People fear that they may be called up for military service or lose the ability to leave the country freely. As a result, some of those who have received draft notices are seeking to travel abroad as quickly as possible, while restrictions on leaving the country have not yet taken effect.
"One acquaintance of mine left Russia two months ago after receiving a summons for data verification from the military enlistment office," one reader wrote.
Unwilling soldiers: A stealth mass draft starting in Russia?
Emigration as 'a fantasy'
Not everyone, however, sees emigration as a realistic option in the event of mobilization.
"As for leaving, that's a fantasy. Where would you go, and more importantly, with what money?" one DW reader wrote.

In June, reports emerged from Russia's Penza region that men were forcibly taken to military enlistment offices and pressured into signing military contracts. According to local reports, the practice became widespread enough that residents organized protests in support of relatives and neighbors. Journalists reporting on the issue say such raids are continuing.

"People are being detained, particularly near the entrances to their apartment buildings," Lena Lemyasova, a journalist with news outlet Important Stories [Vazhnye Istorii], told DW. "Often men who have been drinking. Unknown individuals approach them, or vehicles pull up — often cars provided by local authorities. The men are simply seized and taken away, then their families and neighbors hear nothing more. Later, information sometimes emerges that they were transported to military units. They are often held there before being sent to the front."
Important Stories specializes in investigative journalism. Its publisher, Roman Anin, spent ten years as investigations editor at well-known independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta.
What do Russian lawyers say about the summonses?

Does receiving a military summons mean a person will be sent to war? According to lawyer Artem Klyga, a summons issued "for data verification" does not in itself mean that someone will be drafted, mobilized or deployed. Data verification notices are one of several legally established reasons for calling someone to a military enlistment office.

"These summonses only show that military enlistment offices have significantly improved their military registration procedures. If mobilization begins, such records would help authorities quickly summon the people they need," Klyga explained to DW.

Russians have also increasingly reported receiving mobilization orders issued in advance. In peacetime, such orders do not oblige individuals to take any action. However, if mobilization is declared, recipients are required to report to their designated military enlistment office.

"They were issued before the war and during the war [against Ukraine] as well. But what changed in the first half of 2026 is that, judging by all indications, they began to be distributed in the hundreds of thousands," Russian lawyer Timofei Vaskin told DW. "We do not know the exact figures because the information is classified. But judging from social media reports and the number of inquiries we and our colleagues received, the increase was dramatic, by dozens of times."
At the same time, the 2022 decree on partial mobilization in Russia has never been formally revoked and technically remains in force.
Can Russians who flee partial mobilization come to Germany?

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has repeatedly described reports of a new mobilization wave as "fake stories." Yet critics note that Peskov also denied reports of a possible mobilization beginning in May 2022.
Just eight days before the announcement of partial mobilization, he said: "At the moment, this is not being discussed."
Growing demand for mobilization specialists

As of August 8, DW found several vacancies on the Russian job platform HeadHunter seeking specialists in "mobilization preparedness." 40 such vacancies are available in Moscow and the surrounding region and 13 in St Petersburg.

For example, some companies are looking for specialists responsible for ensuring that the organization has a mobilization plan in place and knows how it would operate if the state were to place the economy on a wartime footing. Their duties also include preparing the company for emergencies and civil defense measures, as well as helping to transition the organization to a special operating regime in the event of wartime conditions.
The positions were advertised by both private companies and state institutions.
Summonses, military training exercises, the expansion of military registration systems and active recruitment efforts help explain why official denials have failed to put the rumors to rest.
Preparing for ‘any decision Putin might make'

"The way to look at this is that bureaucrats have been tasked with preparing the system for any decision Putin might make. And if that decision is mobilization, they are expected to be ready," Artem Klyga said.

In late July, the independent outlet Agentstvo counted 197 vacancies around Russia containing the term "mobilization preparedness" and more than 2,600 vacancies related to "military registration" on the same recruitment platform.

articles.title: Dallas Republican convention: How Trump looms over midterms
articles.summary: Donald Trump is not on the ballot in the midterm elections — but the first Republican midterm convention is putting him center stage. It's a strategy that could prove risky for the party.

image.caption: Republican candidate Donald Trump and his wife Melania at the 2016 Republican National Convention in Ohio, where Trump was officially nominated as the Republican nominee for president for the first timeImage: Kevin Dietsch/newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: In the midterm elections on Nov. 3, US President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot. Nevertheless, his party is putting him at the center of a major convention two months before the election. On Wednesday and Thursday, Republicans are gathering at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, which can hold around 20,000 spectators, for the "Republican Midterm Convention."

In the United States, this sort of large party conventions are normally only held before presidential elections. Democrats experimented with similar gatherings in the 1970s and early 1980s, but for Republicans, the format is a first. In Texas, they want to mobilize Trump supporters for Republican candidates.
How much Trump is too much for the campaign?

Republicans are heading into the campaign with an unpopular president. According to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, Donald Trump had an approval rating of just 33%. On top of that, Democrats are currently much more energized. Nearly half of their supporters say they are especially enthusiastic about the midterm elections, compared with just 31% of Republicans.

Even so, the convention is entirely centered around Trump. The president will appear on both nights, putting him even more prominently in the spotlight than the Republican candidates who will actually be on the ballot for the Senate and House of Representatives in November. But for some of those candidates in particular, being seen as close with Trump poses a risk. A survey of more than 70 Republican candidates and lawmakers by Politico found considerable reluctance toward the convention.

Numerous candidates in competitive districts appear to shy away from being too closely associated with the president. The fact that some candidates are even avoiding their own party's convention altogether highlights the Trump dilemma. On the one hand, he could mobilize the MAGA base. On the other, his presence could also alienate moderate voters and even boost the opposition.

blocks.caption: Only one potential Trump successor is coming to Dallas: Unlike Vice President JD Vance (left), Secretary of State Marco Rubio (right) is not on the convention's speaker list so farImage: Kylie Cooper/REUTERS

blocks.text: A record of achievements or an attack on Democrats?

Despite the president's weak poll numbers, the convention's choreography initially focuses on a positive record of his time in office so far. Topics such as the economy, border security, trade and public safety are intended to show what Trump has already accomplished from the Republicans' perspective.

With segments such as "Two Visions for America" and "The Opposition Contrast," the convention is designed as an attack on the Democrats. Republicans portray them as a party dominated by the political left and a Democratic congressional majority as a threat to Trump's policies so far. In fact, it could block his agenda over the next two years and give Congress significantly more power to oversee and investigate the administration.

blocks.caption: The midterm elections will determine the new House of Representatives and part of the Senate Image: J. David Ake/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Does Trump have an answer to high living costs?
Trump's economic record is a particularly hard sell. The convention program focuses on what Trump has already done: his tax cuts, lower drug prices and efforts to promote domestic production.

Whether he can offer anything substantially new in Dallas remains unclear. Political scientist Sascha Lohmann of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) considers that unlikely. In such campaign settings, Trump's speeches are usually poorly structured and rarely outline specific policy measures, he says.
"What we see there is almost a kind of 'stream of consciousness,'" Lohmann continues. Trump tends to reveal over an extended period "whatever may happen to be going through his mind at the time."

The problem for Trump is that his telling of an economic success story does not match the perceptions of many Americans. In a recent FT/Focaldata poll, nearly two-thirds say the US economy is heading in the wrong direction. A total of 57% even say their personal financial situation has worsened since Trump took office again.
What will Trump say about the Iran war?

Perhaps the most striking element of the planned program is that the Iran war hardly figures in it. Among the 109 announced program items and speakers, there is a segment marking the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks alongside economic topics, but there is no attention paid to the ongoing war with Iran.

The convention organizers seem keen to keep the politically thorny issue out of the limelight as much as possible. Trump himself, however, has so far taken a different approach and continues to portray the war as a success. Lohmann expects him to maintain that line in Dallas as well.

He says that Trump's argument is "that Iran has been weakened to a greater extent than any president before him has ever managed, that its nuclear program has been wiped out and that the Iranians are now virtually begging for an end to the conflict."
No sign of end to US-Iran conflict after six months
Will Dallas set the stage for Trump's succession?

Officially, Dallas is about the midterms, but straight after the midterm elections, talk will move on to the next presidential election. Trump's Vice President JD Vance has been given a prominent role at the convention, while his potentially most important party rival, Marco Rubio, is not on the speaker list so far.
Trump will almost certainly not crown Vance as his successor in Dallas, but his vice president will have an opportunity to present himself to the MAGA audience as a potential heir to the movement.
"It seems likely that the vice president will be a central focus in Dallas," Lohmann says, "not least because Vance has so far had to bear very little political responsibility for the war with Iran."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Andrew Hastie accuses Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce of being ‘lying cowards’ over One Nation ‘traitor’ cartoon
articles.summary: The Canning MP says the cartoon, first posted by Hanson on social media over a month ago, calls him a traitor eight times

blocks.text: Liberal frontbencher and SAS veteran Andrew Hastie has called Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce “lying cowards”, after he claimed a One Nation cartoon portrayed him as a traitor for providing evidence in court against Ben Roberts-Smith.

Hastie further escalated his fight with One Nation on Wednesday, a day after the Canning MP used a letter to supporters to promise to take on Hanson and her chief strategist, James Ashby, directly – even hinting at costly court action.
Hastie told News24 the One Nation cartoon, first posted by Hanson on social media over a month ago and now pinned to the top of her X account, called him a traitor eight times.
“I would say that Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce are lying cowards, and I’ll say it again, so there’s no ambiguity,” he said.
“They are lying cowards … when you start calling me a traitor to my own country, then we have a big, big problem.”

The animated video, called “Don’t be Hastie”, depicts Hastie asking Anthony Albanese for help after people called him a traitor online. When Albanese asks Hastie why people are calling him a traitor, Hastie responds: “I don’t know, all I did was testify against Ben Roberts-Smith and support your evil hate speech legislation.” It has had more than 145,000 views on YouTube.

Hastie served in Afghanistan twice and has attracted the ire of One Nation and Hanson’s billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart, after he gave evidence against Roberts-Smith, the Victoria Cross recipient, in Roberts-Smith’s failed defamation case against Nine newspapers.

Hanson and Rinehart, as well as the former prime minister Tony Abbott, say Roberts-Smith is being unfairly targeted over war crimes allegations related to his service in Afghanistan, between 2009-2012.
The 47-year-old has been charged with five counts of the war crime of murder but strongly denies the allegations.
“Are they saying the same thing of the other 20 SAS combat veterans who gave evidence under oath in the federal court?” Hastie asked.
“Are they also traitors to their country?
“I gave evidence under oath, before God. For that, I’ve been called a rat, a traitor, a dog c—, and many other things. People I trusted have walked away from me or failed to defend me.
“Now I’m calling time on cowards who have never served a day in the Australian Defence Force attacking my service record, my integrity, and my loyalty to Australia.”
Hastie pointed out than Hanson and Joyce had “never, ever served a day in our uniform overseas on operations”.
“They don’t get to define Anzac Day, or Anzac, or the values that underpin our defence force.”
after newsletter promotion
Hanson denied ever calling Hastie a traitor, telling the Nightly: “I will call him a wanker.”
Joyce told Guardian Australia he has never called Hastie a traitor, “nor ventured anywhere close to any such narrative about him”.
“In fact I have never said a bad word about him,” he said.

“This morning in a press conference at Canberra I spoke in support of Mr Hastie and his family. When asked, I noted the fact that Ms Hanson stated she had never called Mr Hastie a traitor. This is now apparent as a fact.
“There has come to my attention now a satirical cartoon that made the claim. I had not seen it nor was aware of it.”

Hastie, the shadow minister for industry and sovereign capability, has spoken publicly about a campaign of threats and abuse targeting him and his family. The federal government boosted security around his home and office earlier this year.
One Nation won this month’s state byelection in the Western Australian seat of Secret Harbour, which overlaps Hastie’s federal electorate of Canning.

The party has flagged a major challenge to oust Hastie at the next election. Hastie is considered the leading alternative to opposition leader, Angus Taylor, but opted not to contest a leadership race earlier this year.

articles.title: TREYNA Group acquires Evident, expands PR capabilities
articles.summary: TREYNA Group scales its offering with the acquisition of Evident, expanding its award-winning public relations practice by bringing in the corporate and advocacy communications specialist. From…

blocks.text: TREYNA Group scales its offering with the acquisition of Evident, expanding its award-winning public relations practice by bringing in the corporate and advocacy communications specialist.

blocks.caption: TREYNA Group Chairman and CEO Mike Trillana with Evident founder Cecile Dominguez-Yujuico

blocks.text: From October 1, 2026, Evident will operate as TREYNA Evident, a business unit of TREYNA PR. The acquisition now positions TREYNA PR as one of the country’s most formidable PR agencies, with capabilities spanning consumer, brand, corporate, public affairs, and advocacy communications.TREYNA PR (previously MullenLowe MARC) has worked with major lifestyle and FMCG brands including Galderma, Monde Nissin, and Unilever. It has placed locally and regionally at multiple PR Agency of The Year award shows and continues to do so with its latest work for Galderma Cetaphil, Nutella, and Scoliosis Philippines.Evident adds deep experience in corporate and public affairs with a client portfolio spanning finance and capital markets, technology, transport, energy, telecommunications, and real estate. On the advocacy front, Evident works with multilateral institutions and local and international nonprofits supporting work in sustainability, public health, gender, and climate resilience, among others. Their work has earned recognition from the Philippine and Asia Pacific Quill Awards, Anvil Awards, and Stevie Awards.

“Evident was built for clients navigating complex regulatory, reputational and public interest terrain,” said Cecile Dominguez-Yujuico, founder of Evident. “Becoming part of TREYNA PR gives us the opportunity to bring that expertise into a broader communications offering and build even more meaningful work at scale together.”

The combination brings together complementary PR strengths: TREYNA’s expertise in building brands and connecting with consumers, and Evident’s experience in navigating stakeholder engagement, public sector advocacies, behavior change communication, and complex issues.

For TREYNA Group, the acquisition is the latest strategic move to build strong capabilities beyond its traditional advertising roots. Its M&A journey began with the acquisition of ARC Public Relations in 2018, followed by its investment in UX/UI specialist Quiddity in 2021 and the acquisition of Xiklab Digital’s digital advertising business in 2024.With that pattern of expansion came a broader reinvention of the agency itself. Formerly known as MullenLowe TREYNA, the company recently rebranded as TREYNA Group in 2026, following the retirement of the MullenLowe brand – adding another chapter to a 48-year agency history that counted Lintas, Lowe, and MullenLowe among its identities.According to TREYNA Group Chairman and CEO Mike Trillana, the acquisition reflects the same philosophy that has guided the agency through successive transformations.“Our challenger mindset has always meant questioning what exists, adapting to where the industry is going, and having the courage to bet on what’s next,” Trillana said. “That means TREYNA Group constantly adds capabilities—such as the expertise afforded by Evident—rather than be relegated to what it has traditionally been.”With TREYNA PR now combining consumer, corporate, and advocacy expertise, the latest move signals an agency group still treating reinvention not as a response to change, but as part of its operating model.For more on TREYNA Group and its latest work, visit treynagroup.com or check out @TREYNAgroup on all major socials.

articles.summary: From September 17 to 19, 2026, the Taiwan Healthcare Pavilion will take center stage at Booth No. 1 the SMX Convention Center Manila as part of the Taiwan Expo 2026. Featuring 21 prominent Taiwanese…

blocks.text: From September 17 to 19, 2026, the Taiwan Healthcare Pavilion will take center stage at Booth No. 1 the SMX Convention Center Manila as part of the Taiwan Expo 2026. Featuring 21 prominent Taiwanese hospitals and companies, the pavilion will highlight Taiwan’s world-class leadership across four key sections: Medical Services, Medical Devices, Regenerative Medicine, and Biotech and Everyday Wellness Solutions.

blocks.caption: Taiwan Expo 2026

blocks.text: Visitors to the pavilion will experience firsthand how Taiwanese healthcare integrates advanced technologies with modern medical science. Attendees are also invited to join an exclusive Product Launch on September 17 from 3:30 p.m. to 4:30 p.m, highlighting advanced medical innovations.

In the Medical Services sector, top-tier institutions—including Shin Kong Wu Ho-Su Memorial Hospital, Hualien Tzu Chi Hospital, Taipei Municipal Wanfang Hospital, Chang Bing Show Chwan Memorial Hospital, and Shuang Ho Hospital—will showcase international patient care, specialized medical services, and integrated healthcare solutions.

Highlighting the power of Medical Devices, Far East Medical Electronics Technology will showcase its latest telemedicine systems and smart care solutions. Quanta Computer is set to feature the QOCA o2b pulse oximeter for continuous blood oxygen monitoring, while Ginkgomed will present 3D anatomical software and digital pathology innovations. The pavilion will also highlight foot health technologies, smart diagnostics, and hearing aids—demonstrating how Taiwan leverages its strong ICT sector to improve the efficiency of patient care.

In the Regenerative Medicine sector, BioGend Therapeutics will showcase its innovative RevoCart One-Step Autologous Cartilage Repair System alongside Norien Biotech’s OsteoFill Gel injectable hydrogel platform, reflecting Taiwan’s growing capabilities in biomedical technology and advanced materials.

Furthermore, the Biotech and Wellness section will feature a wide range of products ranging from health supplements and algae-based formulations to medicated topical essential oils and skincare products. These offerings demonstrate how Taiwan’s healthcare industry extends beyond clinical treatment to preventive care, healthy living, and everyday wellness.

By bringing together Taiwan’s diverse industry strengths across those four sections, the Taiwan Healthcare Pavilion presents a comprehensive picture of Taiwan’s healthcare ecosystem. Taiwanese providers are actively seeking new partnerships to deliver accessible, efficient, and comprehensive healthcare solutions to the Philippine and Southeast Asian markets.

Reflecting the growing partnership between Taiwan and the Philippines, the Taiwan Healthcare Pavilion provides a vital hub for exchanging ideas, advancing medical capabilities, and shaping the future of regional care.

Trade visitors, medical professionals, and prospective business partners are encouraged to pre register for B2B matchmaking sessions and site visits via the official registration link: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdW-h9w0WEvjQKok8r2ywHKpk
uEaCPyvW7vZpRgHFgBvyw/viewform

Over the past few decades, the TITA’s role and responsibilities have undergone numerous adjustments to meet the demands of the ever-changing international business environment.

Headquartered in Taipei, their team of 1,300+ specialists operates across 5 domestic offices and a global network of 60+ branches in conjunction with the Taiwan Trade Center (TTC), Taipei World Trade Center (TWTC), and Far East Trade Service (FETS)—and supported by alliances with 500+ international affiliates—TAITRA provides a borderless service network for real time global trade.

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: Inside sweeping UK sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Ed Miliband has announced the strongest statement on Israel’s actions ever issued by the the UK government, but will it make a meaningful difference to…

blocks.text: Good morning. For almost half a century, British governments have condemned illegal Israeli settlements, acknowledging they represent an obstacle to peace and threaten the prospect of a two-state solution. And yet no government has ever compelled Israel to stop its expansion.

Ed Miliband’s statement in the House of Commons yesterday was an attempt to change that. In a powerful and emotive speech, the foreign secretary recounted childhood memories of picking oranges on his grandmother’s kibbutz, accused Israeli “terrorists” of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank and announced a series of new measures intended to address what he described as a “deeply painful contrast” between rhetoric and reality.

It was the strongest statement on Israel’s actions ever issued by the UK government. But will it make a difference to Palestinians living under the omnipresent threat of violence? Today’s newsletter, with the Guardian’s chief Middle East correspondent Emma-Graham Harrison and our diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour, drills into the details of Miliband’s announcement and explores that question. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK news | Police have been told by the government they expect better intelligence gathering after masked far-right groups took to the streets at the weekend, the Guardian has learned, as the Kent force admitted mishandling warnings of potential trouble.

UK politics | Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth tax, universal free personal social care and bringing gas and electricity networks under public ownership, according to a report from more than a dozen influential thinkers.

Airline industry | Flight delays and cancellations were expected to continue today at UK airports after another air traffic control failure kept planes grounded for hours, affecting hundreds of thousands of passengers.
Iran | Iranian forces claimed to have seized an American underwater drone in the strait of Hormuz that the US military said had “malfunctioned” more than a day earlier.

US news | Donald Trump gave sizeable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration, including $45,000 to executive assistant Natalie Harp.

blocks.text: In depth: Could Miliband’s statement shift what seems politically possible?

blocks.caption: The Israeli settlement of Maale Adumim near the E1 corridor, where a housing project could cleave the West Bank in two. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The number of settlers in the occupied West Bank (including East Jerusalem) has risen from 270,000 in 1993 at the time of the Oslo Accords to about 770,000 today. Settlements are often framed as the project of violent extremists backed by far-right cabinet ministers, but Israel’s annexation enjoys longstanding cross-party support. As Emma Graham-Harrison wrote in January, the idea has “persisted in Israeli political imagination,” and although Israeli politicians have condemned settler violence, roughly half of Israelis think settlements help Israel’s security.

In August, Benjamin Netanyahu’s government opened the tendering process for construction work on the E1 settlement, a vast project for 1,200 homes that would cut across the heart of the West Bank, dividing it in two and jeopardising the prospect of a two-state solution. Final bids for these contracts close days before the Israeli election next month, and the timing is strategic. “Netanyahu is trying to make E1 an election issue,” Patrick Wintour tells me.

Miliband’s predecessors Yvette Cooper and David Lammy condemned the plans for E1, and Cooper backed international sanctions on individual settlers. But neither went as far as Miliband. “He’s a more decisive foreign secretary,” Patrick tells me. “You can’t sporadically say this is an outrage, and then not mention it for two months”.

His stance also reflects Labour’s desire to win back voters on the left. The post-match analysis from Labour’s disastrous May local elections focused on the threat of Reform, but the Greens were a bigger threat to Labour’s vote. Miliband acknowledged yesterday that “Labour has not done enough in the face of what is happening”, and has announced these sanctions just before a pivotal byelection in Holborn and St Pancras, where the leader of the Green party, Zack Polanski, will be contesting Keir Starmer’s former seat.
What has Miliband announced?

It’s worth remembering where we were just two years ago, when Starmer’s government was still resisting calls for a ceasefire in Gaza. Although Starmer became more critical of Netanyahu’s government and ultimately recognised Palestinian statehood, Miliband’s speech marked a significant shift in tone and substance from this equivocating stance. He framed his intervention not as an argument with Israelis, “with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds”, but with the conduct of Israel’s government, its illegal occupation of Palestine, and with “settler terrorists”, while attacking the Boycott, Divest and Sanctions movement that calls to limit all trade with Israel.

The first measure he announced is a widely anticipated ban on the import of goods from illegal settlements. This is important, not least because these settlements violate international law, but the economic impact of the ban will probably be minimal. The settlement economy is relatively small, and its products are already excluded from a 1995 EU free trade deal that reduces the tariffs on Israeli imports to Europe. It’s also kept alive by generous subsidies from the Israeli government. Israeli exporters to Europe regularly hide the origins of produce grow in settlements, something that could be dealt with by the “comprehensive sanctions regime” Miliband is working up with the business secretary.

As significant as the ban itself is the fact France and Canada will join the UK in sanctioning Israeli settlements, a diplomatic coup for Miliband. Far-right ministers such as Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir have come out forcefully against Miliband’s sanctions (on Monday, Ben-Gvir issued a statement in Spanish calling for sanctions on Britain over its “occupation” of the Falkland Islands). Part of the reason is because Israel’s economy is bound far more closely to Europe than to the United States, and they fear a domino effect. “The UK is a permanent member of the security council, and they’re worried that Miliband’s statement could shift the window in terms of what seems politically possible,” says Emma. “Someone else stands up and says it, and suddenly, you aren’t taking an initiative – you’re following another country.”
What will this mean for illegal settlements?

One of its most transformative changes could be Miliband’s pledge to take action against companies and individuals who finance or “facilitate” illegal settlements. Any individual or company that wants to bid for government led construction projects, including new settlement expansion, needs a guarantor to underwrite their new property. Settlement residents also need banking services. Under these changes, banks and other companies that provide services to Israeli settlements will be sanctioned.
“Hypothetically, this could force mainstream financial organisations in Israel to choose between financing settlements, or doing business with the UK,” Emma says.
What has the fallout been?

Israeli ministers have frequently made their intentions in the West Bank clear, but the gap between reality and the reactions of the international community is vast. Miliband’s statement went some way towards closing that. He announced that the British government officially views Israel’s occupation as unlawful (it had previously declared settlements illegal but remained silent on the wider occupation) and that it will refuse all licences for arms that contribute to the occupation. He chose his words carefully, accusing “settler terrorists” of “ethnic cleansing”. As the Israeli human rights lawyer Michael Sfard observed, the recognition of ethnic cleansing triggers legal obligations on the UK to prevent it in the West Bank, potentially dictating “many aspects of British policy towards Israel”.

Israel retaliated by announcing it will be closing the consulate in Jerusalem and banning 11 MPs (on a list topped by Jeremy Corbyn) from entering the country. Meanwhile, the US has threatened “repercussions”. “There is no limit on what Trump could potentially do,” Patrick says. “But it’s worth bearing in mind that he is quite ambivalent about Netanyahu at the moment.” Their relationship has soured over Israel’s refusal to agree to Trump’s peace plan and the ongoing conflict in Iran.

Unquestioning bipartisan support for Israel among US politicians appears to be faltering. Rahm Emanuel, Obama’s former chief of staff who is sounding out a presidential bid, has said he would back sanctions on companies financing illegal settlements. Earlier this week, Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, attacked Miliband for “Jew hate” over the (not yet announced) sanctions plans, but he has also called settler violence an “act of terror”. Miliband’s statement is a powerful recognition of the international law that Israel has relentlessly tried to reject, and comes at a time when itlooks increasingly isolated.
What else we’ve been enjoying

It’s a tough read, but I’m grateful that Tom’s kept the spotlight on children, who need us most and who we, as a society, serve least. Libby
Picture a giant pumpkin, then double its size – Gladys is even bigger. There’s lots of rich detail in today’s pass notes on the 14ft circumference fruit (or is she a vegetable?) Michael

One of the many delights of writing a newsletter is the chance to draw readers’ attention where it might not ordinarily land. So it is with our sister email Moving the Goalposts, discussing a recent blow-up in South Korean women’s football. Libby
A new Elon Musk documentary is doing the film festival rounds, and this roundup of its key takeaways has certainly piqued my interest. Michael
In case you missed it, this Today in Focus episode about Gloria Steinem’s life and legacy is worth a listen for the fabulous archive material and more. Libby

The front pages

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: “UK condemns ‘ethnic cleansing by Israeli terrorists’ in West Bank”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times leads with “Israel reacts with fury to UK curbs on settlements”, the i Paper also has “Israeli fury after UK accuses settlers of ethnic cleansing” and Metro runs “Backlash as UK accuses Israel”. The Mail says “Miliband accused of putting Jews in UK in danger”, and the Express writes “‘You have put an increased target on us’”.

Elsewhere, the FT splashes “Bailey warns of ‘upside’ inflation risks as debt costs pile pressure on Healey”, the Telegraph writes “Air traffic collapse grounds flights”, and the Sun has “That’s another flyin’ mess”.
The Latest

blocks.caption: Photograph: The Guardian

blocks.text: UK condemns Israeli settlers conducting ethnic cleansing in West Bank

The UK has attacked ‘settler terrorism’ deployed in a campaign of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, while announcing sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in occupied Palestine. Foreign secretary Ed Miliband delivered the strongest condemnation of the actions of the Israeli government ever by a British government, including the disproportionate killings in Gaza of at least 70,000 people including 20,000 children. Lucy Hough speaks to chief Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison.
Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron

blocks.caption: Illustration: Ella Baron/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Bogotá has launched a number of initiatives to assist its ageing population. Photograph: Bogotá

blocks.text: Bogotá is not the only city to face the challenges of a rapidly aging population but, with a fertility rate lower than Tokyo, the Colombian capital is taking a creative approach. As multigenerational homes become less common, the mayor opened “care blocks”, where caregivers can drop off a toddler or an elderly relative for a few hours. Reducing social isolation is key, so the city has started prescribing culture and nature-based activities. Last December, a seniors’ grand ball saw about 4,500 older people dancing to live salsa at the city’s Movistar arena.

articles.summary: Taking over the spot initially reserved for Justin Brownlee, Calvin Oftana joins Gilas Pilipinas just a couple of days before it opens its title defense in the Asian Games

blocks.text: VETERAN. Calvin Oftana in action for Gilas Pilipinas in the 2025 FIBA Asia Cup.
FIBA
Taking over the spot initially reserved for Justin Brownlee, Calvin Oftana joins Gilas Pilipinas just a couple of days before it opens its title defense in the Asian Games

items: Calvin Oftana has been added to the Gilas Pilipinas roster for the Asian Games, replacing Justin Brownlee who is dealing with injuries.
Oftana, who plays for TNT in the PBA, last participated in national team duties in March and is now fit to play after returning to practice.
Coach Cone believes Oftana will integrate well into the team due to his extensive experience and familiarity with the system.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Calvin Oftana returns to national team duty as he completes Gilas Pilipinas’ 12-man roster in the Asian Games.

Taking over the spot initially reserved for Justin Brownlee, Oftana flew to Japan on Wednesday, September 9, just two days before the Philippines opens its title defense against Bahrain at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya on Friday, September 11.
“Calvin Oftana is stepping in as our 12th man. He is arriving this afternoon, we hope in time to make our practice schedule today,” Cone said through a Viber exchange.
Oftana, who stars for TNT in the PBA, last suited up for Gilas Pilipinas in March in the second window of the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers before injuries kept him out of national team action.

Cone previously said the Asian Games team is ready to compete with just 11 players if Brownlee, who has been dealing with injuries that sidelined him for the last three Asian Qualifiers games, is unable to play.
But with Oftana becoming available, Cone and his staff decided to bring him in.
“Calvin was always on the list to play, but we were uncertain of his health status. He has since returned to TNT’s practice and is good to go,” said Cone.
Despite Oftana coming in at the last minute, Cone sees him fitting seamlessly into the squad, with the 30-year-old forward boasting extensive national team experience.
In fact, Oftana is the only remnant of the 2023 crew that won the Philippines its first men’s basketball gold medal in the Asian Games since 1962.
“Because of the system we are running and his previous experience in the window teams, he’s a plug and play player and will fit right in,” said Cone.
After Bahrain, the Philippines will battle Kazakhstan and China on September 12 and 14, respectively. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Who can use the Lido name? SC cancels ‘Lido Cocina Tsina’ trademark
articles.summary: Years after the falling out between old partners, the Supreme Court says the trademark still belongs to the partnership they left behind

blocks.text: Years after the falling out between old partners, the Supreme Court says the trademark still belongs to the partnership they left behind

items: The Supreme Court of the Philippines ruled that the trademark registrations for 'Lido' held by Panciteria Lido Chinese Cuisine Co. were canceled due to bad faith registration, affirming that the rights belong to Eng Son Co.
The dispute arose from a split between former partners Alipio and the King family, leading to the creation of two separate Lido-branded restaurants and subsequent trademark conflicts.

The ruling clarified that while the King heirs have a legal interest to challenge the registrations, they do not automatically own the Lido trademark, which remains a partnership property until its affairs are resolved.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Just as Lido, a household name in Chinese dining, marks its 90th year, the Supreme Court settled a decades-long dispute over who owns the restaurant’s name.
The SC canceled two Lido trademark registrations held by Panciteria Lido Chinese Cuisine Co., including one for “Lido Cocina Tsina,” after finding that the company registered the marks in bad faith.
“Through Alipio, respondent knew that the right to register the Lido mark belonged to Eng Son Co., yet it caused the registration of the subject marks in its own name,” read part of the SC ruling.

But the SC did not award the Lido name to the King family, whose heirs brought the case. It instead upheld the earlier finding that “the right to register the trademark ‘Panciteria Lido’ is vested to the partnership” Eng Son Co., with no proof that the partnership had been wound up or that the marks had been transferred elsewhere.
Lido traces its roots to 1936. King and Alipio later formed Eng Son Co. in 1997 to operate Lido Restaurant.

The two were once close business partners, but their relationship eventually soured. The falling out also divided the restaurant business, with some franchisees going with Alipio and others with the King family. The Alipio side eventually became Lido Cocina Tsina, while the King side operated as Salido.
The trademark fight soon followed.
Alipio applied in 2008 to register Panciteria Lido in her own name. King opposed the application, and the Intellectual Property Office ruled in 2010 that the right to the mark belonged to Eng Son Co.
King died that same year. His death dissolved the partnership, but under the Civil Code, dissolution did not terminate it. The partnership continued to exist until its affairs were wound up.
Alipio later formed PLCCC with other partners, and the new partnership obtained two Lido trademark registrations in 2012. King’s sons Albert and Arthur eventually challenged them.

blocks.caption: Cyma drama: SC ends Greek restaurant’s trademark dispute

blocks.text: The SC sided with the King heirs and ordered the registrations canceled, but it made clear that winning the case did not make them owners of Lido.

“While such hereditary interest did not automatically vest in petitioners ownership over specific partnership assets prior to liquidation, it nevertheless gave them a sufficient legal interest” to challenge the registrations, the High Tribunal said.
The SC found no evidence that Eng Son Co. had ever been liquidated, that its affairs had been wound up, or that ownership of the Lido marks had been lawfully transferred elsewhere.
That leaves the Lido trademark in the unusual position of remaining a partnership property even though the business relationship behind that partnership fell apart years ago.

The ruling does not order either Lido Cocina Tsina or Salido to close. It also does not resolve who may ultimately use, license, or assign the Lido name once the old partnership’s affairs are finally settled. – Rappler.com

articles.title: South Park creators rename show 'South America' in apparent dig at Trump
articles.summary: Since beginning his second term, the US president has said he wanted to use the word 'America' to rename a lake, a gulf and even a US state.

blocks.text: The creators of South Park, the animated TV show, have announced that its new series will be named South America, in an apparent reference to US President Donald Trump's attempts to rename a lake and a gulf.
"Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google, we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA," creators Matt Stone and Trey Parker wrote in a statement.
Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America, and last year declared that the Gulf of Mexico be known as the Gulf of America.
The announcement from South Park, now in its 29th season, comes after the show won an Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday.
The official name change shared to the show's official social media account featured an image of the South Park sign with the word 'Park' replaced with 'America'.
"We especially want to thank our parent company Paramount - a Skydance Capitulation," its creators said in the post.
Paramount Skydance is the show's parent company. The Trump administration this year approved a $111bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery - one of the biggest media deals in history.
But the merger has since been paused until June 2027, after 12 US states filed lawsuits against the deal for fear of it harming competition and leading to higher prices for consumers.
A day before the show's announcement, Trump shared an AI-generated video of him placing the word 'America' over 'Mexico' on a "Welcome to New Mexico" sign.
In August, as trade tensions escalated between the US and Canada, Trump ordered a similar change for Lake Ontario - renaming it Lake America.
Apple and Google subsequently changed the name in their respective Maps apps for US-based users.
And last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico be renamed as Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
South Park, which has run since 1997, has regularly mocked the US president during his two presidency terms.
Both its creators, Stone and Parker, have repeatedly drawn criticism from Trump, the White House and MAGA supporters for its jabs at the president.

During its 27th season, the White House described South Park as a "fourth-rate" show that was "hanging on by a thread with uninspired ideas in a desperate attempt for attention", after an episode depicted Trump naked in bed with Satan.
After winning the award for Outstanding Animated Program on Sunday, South Park also shared an image depicting a fictionalised Donald Trump with the words: "You finally got your Emmy."
The new season of South Park will premiere on 16 September.

articles.title: PNP prepares room for Romualdez's possible hospital detention
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Wednesday said it has prepared a room for former Speaker Martin Romualdez in case he is allowed to remain under hospital detention following his arrest on…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 1:37pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Wednesday said it has prepared a room for former House Speaker and Leyte 1st Dist. Rep. Martin Romualdez in case he is allowed to remain under hospital detention following his arrest on plunder charges.

"We have already undertaken the necessary preparations for the possible transfer. We requested that he be transferred to the PNP General Hospital, so we have already made the initial preparations," PCol. Allen Rae Co said.
"A room has already been prepared for him,” he added..
Co said PNP doctors are also coordinating with the management of Cardinal Santos Medical Center for an independent health assessment of Romualdez.
"[This is] for us to be able to assess if the former Speaker [is] physically fit to face the Sandiganbayan," Co said.

Romualdez was arrested Monday at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, the same day the Office of the Ombudsman filed a P7.4-billion plunder charge against him and three others over their alleged involvement in a kickback scheme involving flood control projects.

Police have since secured Romualdez at the hospital, where he was taken Monday afternoon after suffering "a cardiovascular event, unstable blood pressure, and an anxiety attack," Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said.
Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said the Office of the Ombudsman would "strongly oppose" Romualdez's motion for hospital detention.

"The prosecutors will strongly oppose the motion. In fact, the prosecutors will ask that not just one doctor but a team of government doctors assess whether or not the illnesses declared need confinement or can be managed outside of the hospital," Clavano said.

"If his illnesses can be managed from outside of the hospital, the prosecutors will move that he be immediately transferred to the regular detention facility as all other accused in non-bailable cases," he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: [In this Economy] PISA 2025: Much better scores, but the learning crisis remains
articles.summary: The improvements are real, but that’s what you get from intense preparation. As with any student determined to ace an exam, preparation is key.

blocks.text: After a long wait, on September 8, we now have the results of the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) which measures the skills of 15-year-old students.
There’s good news all around. Philippine scores have improved in all three subjects tested: our reading score rose from 347 in 2022 to 367, math from 355 to 371, and science from 356 to 373.

All three increases were statistically significant, meaning the analysis finds evidence of improvement beyond sampling and measurement uncertainty. PISA noted that we were among eight participating education systems that exhibited significant gains in all three subjects. Great!
In addition, the share of Filipino students below baseline proficiency in science, or PISA’s minimum expected skill level, also fell by a significant 8.9-percentage points between 2022 and 2025.
All of this is welcome news, and our teachers and students deserve recognition.
What accounts for the improvement? On the one hand, such a result should be hardly surprising, given the intense preparations of the Department of Education (DepEd).

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. himself directed DepEd, as early as 2024, to improve its PISA ranking. In response, DepEd formed a “Task Force PISA” whose job was to help teachers and especially students prepare for the computerized tests. They provided computers to the hundreds of schools which would potentially be sampled at random by the PISA test administrators, and took pains to allow students to practice on “PISA-type reviewers”—so that they’re less anxious to take the PISA test in case they are chosen to take it. These were so-called “familiarization sessions.” During test day itself, DepEd also made sure to put in place a “festive” mood in the schools, to make the exam less scary for students.

In 2024, DepEd also rolled out a “special science program” which involved teachers training their students in PISA-type questions. (This raised concerns that selected students were being trained for the sake of PISA 2025, a phenomenon called “teaching to the test.”)

Meanwhile, within the DepEd hierarchy, certain regional offices proferred incentives (e.g. awarding of plaques in special events) for “PISA Participating SDOs and Schools” after the exam was administered. The idea was to “recognize the efforts and commitment of PISA-participating schools” and, prospectively, “incentivize continued improvement in learning outcomes to drive future enhancements in educational performance.”

The singular focus of the public education system on PISA 2025 seems to have paid off. The improvements are real, but that’s what you get from intense preparation. As with any student determined to ace an exam, preparation is key.

The Philippines’ improvement is especially amazing given the broader trend in rich countries showing a significant deterioration especially in reading and math scores. According to the official press release, “Average reading scores fell by 28 points across OECD countries between 2015 and 2025, equivalent to about one and a half years of learning. Mathematics scores fell by 22 points, equivalent to just over one year of learning. Among non-OECD PISA participants, reading scores fell by 16 points and mathematics scores by eight points over the same period.”
Whether this unsettling result is because of worsening digital distractions or greater use of AI, we don’t quite know yet. At least for us, we seem to be bucking this global trend—for now.
Of course, there’s much more to say about the Philippines’ PISA results beyond the headline-grabbing gains.
First, our 2025 reading score of 367 is still quite low compared to the OECD average of 461. In math, the comparison is 371 versus 463, and in science, 373 versus 482.

Our ranking in ASEAN also still leaves much to be desired (Figure 1). While we managed to overtake Indonesia in reading and math, the differences are not statistically significant. Cambodia managed to overtake us in science, so that in the region we’re now last in science. Vietnam, which became an upper-middle income country this year (like us) is also way ahead of us in terms of math and science.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.

blocks.text: While the DepEd was gleeful to list the countries that now rank below us, we cannot treat every country below us as a country we overtook. Some countries and economies below us in 2025 were absent in 2022.

More troubling, the vast majority of Filipino students are still below the baseline proficiency level called Level 2 (Figure 2). As much as 70% are below-proficiency in reading, 79% in math, and 68% in science. Meanwhile, 64.3% of Filipino students, or nearly two in three, were below baseline proficiency (Level 2) in all three subjects simultaneously.

blocks.caption: Figure 2.

blocks.text: The gains were also unequal. Between 2022 and 2025, science scores rose by 36 points among the most socioeconomically advantaged quarter of Filipino students, versus 10 points among the most disadvantaged quarter. The latter increase was not statistically significant, while the gap widened by a significant 26 points.

Naturally, DepEd was in a self-congratulatory mood when the PISA 2025 results were announced. But higher scores do not, by themselves, establish which specific DepEd program worked, how much it contributed, or which specific official deserves credit.

Better instruction could have contributed, alongside greater familiarity with the computer platform and question formats. Preparation can include actual teaching, too, which means learning and test preparation are not always separable. The score increase alone cannot tell us how much came from each.

DepEd’s preparation materials warrant scrutiny. Since we joined PISA 2022, resources already included computer-based familiarization and practice materials, so these may have helped in the most recent round.

Some people allege that DepEd handpicked good students and schools. But PISA follows a prescribed sampling process, and the OECD says Philippine data met its quality standards. The 2025 sample included 8,072 students in 208 schools.

Nonetheless, since DepEd knew weeks in advance which specific schools would participate, it’s worth asking: did PISA-participating schools receive substantial extra support that comparable schools elsewhere did not?

Till now, we don’t exactly know what happens after random selection, and how much additional resources were poured to sampled schools. Maybe DepEd should publish the coverage, timing, and intensity of its preparations so that researchers can study their contribution. Establishing which measures helped would also inform whether they should reach more schools.
PISA’s coverage has limits, too. The Philippine sample represented about 82% of the country’s 15-year-old population, leaving young people outside its coverage whose learning also deserves attention.

More research needs to be done. A 2023 study published in the Economics of Education Review studied Vietnam’s exceptional PISA performance despite being an emerging economy. They found that Vietnam’s advantage persists even after adjustments for better-off students being overrepresented, adolescents outside school being excluded, and possible differences in test preparation and effort. Measured household and school characteristics explain only part of Vietnam’s exceptional performance, and much remains unexplained.

For the Philippines, that study suggests that poverty alone need not determine educational outcomes. Researchers must find out: how much of our learning gap persists after accounting for family circumstances and who gets tested? And what could explain the remainder?
Finally, by no means do the new results tell us that we have eradicated our long-standing learning crisis.

Apart from the 90% learning poverty rate that previously shocked the country, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) also reported that proficiency rates plummet from 30% in Grade 3 (abysmal as it already is) to as low as 0.47% by Grade 12.

EDCOM 2’s executive director, Karol Mark Yee, also lamented recently on social media that the national government’s budget documents for 2027 are replete with the phrase “at least nearly proficient”—meaning that DepEd’s performance indicators are considered met if students are “at least nearly proficient” (not quite “proficient”). Karol argues that this is too low a bar, and may serve to mask systemic underperformance.

On top of this, Education Secretary Sonny Angara also divulged that for 2027 the budget proposed by the executive for the ARAL Program amounted to zero. ARAL involves remedial interventions for students lagging in reading. As things stand, there’s also no budget yet to hire teachers next year.

Worse, the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism (PCIJ) recently reported that politicians have made schools their milking cows as well. They said, “Data from the DPWH Transparency Portal reveals that contractors tied to the flood control scandal were the same ones awarded a large share of school infrastructure contracts.” Moreover, “Construction tycoons Curlee and Sarah Discaya bagged some P13.4 billion worth of school building and facility contracts from 2016 to 2026–the largest haul among all contractors.”

In sum, let’s celebrate the recent PISA gains. But that should not lull us into thinking that the education crisis is now gone. DepEd still needs to establish what caused the improvement and whether the measures behind it can help students across the country, especially those who remain below baseline proficiency.
Most importantly, the DepEd must ensure that these gains are persistent and not just one-off. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Intent to nab dela Rosa not waning amid ‘negotiations’ – PNP
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) maintained that its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa were not waning despite purported ongoing negotiations with “protectors”…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) maintained that its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa were not waning despite purported ongoing negotiations with “protectors” for his surrender.
“It will take as long as it will take,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co said in a press briefing in Camp Crame on Wednesday.
“Our efforts did not wane, will not wane, and we will not deviate from serving the warrant of arrest,” he insisted.
Dela Rosa was ordered arrested by the International Criminal Court in a warrant issued last November.
The warrant was only publicized in May and it was in connection with his alleged involvement in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war against illegal drugs.
On Tuesday, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that the government was in negotiations with dela Rosa’s “protectors,” whom he only identified as “powerful people.”
The senator’s legal counsel, Israelito Torreon, however, denied any personal knowledge of the supposed negotiations nor the protectors.
For its part, Co said the PNP’s search for dela Rosa are continuous, but the spokesperson refused to provide further details, citing operational matters.
He further noted that 91 of the 117 firearms registered to dela Rosa are still unaccounted for.
“Our FEO is continuously coordinating with the family for the surrender of the guns. Legal police action will be initiated,” Co explained.
The PNP FEO revoked dela Rosa’s firearms license and gun registrations in June as part of the bid to capture him.
Dela Rosa was last seen leaving the Senate premises and was supposedly dropped off in Makati City in the early hours of May 14, after a shooting in the chamber.
Remulla previously said dela Rosa’s last known location was in Mindanao. /apl

articles.title: Zamboanga City marks ‘Day of Remembrance’ for bloody 2013 siege
articles.summary: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Zamboanga City government observed a “Day of Remembrance” on Wednesday for the 2013 bloody Zamboanga Siege that killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands…

blocks.text: PAGADIAN CITY, Zamboanga del Sur – The Zamboanga City government observed a “Day of Remembrance” on Wednesday for the 2013 bloody Zamboanga Siege that killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands of residents.
Mayor Khymer Adan Olaso issued Executive Order KHYM 183- 2026 on Tuesday, declaring Wednesday a “Day of Remembrance” to honor the lives lost and the sacrifices made during the 2013 Zamboanga Siege.
The order recognizes the heroism of the security forces who defended the city and remembers the civilians caught in the crossfire during the three-week conflict 13 years ago.
Olaso highlighted the selflessness of the military, police, and emergency personnel who stood on the frontlines to safeguard the city’s democratic ideals and way of life.
Pursuant to Sangguniang Panlungsod Resolution No. 1019, dated Sept. 2, 2014, the declaration formalizes Sept. 9 as an annual day of commemoration.

The mayor urged local businesses—including major department stores, restaurants, public conveyances, entertainment centers, and resorts—to observe the occasion by offering customers a 20% discount every September 9, with special emphasis on active security personnel, as a gesture of solidarity and appreciation.
The September 2013 siege remains one of the darkest chapters in the city’s history.

Sparked by an influx of Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) fighters identified with the Nur Misuari faction, the three-week standoff directly affected six barangays and displaced 22,196 families—or 122,226 individuals.

The urban armed conflict claimed the lives of 25 military and police personnel, alongside 13 civilians, while 266 others were wounded. Rebel casualties were reported at 153 killed in action, with 278 individuals arrested.
The physical and economic destruction was massive.

At least 9,722 homes were burned or destroyed, causing an estimated P200.83 million in damages, while the closure of the city’s airport and seaport paralyzed trade links across Basilan, Sulu, Tawi-Tawi, and the broader Zamboanga Peninsula, resulting in an estimated P331 million in daily economic losses.

Despite the lingering scars, local officials emphasized the resilience of the city’s constituents. Rebuilding and recovery efforts have relied heavily on support from the national government, non-governmental organizations, civil society groups, and international partners.

In his declaration, Olaso offered eternal prayers and condolences to the families of the victims, reassuring residents that the memory and heroism of those who served—including prosecutors from the Department of Justice who pursued legal accountability—will remain permanently etched in the hearts of every Zamboangueño./ca

articles.title: 68 Itogon families evacuate amid prolonged rains in Benguet
articles.summary: BAGUIO CITY – Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the…

blocks.text: BAGUIO CITY – Sixty-eight families (351 people) have voluntarily evacuated their homes in the Benguet municipality of Itogon as prolonged rains from a succession of weather disturbances and the enhanced southwest monsoon raised safety concerns in several communities.

As of Monday, a total of 227 families, or 874 individuals, have been affected by the continued rains across Itogon’s nine barangays, according to the Municipal Social Welfare and Development Office (MSWDO). It said 81 houses were also reported damaged.

The evacuations were carried out as residents in high-risk areas responded to government advisories to seek safer locations amid weeks of rainfall brought by weather disturbances Luis, Maymay, Neneng, Obet, and Pilandok, as well as the monsoon.

Barangay Ampucao recorded the highest number of affected families at 65 (256 individuals, followed by Loacan with 47 families (211 people). Gumatdang reported 46 affected families, while Poblacion had 44 families (134 individuals).

The MSWDO distributed 238 family food packs and hygiene kits to affected residents. The provincial government also provided 200 five-kilogram rice packs, while the Office of Civil Defense in the Cordillera provided nonfood items and fuel assistance for emergency response operations.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development also extended cash assistance to affected families in Gumatdang, Virac, Tuding, and Tolibeng in Loacan. The Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office provided additional nonfood items to families in Tolibeng.

Mayor Bernard Waclin, together with the MSWDO and disaster risk reduction councils, led the assessment and relief efforts. The municipal government said no casualties had been reported in Itogon amid the prolonged rains and successive weather disturbances. Maureen Matayew / Contributor/coa

articles.title: Voting threshold in impeachment trial too early to be tackled --UP prof
articles.summary: It is too early for the Senate impeachment court to be discussing the 16-vote threshold set to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, said Paolo Tamase, University of the Philippines-College of Law…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 1:29pm

It is too early for the Senate impeachment court to be discussing the 16-vote threshold set to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, said Paolo Tamase, University of the Philippines-College of Law associate dean.
In a Super Radyo dzBB interview on Wednesday, Tamase said it must first be clear how many senators will actually be able to vote before the Senate can make a decision regarding the voting threshold.
"Hindi pa ho hinog pa rin in that sense dahil inaantay natin na lumapit na doon sa pagboboto mismo," Tamase said.
(It’s still too early to make that assessment because we’re waiting until we get closer to the actual voting.)

"Kasi malayo pa, maaga pa ang stage 'yung usapin ng pagbaba ng threshold or pagtaas ng threshold. Minsan kailangan na mas malinaw 'yung circumstances, 'yung situasyon kung ilan talaga makakaboto bago makarating sa intelihenteng desisyon 'yung Senado ukol dito," he added.

(Because we are still far from that point. It is too early to discuss lowering or raising the threshold. Sometimes, we need a clearer picture of the circumstances, particularly how many senators will actually be able to vote, before the Senate can make an informed decision on the matter.)

However, Tamase clarified that discussing the voting threshold is a good way to gauge the sentiments of the senator-judges and strengthen the principle that the impeachment is under their jurisdiction.

"Bagamat hindi normal course 'yun sa impeachment, maganda na rin magkaroon ng debate or oral argument 'di dahil kinakailangan ng Senado para magdesisyon but I think nag-e-evolve 'yung proseso natin," Tamase said.

(Although this is not the usual course of an impeachment proceeding, it is still good to have a debate or oral arguments, not necessarily because the Senate needs them to make a decision, but because I think our process is evolving.)
"Na una, makita talaga natin 'yung sentiments ng Senado ukol dito at pinatitibay 'yung principle na 'yun dapat nagkokontrol dito sa proseso na ito at hindi ang Korte Suprema," he added.
(First, it allows us to see the sentiments of the Senate on the matter and reinforces the principle that they're controlling the process and not the Supreme Court.)
'The earlier the better'
Meanwhile, for UP College of Law Assistant Professor Michael Tiu Jr., it is better to tackle the voting threshold as early as possible since it may affect the impeachment trial.
"I think, dahil marami nang lumipas sa trial na ito, marami nang naganap, I think, the earlier the better," Tiu said in a separate Super Radyo dzBB interview on Wednesday.
(I think, since a lot of time has already passed in this trial and a lot has happened, I think, the earlier the better.)

"They should have been asked earlier itong question on the voting threshold. But since it's happening now, under the best circumstances, ito na 'yung pagkakataon bago pa sila magpatuloy at masagot na ito bago pa sila dumating sa pagkakaton na nangyari na 'yung buong trial tapos hindi pa pala nasasagot 'yung tanong na ito," he added.

(They should have been asked about the voting threshold earlier. But since it is happening now, under the circumstances, this is the best opportunity to resolve the issue before they proceed further and reach a point where the entire trial has already concluded, only to find out that this question has not yet been answered.)

On Tuesday, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said oral arguments between the defense and prosecution will be held on September 23 to discuss the 16-vote threshold required to convict the Vice President.
This came after Senator-Jude Erwin Tulfo sought clarification on the voting threshold, given that four senator judges are not attending the trial.

Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder charges, Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, and Senator Loren Legarda has been on medical leave since August 3, and is currently abroad. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: Google warns of lower quality as it revamps Europe search results to avoid EU fines
articles.summary: Google says the changes mark the largest reduction in quality of service at the world's most popular internet search engine in its 29-year search history

blocks.text: BRUSSELS, Belgium – Alphabet’s Google on Tuesday, September 8 (September 9, Philippine time), rolled out changes to its online search results in Europe to satisfy EU antitrust regulators that it said will degrade users’ experience and ratchet up costs for European businesses.
Google told Reuters the changes mark the largest reduction in quality of service at the world’s most popular internet search engine in its 29-year search history.
The company said the EU pitched the changes as levelling the playing field for companies to be displayed on Google.

However, it said in its view the changes favour price comparison sites, also known as vertical search services (VSS), linked to sectors including hotels, airlines and restaurants, such as Expedia or Booking.com.
They get more prominence in search results over companies in those sectors that are listed with just a link to their websites, telephone numbers and addresses.

The US tech giant was hit with a €460-million ($534 million) fine in July for favoring its own services in shopping, hotels, transport, and sports results in search results, in breach of the EU’s Digital Markets Act seeking to rein in the power of Big Tech.
The European Commission gave it 60 days to comply with the DMA or risk periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of its total worldwide turnover.

The revamped search results will highlight one specialised search engine at the top of the page, followed by two others with fewer details. A carousel of hotels, airlines and restaurants, for example, will sit below them with key features such as real-time prices stripped out.
The rankings will be determined by Google’s algorithm.
“To comply with DMA requirements, we’re making significant changes to Search in Europe,” Nick Fox, Google’s senior vice-president, knowledge & information, said in a statement to Reuters.

“These changes degrade the user experience for Europeans — boosting online intermediaries at the expense of local businesses, and removing helpful features people rely on every day. Users outside the EU will not be impacted by these changes,” he said.
Google said past changes to comply with the DMA led to a 30% drop in free, direct booking traffic to European businesses, and the latest changes are expected to hit them.
The company said it has tested the changes with millions of users in Europe, which show a high level of dissatisfaction as they have to retype queries to find what they want.
EU regulators handed out a separate €430-million fine in July for restrictions preventing app developers from steering users free of charge to cheaper offers on rival app stores or websites.
On how Google Play plans to comply with the DMA with regard to that, the company said it has already updated its external offers program.
It announced tweaks in August last year to make it easier for app developers to direct customers to other channels and choose a fee model.
Google has racked up total EU antitrust penalties of €10.38 billion in its near two decade-long fight with EU antitrust regulators.
The EU fines drew fire from US President Donald Trump, who threatened to launch a probe into the bloc’s “robbing” of American companies. – Rappler.com
