articles.title: Mans Carpio eyes filing Ombudsman complaint over bank records disclosure --camp
articles.summary: The camp of lawyer Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, said Wednesday it is eyeing to refile with the Ombudsman the complaint he earlier filed against lawmakers and other…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 1:14pm

The camp of lawyer Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, said Wednesday it is eyeing to refile with the Ombudsman the complaint he earlier filed against lawmakers and other government officials over the disclosure of their bank records.
This was after the Quezon City Prosecutor's Office dismissed the complaint, saying the acts of the respondents were done in relation to their office, and such acts “are not inherently immoral.”

In a statement, Atty. Peter Paul Danao, counsel for Carpio, said the disclosure and handling of confidential and sensitive financial information deserve to be fully examined on the merits by the proper authority.
“We acknowledge the September 7, 2026 Resolution of the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office. We are still awaiting and will carefully review the official copy of the Resolution,” he said.

“Once received, our client reserves the right to exhaust all available legal remedies to challenge the Resolution, consistent with his right to seek appropriate relief under the law and existing rules. At the very least, our client retains the option to refile the complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman, which the Resolution itself identifies as the proper forum based on its jurisdictional finding,” he added.
Danao said the complaint was dismissed based on technicality, not merits.

“It is important to emphasize that the complaint was recommended for dismissal without prejudice and on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. The Resolution therefore does not constitute a final determination on the merits of the allegations raised in the complaint,” he said.
“The finding that the acts complained of were allegedly committed in relation to public office also leaves open the appropriate legal remedy and forum for pursuing the matter,” he added.
One of the impeachable offenses that the prosecution alleged against the Vice President is accumulation of unexplained wealth.
The prosecution intends to present the bank accounts of the Vice President and Carpio as evidence for Article 2. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Who is Atty. Paolo Panelo?
articles.summary: Attorney Paolo Panelo on Wednesday was appointed as the new spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte, replacing Ruth Castelo.

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 1:11pm
Attorney Paolo Panelo on Wednesday was appointed as the new spokesperson of Vice President Sara Duterte, replacing Ruth Castelo.
But this is not the first time that Panelo will be working with Duterte as he serves as legal counsel for the Vice President in connection with the multiple perjury complaints filed against her.
Panelo is the son of Salvador Panelo, who served as presidential legal counsel and spokesperson of former President Rodrigo Duterte.
The younger Panelo founded his own law firm, the Panelo Law Office, in 2018.
But he started his legal career with the Migallos and Luna Law Offices in 2011 after passing the Bar exam.
In 2016, Panelo also worked as consultant and acting chief of staff to his father under the Office of the President.
Panelo graduated with a degree in Development Studies in the Ateneo de Manila University in 2005.
He began his law studies also in the Ateneo Law School before completing it in Arellano University School of Law in 2010.

The OVP said that as the newly appointed spokesperson of the vice president Panelo “will serve as the official point of communication, representing the views and positions of the Vice President and engaging with the media and public on relevant matters.”
The OVP also said that Panelo is expected to make “important information more accessible, clear, and easier for the public to understand.” — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: US accuses Chinese AI firms of ‘malicious’ copying of AI technology
articles.summary: The Chinese companies copied US AI labs’ intellectual property through a technique known as distillation, US law enforcement and intelligence officials say

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, USA – The US government on Tuesday, September 8, accused Chinese artificial intelligence companies of maliciously copying technology from American AI firms, potentially complicating relations ahead of a planned meeting between leaders of the world’s two biggest economies later this month.

The Chinese companies copied US AI labs’ intellectual property through a technique known as distillation, according to a statement from US law enforcement and intelligence officials. Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using output from larger, more expensive ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a new AI tool.

US officials accused six Chinese companies, including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, and Alibaba, of tapping variants of American-made AI models to train their AI products more quickly. The companies did so “likely with Chinese government awareness,” according to the statement from US officials, who added that the Chinese companies targeted AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet’s Google, and SpaceX.
“China-based AI companies are engaging in aggressive, malicious and targeted distillation activities at an industrial scale,” the officials said.

US officials made the allegations as the administration of President Donald Trump prepares for Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US in late September. The US and China are also gearing up to discuss AI safety risks during a dialogue planned for mid-September, Reuters previously reported.
The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the distillation allegations.
The US made a similar accusation in April ahead of Trump’s visit to Beijing.

The Tuesday statement alleged that the distillation not only reduces research and development costs for Chinese AI firms, but also enhances China’s “military and cyberattack capabilities that could be used against the US and our allies.”
Reuters reported on July 31 that Chinese military researchers have used outputs from leading US AI models to train domestic Chinese AI systems and advance China’s defense capabilities. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Philippines trails Southeast Asian peers in good governance index
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines ranked 59th out of 133 governments in the 2026 Chandler Good Government Index, placing sixth among eight Southeast Asian countries covered by the global…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines ranked 59th out of 133 governments in the 2026 Chandler Good Government Index, placing sixth among eight Southeast Asian countries covered by the global assessment.
The country ranked ahead of only Cambodia and Laos in the region. Malaysia placed 40th, Indonesia 48th, Vietnam 49th and Thailand 58th, while Singapore topped the global rankings.

The index evaluates governments using 35 equally weighted indicators across seven pillars: Leadership and Foresight, Robust Laws and Policies, Strong Institutions, Financial Stewardship, Attractive Marketplace, Global Influence and Reputation, and Helping People Rise.

“The country generally trails its stronger regional peers across the index’s seven dimensions of good governance, although its performance is uneven,” said Dr. Rogelio Alicor Panao, an associate professor at the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman and an Inquirer data scientist.
Financial management a relative strength
The Philippines’ strongest showing was in Financial Stewardship, where it ranked 32nd globally.
“Surprisingly, the strongest area appears to be in Financial Stewardship, which measures how effectively public finances are managed,” Panao said.

blocks.caption: inqmetrics

blocks.text: The country also ranked relatively well in Strong Institutions, placing 53rd, followed by Leadership and Foresight at 57th and Robust Laws and Policies at 59th.
Panao, however, noted that the stronger showing in financial stewardship did not extend to investment conditions.
“This notwithstanding, the Philippines ranks 67th in Attractive Marketplace, which assesses the conditions for investment and economic activity,” he said.

The country ranked 65th in Helping People Rise, which measures the government’s contribution to improving people’s social and economic opportunities, and 75th in Global Influence and Reputation, which looks at international standing and influence.
Panao noted that the Philippines’ score in Helping People Rise improved slightly from last year, although it remained ranked 65th in the area.
Vietnam posts biggest regional improvement
The Philippines also trailed Vietnam, which recorded the largest overall improvement in the Asia-Pacific region since the index began.
“Vietnam recorded the largest overall improvement in Asia Pacific since the index began, moving from 58th to 49th globally and improving in six of the seven pillars,” Panao said.
Vietnam ranked 34th in Attractive Marketplace, well ahead of the Philippines at 67th. Indonesia also ranked higher than the Philippines in the area, at 47th.
In Global Influence and Reputation, Indonesia ranked 65th, compared with the Philippines’ 75th.

The Chandler Governance Group, which produces the index, found broad-based improvement in government performance in the 2026 edition, with the global average reaching its highest level since 2022. Singapore remained No. 1 for the fourth consecutive year. /dm

articles.title: Europeans want a united Europe but question whether it can get there, study finds
articles.summary:
A continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline, report suggests

Europeans overwhelmingly want a strong, united and independent Europe…

blocks.text: Europeans overwhelmingly want a strong, united and independent Europe but question whether it can get there, according to a study that suggests a continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline.

The report, based on 5,800 interviews in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and the UK and analysis of the way Europe is discussed in the politics and media of 15 countries, paints a picture of an ambitious but disillusioned public.

It found that 68% of respondents spoke about Europe in terms of a “general deterioration or loss of normality”, compared with just 12% who said they viewed the present moment as a time of “European awakening and renewal”.

Many recognised the major challenges facing Europe, including war (43%), economic pressures (33%) and the need for greater international autonomy (29%). But 74% said Europe was not dealing well with them, and 56% believed its future was “in danger”.

The problem is not lack of ambition: an overwhelming 73% of respondents harbour a strong European vision of unity and political integration (35%), peace and security (28%) or prosperity (19%), while only 13% hope for “less Europe” or EU dissolution.

For many, said the study’s author, Pawel Zerka, a senior fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) thinktank, the problem was “not that they’ve stopped wanting a stronger Europe, but that they no longer believe it’s achievable”.

The result, Zerka added, was an “imagination gap. People can picture the kind of Europe they want, but struggle to imagine a credible path from where it is today to where they want it to be. These are matters of policy, not just communication.”

blocks.caption: Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission. Photograph: Mads Claus Rasmussen/Reuters

blocks.text: A week before the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, is due to deliver her annual “state of the union” address in Brussels, Zerka said the evidence suggested the bloc needed “fewer grand promises” and more “proof of trajectory”.

The study cites dozens of conversations with Europeans. “I’m regularly relieved I live in Europe. It’s not perfect and some things are going in the wrong direction, but no region in the world is safer, freer and more democratic,” one German said.

However, while he identified the climate crisis and far-right parties as the continent’s greatest challenges, he said they were not being tackled effectively. “Elections focus too much on the here and now, and not enough on the future,” he said.

The respondent said he would like Europe in 20 years’ time to be “free, democratic, sustainable, less indebted, politically further to the left [and] peaceful”. Asked whether he thought that was likely to happen, he said: “No.”

The study classed Europe’s voters in four categories. The Positives (19%) are staunch pro-Europeans who view current crises as a catalyst for a stronger, more integrated union. The Negatives (39%) believe Europe’s best days are behind it.

Almost half of people in France, Germany and Italy – and almost all who voted for radical-right parties such as Germany’s AfD, France’s RN, the Dutch PVV and Reform UK – were Negatives, with 83% speaking of Europe in terms of loss and decline.
after newsletter promotion

The Disconnected (12%) are generally apathetic voters for whom EU integration is distant background noise, and the Uncertain (31%) share pro-European values but doubt the continent’s ability to act decisively, keep citizens safe or uphold its values.

Almost a third (32%) of respondents across all countries surveyed mentioned “Europe’s slowness” in their responses. As one young Polish citizen, born in the 2000s, put it bluntly: “The EU fundamentally discusses a lot, but does nothing.”

The bloc’s failure to stand its ground when confronted by powerful actors was also a recurring theme, mentioned by almost a third (30%) of all respondents, with the EU’s recent tariff concessions to Donald Trump a particularly humiliating symbol.

Zerka said the Uncertain group was key to the future trajectory of Europe. “Leaders tend to preach to the Positives or bow down to the Negatives,” he said, but it “is among the ‘uncertain’ where belief in Europe’s future remains up for grabs.”

Unlike hardened Eurosceptics, Uncertain voters retain a strong emotional attachment to the European project, the report argues, but are alienated by institutional inertia, bureaucratic slowness and perceived geopolitical weakness.

Winning back those doubters would require politicians to demonstrate that collective European action can solve tangible domestic crises, from energy security and defence to climate change and the cost of living crisis, Zerka said.

articles.title: Burnham urged to tackle inequality with policies including wealth tax
articles.summary:
Key thinkers suggest other radical measures in Compass report such as free personal social care and abolishing Lords

Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham should tackle inequality in the UK by introducing a wealth tax, universal free personal social care and bringing gas and electricity networks under public ownership, according to a report from more than a dozen influential thinkers.

In the lead-up to the first budget of the chancellor, John Healey, this autumn, the Compass thinktank has collated 70 policy options from 15 leftwing thinkers that they argue would deliver on the prime minister’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.

Introducing the report, Ending Business as Usual, Michael Jacobs, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, and Neal Lawson, director of Compass and a close friend of Burnham, praise what they call the prime minister’s “invaluable aura of authenticity”.

However, they warn that while he has ambitious plans “there is no guarantee that he will be given any longer to deliver results than his immediate predecessor”. The authors argue that it is “simply not the case that a British government can no longer govern from the left of centre”.

Among the policy proposals, which the organisation states is “a menu of policy options, not a manifesto”, are a £50,000 cap on political donations, the abolition of the House of Lords and an immediate cost of living package.

The plans also include a raft of far-reaching tax policies, including the introduction of a wealth tax on net assets of more than £10m, which would raise about £24bn a year, according to Caitlin Boswell from Tax Justice UK.

Other mooted policy ideas include equalising capital gains tax with income tax, which would raise a further £11.3bn a year – enough “to fund the building of 90,000 new social homes”. The Institute for Fiscal Studies has argued such a move would risk lowering total tax revenue and investment, and lead wealthy individuals to move their money or leave the country.

The essay also calls for what it describes as the “regressive, outdated and unfair” council tax as well as stamp duty to be replaced with a proportional property tax, noting such a move would result in 23% of households – concentrated in London and the south-east – paying more.

“If the new Labour government is serious about rebuilding public confidence and delivering material improvements to people’s lives, it must be prepared to address one of the structural causes of inequality: a tax system that favours wealth over work,” writes Boswell.

Suggested social policy changes in England include introducing free personal social care, paid for by a surcharge on income tax rates for people aged over 40, and a contribution from housing wealth. Sebastian Rees, from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) argues that personal care needs, such as washing, dressing and eating should be covered by the state with accommodation or ordinary living costs, remaining the responsibility of the individual and their family, a model currently in place in Scotland.

Stating that a 1% surcharge on income tax for the over-40s would raise between £8bn and £9bn, it also argues that care costs could be secured against a property and recovered after sale or death. This would “would allow housing wealth to contribute to the cost of reform without requiring people to sell their home when they first need care,” says Rees. Elsewhere, the report calls for universal free childcare, which it argues would “boost the economy, support children’s development, help families and promote gender equality”.

Chris Hayes, from Common Wealth, calls for government-owned companies to be put in charge of running energy networks, as well as the setting up of regional energy boards, while the director of politics at Green Alliance, Holly Brazier Tope, argues for a climate resilience standard for critical infrastructure.

Michael Jacobs, professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, said Burnham and his chancellor must resist pressure to conform to the “moderation and orthodoxy” that he argues ended the tenures of Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves.

“There are a wealth of alternatives,” he says. “As Burnham knows, the public is disillusioned with politics and angry with their politicians. He does not have long to prove to voters that, when he says he wants to end business as usual, he means it.”

articles.title: Over 9.6M people affected by Habagat, 4 cyclones -- NDRRMC
articles.summary: More than 9.6 million people have been affected by the combined effects of the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng and Pilandok, according to the National Disaster…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 12:58pm

More than 9.6 million people have been affected by the combined effects of the enhanced southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay, Neneng and Pilandok, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC).

In its Situational Report No. 37 issued at 8 a.m. Wednesday, the NDRRMC said a total of 9,614,020 people, or 2,781,245 families, were affected in 10 regions, 39 provinces, 468 cities and municipalities, and 6,551 barangays.
Of the affected population, 162,057 people were displaced and were staying in 820 evacuation centers.
The report also said 7,478 people were pre-emptively evacuated, including 2,472 individuals from Regions 1, 3, CALABARZON and MIMAROPA.
The disasters have left 44 people dead, 18 injured and five missing, the council said.
Of the reported deaths, 12 have been confirmed while 32 remain for validation. Twelve injuries have been confirmed, while six are still being validated.
All five missing persons have been confirmed as missing, the NDRRMC said.
The combined effects of the weather disturbances also resulted in 1,830 flooded areas across Regions 1, 3, CALABARZON, MIMAROPA, 6 and 9, as well as the National Capital Region.
The NDRRMC also recorded 79 other related incidents, including rain-induced landslides, collapsed structures, and tornadoes or destructive and strong winds.
A total of 4,361 houses were damaged, including 3,758 partially damaged and 603 totally damaged houses.
Meanwhile, infrastructure damage was estimated at P8.30 billion, involving 1,383 facilities, including flood-control structures, government facilities, bridges, schools, roads and health facilities.
The agricultural sector also sustained an estimated P4.12 billion in damage, affecting 92,953 farmers and fisherfolk and 80,274.44 hectares of crops, according to the report.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: BARMM election faces low-turnout risk amid violence, voter uncertainty
articles.summary: Some of the forces the peace process was meant to overcome remain powerful enough to influence whether people turn out to vote in the BARMM on September 14

items: The upcoming parliamentary election in the BARMM faces challenges due to fears of violence and distrust in the electoral process, potentially leading to low voter turnout.
Despite a gun ban and military presence, violence has persisted in the region, with an increase in gun-related incidents and deaths, highlighting ongoing clan rivalries and political polarization.

Voter uncertainty about the new parliamentary system and lack of proper voter education may further hinder participation, reflecting deeper issues of skepticism toward the BARMM government and its political entities.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – The first parliamentary election in the seven-year-old Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) is approaching with this possibility: Voters may be too frightened, distrustful, or uncertain about the new political system to turn out in the numbers election officials are counting on.

Climate Conflict Action Asia (CCAA), a group that monitors conflict in the predominantly Muslim region, warned that violence and low public confidence in the electoral process could depress turnout and undermine the credibility of the September 14 election.
The warning carries particular weight because the Commission on Elections (Comelec) is targeting a turnout of at least 70% to 75% among the BARMM’s 2.39 million voters.

Next week’s parliamentary election is meant as a start of a new chapter for the region that emerged from decades of armed conflict through a 2014 peace agreement between the government and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), which resulted in BARMM’s creation in 2019.

But CCAA’s monitoring in the weeks before the vote suggests that some of the forces the peace process was meant to overcome — guns, clan rivalries, political polarization, extremist violence and distrust of government — remain powerful enough to influence whether people go to the polls.
The numbers offer one of the clearest warnings.

CCAA’s Critical Events Monitoring System recorded 58 gun-related incidents from July 16 to August 31, after the election gun ban in the region took effect. That compared with 44 incidents from June 1 to July 15, before the ban.
Deaths from gun-related violence also increased, from 34 before the ban to 39 afterward.
CCAA recorded 14 more gun-related incidents, an increase of about 32%, and five more deaths, or about 15%, after the ban took effect.

The figures do not mean that the gun ban factored in any way to the increase. But they show that, during the period monitored by CCAA, restrictions on firearms had not produced the reduction in violence voters might expect from an election security measure.
Instead, violence continued in communities where politics, clan loyalties and access to firearms overlap.

CCAA is not the first to point out that the persistence of violence shows a problem that goes beyond election security. An earlier assessment by the Brussels-based International Crisis Group found that more than a decade after the peace agreement, clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal networks continued to thrive where state institutions remained weak.

blocks.caption: 12 years after peace deal, violence still stalks Bangsamoro

blocks.text: On Tuesday, September 8, the Lanao del Sur-based Moro Consensus Group (MCG) called on candidates, security forces, and voters in the region to help ensure a peaceful and credible first parliamentary election in the BARMM.

In a statement, MCG chairman Drieza Lininding called on the region’s political parties and candidates to avoid violence, vote-buying, harassment and intimidation, and to respect voters’ right to make their choices freely.

The civil society group also called on the military, police and other security agencies to remain neutral, protect polling centers and election workers, and enforce election laws without political bias.
MCG said Bangsamoro voters, including Muslim Filipinos, indigenous peoples, Christians, women, and young people, should be able to take part in the election without fear or coercion.
It urged BARMM leaders and politicians to respect the outcome and accept the choice of voters.
“Peace is our shared responsibility,” the group said, urging Bangsamoro voters to take part in the election “with courage, discernment, and peace.”

CCAA said tensions worsened after Bangsamoro interim Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua was ambushed on August 15, an attack it said deepened divisions within the MILF and intensified political polarization.
In Shariff Saydona Mustapha in Maguindanao del Sur, a recurring rido (clan feud) displaced about 30 families in late August.

In Basilan, arrest warrants were issued against the mayor and seven others over an ambush involving supporters of a former mayor during the 2025 midterm elections. The warrants were issued about a month before the parliamentary election, CCAA said, after the incumbent mayor aligned herself with a political camp opposed to the governor.
The government has imposed a gun ban and deployed large numbers of military personnel to secure the election.
But CCAA said armed groups, political parties and local power structures remained closely linked in parts of the region.
It also raised questions about the weapons and armed capability of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), the MILF’s political party.
CCAA said there had been no concrete steps toward decommissioning the weapons and armed forces linked to the MILF.

The government and the MILF signed guidelines on August 31 governing ceasefire-related functions during the election. Two days later, the military stopped an MILF convoy in Kolambugan, Lanao del Norte, because most of its members were armed.
Lanao del Norte, a province led by the Dimaporos – a Muslim Filipino family – did not join BARMM and is part of the predominantly Catholic region of Northern Mindanao.
As a result, the military called on the MILF to coordinate movements through mechanisms established under the Bangsamoro peace process.
Security is only part of the problem. CCAA’s monitoring also found uncertainty among voters about how to participate in the new parliamentary system.

In interviews with residents, CCAA said it found people who were still unsure how to vote and others who said they had received little voter education. Some said political parties had turned voter education into another form of campaigning, telling people whom to support rather than explaining how the new parliamentary system was supposed to work.

For generations, elections in Muslim-majority areas of Mindanao had been more personal and familiar. Voters knew local candidates, their families and often the clans and political alliances behind them. Now, they are being asked to choose representatives to a regional legislature through regional political parties and parliamentary districts – a system that remains unfamiliar to many.

That lack of understanding carries another risk. CCAA said local electoral boards had come under pressure in previous elections from political groups seeking to influence or intimidate voters. A voter unfamiliar with the system and looking to an electoral official for guidance could therefore be especially vulnerable.
The question is what that uncertainty will mean on election day.
CCAA said weak participation could signal more than confusion over a new ballot, and it could show a deeper lack of faith in the BARMM government and the political groups competing to control it.
That skepticism has a tangible backdrop of poor health and education services and corruption allegations involving the BARMM education ministry.
Poverty has declined but economic hardship remains widespread, CCAA said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘It’s hell’: father of slain Australian surfers tells Mexico homicide trial about identifying sons’ bodies
articles.summary:
Three men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend, US citizen Jack Carter Rhoad, in Ensenada

The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico…

blocks.text: The father of two Australian surfers killed in Mexico two years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.

Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.
Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.
“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”
“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.
Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.
Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.
“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”
Authorities say the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.
A protected witness testified Monday that they accompanied one of the defendants to the crime scene and fled after hearing gunshots, and were later threatened into silence.
The surfers’ disappearances and deaths sparked widespread outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, prompting a major social media search for their bodies.
“We hold no resentment toward the people who did this, but we cannot understand how they could have taken the lives of two beautiful people,” Martin Robinson told the court.
The trial is expected to run until the end of September.
Rhoad’s widow, Natalie, is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.

articles.title: Wage board clears P60 NCR wage hike while P85 order remains frozen
articles.summary: Metro Manila's wage board approved a new P60 daily minimum wage increase while the earlier P85 hike remains tied up in court.

blocks.text: September 9, 2026 | 12:33pm
Workers are seen at the construction site of the Metro Manila Subway Project (MMSP) during an inspection in Quezon City, Metro Manila on August 28, 2025.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa
MANILA, Philippines — Metro Manila's wage board approved a new P60 daily minimum wage increase in an attempt to deliver the first tranche of a P85 hike tied up in court since July.

The new Wage Order NCR-28 could raise the non-agricultural minimum wage from P695 to P755 later this month if affirmed by the National Wages and Productivity Commission. But lawmakers warned that issuing a second wage order could complicate the continuing legal fight over Wage Order NCR-27, which also provides another P25 increase in January.

During a House hearing on the Department of Labor and Employment's proposed 2027 budget Tuesday, September 8, DOLE-National Capital Region Director Roy Buenafe said the regional wage board approved Wage Order No. NCR-28 on Monday night.
The order has been forwarded to the NWPC for review.
Buenafe said the P60 increase would be implemented in a single tranche and could take effect around September 26 or 27 if affirmed by the commission and published as required.
The increase would bring the daily minimum wage for non-agricultural workers from P695 to P755.
For agricultural workers, as well as employees of small retail and service establishments and small manufacturing firms covered by the lower NCR minimum, the rate would rise from P658 to P718.
The wage board approved the order in a 4-3 vote, with two labor representatives and one employer representative dissenting.
P85 wage order remains in court
Wage Order NCR-27 granted an P85 increase in two tranches: P60 beginning July 25 and another P25 on Jan. 20, 2027.
Its implementation was blocked before the first tranche could take effect following court challenges filed by employers.

"The non-implementation of Wage Order No. NCR-27 resulted from the successive issuance of judicial injunctive reliefs, specifically a Status Quo Ante Order (SQAO) issued July 24, 2026, a Temporary Restraining Order, and a Writ of Preliminary Injunction," Wage Order No. NCR-28 stated.
DOLE and the wage authorities continue to challenge the injunction and maintain that wage order remains valid.
The Supreme Court is also considering a separate petition by labor groups seeking to nullify the lower court orders that blocked its implementation.
Lawmakers question new order

Rep. Sarah Elago (Gabriela party-list), Elijah San Fernando (Kamanggagawa party-list) and Deputy Speaker Raymond Mendoza (Trade Union Congress Party-list) questioned why another wage order was issued while the P85 increase remains the subject of pending litigation.
They warned that the new order could be seen as accepting the court injunction and settling for P60 instead of pursuing the full P85 increase under the original order.
"Mali ang naging injunction sa Wage Order 27 at kapag tinanggap ito ng DOLE, at ngayon meron nang Wage Order 28, para na rin silang pumayag na legal ito," Elago said.
("The injunction against Wage Order No. 27 was wrong, and if DOLE accepts it and now there is Wage Order No. 28, it would be as if they agreed that the injunction was legal.")
Labor groups have argued that the lower courts had no authority to restrain the wage order, citing Article 126 of the Labor Code.
The provision prohibits courts, tribunals and other entities from issuing injunctions or temporary restraining orders against proceedings before the NWPC or regional wage boards.
Whether that prohibition invalidates the court orders blocking Wage Order NCR-27 is among the issues raised in the pending legal challenges.

articles.title: ‘No executive suite for Romualdez if transferred to PNP hospital’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will not be confined in an executive suite if he is transferred to the Philippine National Police General Hospital…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former House Speaker and incumbent Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez will not be confined in an executive suite if he is transferred to the Philippine National Police General Hospital (PNPGH) in Camp Crame.
“May room nang naka-ready sa kanya,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co explained in a press briefing in Camp Crame.
(There is a room waiting for him already.)
“Wala ditong executive suite. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms,” he stressed.
(There is no executive suite here. Rooms are rooms. Ordinary rooms.)
Romualdez was arrested on plunder charges on Monday night while confined at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for various purported ailments.

On Tuesday, however, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the PNP will ask the Sandiganbayan to transfer Romualdez to the PNPGH to show that the former speaker is not receiving special treatment.
“Our doctors have been coordinating with the doctors of Cardinal Santos for practicing rights so we can assess him independently,” Co said.
“And then, they will confer for us to be able to assess if the former Speaker will be physically fit to face the Sandiganbayan,” he added.
Romualdez has since requested the Sandiganbayan to allow his continued hospital confinement.
But earlier on Wednesday, the Office of the Ombudsman opposed the motion while asking that another team of government doctors assess whether he needed to be confined.
“We welcome them to erase any doubts or suspicions of special treatment,” Co said.
“The more, the merrier. We very much welcome additional doctors to assess the situation or the health status of our former speaker,” he added.
Romualdez is charged in connection with over P7 billion in alleged kickbacks in various government projects from 2022 to 2025. /gsg

articles.title: Iloilo City mayor secures power pledges to strengthen local grid
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY — In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build…

blocks.text: ILOILO CITY — In response to recurring power interruptions across Panay Island, Iloilo City Mayor Raisa Treñas has secured critical commitments from energy providers to boost power capacity and build grid redundancy for the fast-growing city.

In a statement released on Wednesday from South Korea, where she is currently on official travel, Treñas said the city government is proactively pursuing long-term solutions to safeguard local power stability despite regional supply challenges.
“We know how frustrating these continuing interruptions and rotational brownouts are for our people,” Treñas noted.

She added: “Even while the manual load shedding implemented by the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) is not directly within the control of the city government, we will not just wait around.”
To address Panay Island’s vulnerability as it sits at the tail end of the national power grid, the mayor outlined three major power generation projects to strengthen the island’s electricity supply.

The mayor said Panay Energy Development Corporation (PEDC) has committed to expanding its generation capacity, with the additional power targeted to become fully operational by 2028. Meanwhile, cleaner energy provider PH Natural Gas is preparing to establish operations in Iloilo City, which is expected to help diversify the local energy mix.

In nearby Guimaras, MORE Power is also set to operate a 40-megawatt (MW) floating power barge by the first quarter of 2027. The facility is expected to provide immediate backup power and help improve the reliability of electricity supply in Panay.
Treñas noted that building redundancy—having multiple, independent sources of electricity—is essential to sustaining Iloilo’s rapid economic expansion and insulating it from wider grid failures.

“These are the investments we must continuously pursue because we cannot depend on just one source of power,” Treñas stressed. “Especially here in Panay, being at the tail end of the grid, having more generation, more sources, and more redundancy is vital.”

To ensure these projects proceed without unnecessary delays, the mayor called on the national government and regulatory bodies to fast-track the required permits and approval processes so construction can begin immediately.

She reaffirmed that the city administration will continue engaging with power utilities, private investors, and regional stakeholders to build a more resilient energy infrastructure for Iloilo City./coa

articles.title: US strikes Iranian oil tankers as Tehran targets American base in Jordan
articles.summary: Oil prices edged closer to $100 a barrel after an escalation in the tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran.

blocks.text: US forces struck five Iranian tankers on Tuesday, sinking one, in response to Tehran twice targeting an American warship, US Central Command (Centcom) said.

Four Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) were targeted, as well as another near Kharg Island, a major oil terminal off Iran's coast, Centcom added.
Tehran responded by launching missiles at a US base in Jordan - most of which were shot down - and said it attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tit-for-tat strikes between the two countries have escalated in the past week, more than six months after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on 28 February.
Oil prices rose in Asia trading. Benchmark Brent crude was up by 1.5% at $99.35 (£73.35) a barrel, while US-traded oil was 1.3% higher at $94.23.
Jordan said it had shot down 18 of the 20 Iranian missiles, while two of them fell in unpopulated areas, an official spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said.

After warning of further retaliatory strikes, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they had attacked two US vessels, eight oil tankers and 10 "non-compliant vessels" trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.

The latest round of escalation comes after Iran targeted a US warship with ballistic missiles, which Centcom said were "successfully evaded". It added that no American troops were harmed during the attacks.
In response, the US said that the five Iranian oil tankers it targeted were "part of a multi-billion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies".
One of the ships it had struck, the M/T Riesco, sunk in the Gulf of Oman, Centcom later said, posting a video on X of the damaged vessel.
Kharg Island - where one Iranian tanker was attacked in the latest round of US strikes - hosts Iran's main terminal for exporting oil.
Some 90% of the country's crude oil passes through the island in the Gulf, transported through pipes from the mainland.
Pressure on oil prices has been exacerbated by wider regional instability.
Also on Tuesday, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement attacked energy facilities and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 people, according to Saudi authorities.
The drone and missile attack caused fires at oil facilities and installations that led to a temporary halt in operations, Saudi Arabia's military and energy ministry said.
When asked by reporters about the latest tit-for-tat strikes between the US and Iran, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the situation was "pretty straightforward".

"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And, for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters during a trip in Colombia.
The US strikes on Tuesday came hours after Iran's navy claimed it had seized an uncrewed US submarine in the Strait of Hormuz.

US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, said that the "underwater drone operated by US forces malfunctioned more than a day ago" and was used to survey regional waters "in support of ongoing operations".
The defective drone was "an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment", he said, adding that US operations in regional waters were ongoing.
With additional reporting from Peter Hoskins.

articles.title: Trump gave $45,000 to Natalie Harp and other White House aides as holiday gifts
articles.summary:
The president’s substantial holiday gifts to four White House aides were made public via financial disclosures released by the administration

Donald Trump gave sizable holiday gifts to four…

blocks.text: Donald Trump gave sizable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration, including $45,000 to executive assistant Natalie Harp.

Communications adviser Margo Martin and deputy director of Oval Office operations Chamberlain Harris also received $45,000, while director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta received a $20,000 gift.

The gifts were noted in the staffers’ annual financial disclosure forms that were published by the administration last week. Harp, Martin and Harris make $150,000 annually and Nauta is paid $175,000 a year, according to the White House’s salary disclosure report to Congress.

A White House official told the Associated Press that Trump “has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector.”

The official did not say if any other staffers were given similar gifts from the president, but added that the cash gifts were not related to the “individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.”
The disclosures of the gifts were first reported earlier on Tuesday by The Washington Post.

Harp is a constant presence by Trump’s side and is known for carrying a portable printer with her so she can print out favourable media coverage and social media posts for the president, who prefers reading important information on paper rather than on a screen.

Martin has been working for Trump since his term in the White House. She started as a White House press assistant and followed the president to Palm Beach, Florida, to help run his media operations after he lost the 2020 election to Joe Biden. She returned to the White House with Trump after his 2024 victory.
Earlier this year, Trump appointed Harris to serve on the US Commission of Fine Arts, which has oversight over the president’s White House ballroom project.

Nauta, who previously served as a valet to Trump, and Mar-a-Lago property manager Carlos De Oliveira were charged in 2023 with conspiring with Trump to obstruct an FBI investigation into classified documents that the Republican took with him when he left the White House after his first term.
The charges were dismissed in 2024.

articles.title: [Pinoy Criminology] Like Martin Romualdez, can ordinary accused avail themselves of hospital arrest?
articles.summary: I cannot help but comment on the arrest of former House speaker Martin Romualdez. He was arrested for plunder involving

blocks.text: I cannot help but comment on the arrest of former House speaker Martin Romualdez. He was arrested for plunder involving allegations of billions of pesos in kickbacks. When the warrant was served, however, he was already confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center after allegedly experiencing a cardiovascular event, and his lawyers subsequently asked the Sandiganbayan to allow his continued hospital confinement.

There is nothing inherently wrong with that. If Romualdez truly has a medical condition, then he deserves to be medically attended to. He is not yet convicted guilty, and preventive detention should not be punishment, much less medical deprivation that could lead to death.

The problem is not that Romualdez is receiving medical attention. The problem is whether the same consideration is available to everyone else. Because, right now, how many old, sickly, and terminally ill accused are languishing in our jails, undergoing trial for offenses far less serious than plunder? (READ: [Pinoy Criminology] Protecting the old and sickly from prolonged pre-trial detention)Some have been there not for one month but for years, with no end in sight. Some suffer from diabetes, hypertension, cancer, tuberculosis, heart disease, and other debilitating illnesses. They are also presumed innocent, except that poverty seems to make that presumption considerably less comfortable.

Where is their hospital detention? Where is their humanitarian consideration? Where is the urgent medical attention when the person asking for it has no money, no powerful lawyers, and no famous surname?

We have been pushing for medical and humanitarian release for individuals with serious medical conditions. They can be supervised, required to report regularly, prohibited from traveling, and monitored by authorities. They can also be returned to detention when they violate the conditions of their release.

Medical considerations, however, have appeared selectively available to the rich and powerful. We saw humanitarian considerations invoked in the case of Juan Ponce Enrile, when the Supreme Court considered his advanced age, health, and flight risk in granting bail (Enrile v. Sandiganbayan, G.R. No. 213847, August 18, 2015). We have likewise seen former presidents Joseph Estrada and Gloria Macapagal Arroyo receive special detention or medical arrangements.

The answer is not to deny these accommodations to powerful people simply because poor people suffer in jail. The answer is to make humanitarian consideration available to poor people under the same objective standards. Humanity should not become a privilege that depends upon one’s bank account, political position, or surname.

That is where risk assessment becomes important. A rational criminal justice system should not merely ask what crime an accused allegedly committed. It should also ask whether the person poses a flight risk, threatens witnesses, presents a danger to the community, or can be safely supervised outside jail.

Congress should therefore pass a law expanding alternatives to pretrial detention, including medical recognizance and humanitarian release based on medical need and criminogenic risk assessment. The Supreme Court should likewise promulgate clear rules governing medical release for pretrial detainees. Who can avail, what are the criteria, what are the procedures, how can they be applied equally, and how can abuse be avoided?

The placement of Romualdez under hospital confinement may be entirely appropriate. He may truly have a heart condition, and if he does, let him receive the treatment he needs while remaining accountable to the courts. But whatever criteria apply to Romualdez should also apply to thousands of poor Filipinos now languishing in overcrowded jails nationwide.

Not automatically, and certainly not indiscriminately, but rationally, transparently, and equally. If humanitarian justice is good enough for the powerful, it should be good enough for the poor. That is not special treatment; that is equal treatment. – Rappler.com
Raymund E. Narag, PhD, is an associate professor in criminology and criminal justice at the School of Justice and Public Safety, Southern Illinois University, Carbondale.
The author originally posted this to Facebook on September 8, 2026.

articles.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
articles.summary:
Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems

Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in…

blocks.text: Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.
Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.

More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.

On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.
Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.

“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.

The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.
Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.

“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”
The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.

The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.

The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.

The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.
While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.
“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.
The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.

It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.

Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

articles.title: DTI-Bukidnon cracks down on social media promos, flags 5 firms
articles.summary: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Five business establishments in the cities of Valencia and Malaybalay have been slapped with show-cause orders by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Bukidnon…

blocks.text: MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — Five business establishments in the cities of Valencia and Malaybalay have been slapped with show-cause orders by the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) Bukidnon provincial office for allegedly running unauthorized sales promotions on social media.

The DTI-Bukidnon, through its Consumer Protection Division (CPD), intensified its monitoring after noticing a spike in online promotional offers, including contests and discounts advertised digitally.
Junar Merla, DTI-Bukidnon CPD chief, said that digital campaigns must not bypass regulatory frameworks.

Operating a sales promotion without a valid DTI permit violates Article 116 of Republic Act No. 7394. Violators face potential administrative fines ranging from P500 to P300,000 under Article 164, alongside penalties upon conviction under Article 123(b).

While the show cause orders demand formal explanations from the establishments to ensure due process, DTI-Bukidnon emphasized that the enforcement actions aim to uphold fair marketplace transparency and protect consumers from unlawful practices.
It did not name the five business establishments ordered to explain.
The provincial office plans to sustain its monitoring efforts across online and physical platforms./coa

articles.title: Yellow rainfall warning up in Metro Manila, 5 areas in Luzon
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The state weather bureau placed Metro Manila and five other areas in Luzon under a yellow rainfall warning on Wednesday due to the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The state weather bureau placed Metro Manila and five other areas in Luzon under a yellow rainfall warning on Wednesday due to the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat.

In its Heavy Rainfall Warning No. 18 issued at 11 a.m., the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said the following areas were under the yellow warning level:

items: Metro Manila: Caloocan, Malabon, Navotas, Valenzuela, Quezon City, Makati, Mandaluyong, San Juan, Pasay, Marikina, and Manila
Zambales: Olongapo, Subic, Castillejos, San Marcelino, San Narciso, San Antonio, Iba, Botolan, Cabangan, Palauig, San Felipe, Masinloc, and Candelaria

blocks.text: Areas under yellow warning tend to experience rainfall between 7.5 mm and 15 mm within one hour and can continue in the next two hours.
The yellow warning level likewise indicates a need for the public to “be alert,” with flooding in flood-prone areas identified as its associated hazard, Pagasa said.
Several local government units have already suspended in-person afternoon classes this Wednesday due to the forecast rains.
Meanwhile, according to Pagasa, light to moderate rains with occasional heavy rains were expected within the next three hours over Laguna, portions of Rizal, Bulacan, Tarlac, Batangas, and Quezon.
The same rainfall conditions were affecting portions of Nueva Ecija, Zambales, Pampanga, Cavite and Metro Manila, which may persist within three hours and could affect nearby areas.
Pagasa will release its next rainfall warning at 2 p.m. /jpv

articles.title: Northern Mindanao cops seize P19-M contraband, net 126 drug pushers
articles.summary: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — The Police Regional Office-10 (PRO-10) seized around P19 million from alleged illegal activities and netted 126 suspected drug pushers in a span of about two weeks. Brig. Gen.…

blocks.text: CAGAYAN DE ORO CITY — The Police Regional Office-10 (PRO-10) seized around P19 million from alleged illegal activities and netted 126 suspected drug pushers in a span of about two weeks.

Brig. Gen. Nestor Babagay Jr, newly installed PRO-10 director, shared the achievement as he marked 12 days in office during his first press briefing on Tuesday at Camp 1Lt. Vicente Alagar in Barangay Lapasan here.
He sent a message to criminals that “they will not find any breathing room” in the region.
“Our provincial and city directors are very good. These first days have set the direction for my leadership of PRO-10,” Babagay told reporters in mixed Filipino and English.

He noted that consistent with the priority agenda of PNP Chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. and the directives of Interior and Local Government Secretary Juanito Victor “Jonvic” Remulla Jr., PRO-10 will remain focused, visible, intelligence-driven, responsive, and accountable.
“We will prioritize sustaining efforts to make Northern Mindanao peaceful,” Babagay said.

Under the Enhanced Managing Police Operations framework, PRO-10’s anti-narcotics campaign chalked the biggest haul, confiscating 1,141 grams of suspected shabu valued at an estimated P7.7 million and arresting 126 drug suspects across 104 operations.
Babagay said P6.7 million worth of suspected smuggled cigarettes and P4.4 million worth of equipment and minerals from alleged illegal mining activities were seized in just about two weeks.

The region-wide campaign also curbed loose weapons and underground betting. Under Oplan Kontra Boga, police carried out 73 operations, arresting eight individuals and seizing 71 firearms. In contrast, 10 anti-illegal gambling operations resulted in 18 arrests and the recovery of P5,911 in proceeds and gambling paraphernalia.

Manhunt operations accounted for 107 wanted individuals, including 32 classified as most wanted persons. On the counterinsurgency front, Babagay reported that five communist personalities surrendered, turning over three firearms to authorities.

Babagay also highlighted urban order under the “Safer Cities Initiative,” which logged 10,030 ordinance violators, with 4,853 individuals fined and 4,897 issued warnings. He said that PRO-10 will maintain maximum visibility patrols, checkpoints, Oplan Bakal, Oplan Sita, Oplan Bandillo, and other area-specific policing interventions.
According to him, only one of the 10 most wanted persons in the region has not been arrested./coa

articles.title: Ombudsman opposes Romualdez’s bid for continued hospital arrest
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday said it will oppose the motion of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez for extended hospital confinement after his arrest, adding that…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman on Wednesday said it will oppose the motion of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez for extended hospital confinement after his arrest, adding that it will request a team of government doctors to assess whether his declared illnesses could be managed outside the hospital.

This was the response of Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano after Romualdez on Monday filed a Manifestation of Hospital Confinement and Urgent Motion ad Cautelam for Continued Hospital Confinement for continuous lawful custody at the hospital “for so long as inpatient confinement remains medically necessary, certified by his attending physical, until he is medically cleared for transfer.”

“The prosecutors will strongly oppose the motion. In fact, the prosecutors will ask that not just one doctor but a team of government doctors assess whether or not the illnesses declared need confinement or can be managed outside of the hospital,” Clavano said in a statement.

Clavano also said that if Romualdez’s illnesses could be managed outside the hospital, the prosecutors would move for his transfer to a regular detention facility, including the other co-accused in the charges.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former lawmaker Zaldy Co, and two others last Monday for plunder over allegations that they received more than P7 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.
Romualdez was arrested in the hospital and he is currently confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla on Monday said that according to the former House Speaker’s doctors, he suffered from a cardiovascular event, and was having an anxiety attack and unstable blood pressure. /jpv

articles.title: Australia: Longer hospital wait times as health feud deepens
articles.summary: MELBOURNE — Patients are contending with extended emergency department stays, as one state minister again points his finger at federal counterparts. Visitors to New South Wales (NSW) emergency…

blocks.text: MELBOURNE — Patients are contending with extended emergency department stays, as one state minister again points his finger at federal counterparts.

Visitors to New South Wales (NSW) emergency departments during the April quarter logged stays five minutes longer than those of 2025, according to Bureau of Health Information data released on Wednesday.
The median visit was three hours and 49 minutes, despite overall attendances going down.
Time for treatment in emergency, however, improved on the April quarter of 2025, but still just more two-thirds of patients were seen on time.
Elective surgeries delivered on time improved eight per cent on the previous year, to 86 percent.
NSW Health Minister Ryan Park welcomed improvements in emergency department wait times, claiming them as a win for previous investment.
But he turned on federal counterparts for crowding in the state’s hospitals, raising NSW’s ongoing bed-block dilemma.
“The number of people waiting for aged care and NDIS placements stranded in NSW hospitals is growing at an unprecedented and unsustainable level,” he said.
“For the first time, NSW Health has confirmed that one in eight ED accessible beds in NSW public hospitals cannot be used as a result.
“Waiting indefinitely in a hospital is not good for patient mobility, recovery or quality of life.”
The equivalent of one in every eight accessible beds in NSW emergency departments is medically fit to leave but otherwise cannot, his department claimed.That figure rose from about one in 10 in 2025.
The number of older people waiting for aged care factored into the increase, it said, rising 40 percent in a year from 761 to 1063 patients.
Australian Medical Association NSW president Fred Betros called the latest data a warning sign, saying the obvious answer was to invest in preventative healthcare.
“We need more doctors and staffed beds today, alongside investment in prevention and early intervention to reduce avoidable demand tomorrow,” he said.
“The system needs help now … patients cannot keep paying the price for governments’ failure to plan.”
The rift between state ministers and Mark Butler deepened last week.
They aired their frustrations directly with the federal health minister on Friday.
Australia required 10,000 new beds every year, South Australian Health Minister Blair Boyer said.
But he stared down calls for urgent intervention and referred to his government’s previous investment, adding the aging population was driving unprecedented demand for healthcare.
“We release our budgets and our budget updates in May and December (but) the increases we have made to aged care in our time in office have been eye-watering,” Mr Butler told reporters. /dl
