articles.title: Sudan's healthcare system on brink of collapse after cuts, medical charity warns
articles.summary: Médecins Sans Frontières is urging world leaders to increase funding to help the millions who need aid.

blocks.text: Sudan's fragile health system is on the brink of collapse as global funding cuts have led to the closure of healthcare facilities across the country, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned.
Dozens of organisations were unable to find alternative funding after the US - the largest donor to Sudan - closed USAID, its body for delivering foreign aid, last year, the medical charity said.
MSF urged world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly in New York to take action.

The war that erupted in April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with more than 33 million people needing medical assistance.
MSF said while the US was still the largest donor to Sudan, existing grants to many USAID-funded organisations ran out in June - as European governments were also reducing international assistance.
According to the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), international aid fell globally by 21.3% in 2025 compared to the previous year.
"War is driving Sudan's needs; funding cuts are shrinking the response," said Muhammad Ibrahim, the head of charity in Sudan.

"MSF's work in Sudan is privately funded. But when funding disappears from other health services, clinics close, patients have fewer places to go, and pressure shifts to the facilities that remain, including ours."
This has meant that patients often have to make dangerous and long trips to get treatment.

"After a longer and more expensive journey, patients often arrive in a much more serious condition, and the hospital may already be full," explained Sebastián Traficante, MSF's emergency co-ordinator in the western region of Darfur, which has experienced much of the fighting over the last three years.
Between January and April 2026, MSF saw admissions jump by 22.5% in facilities it supports in central Darfur, when compared to the same time last year.
In May alone, 45 healthcare centres in the area had stopped receiving funding, it said.
According to MSF, the closure of frontline services was putting other hospitals under severe strain - as they were losing their capacity to function and medicines were disappearing.

It gave Gedaref state's Tanedba camp, where 18,400 people who have fled their homes live, as an example. Its maternity and surgical wards have closed down after a humanitarian organisation left in June.
As a result, MSF is now running an emergency room there, but pregnant women who need surgery to deliver a baby, have to travel three hours to the nearest city.
In the Um Rakuba camp - also in Gedaref - the number of aid agencies working there has dropped from 35 in 2021, to less than 10.
According to the charity, the camp currently hosts around 17,000 people, most of whom are women and children.
"If support does not increase, more patients will face longer journeys, fewer treatment options and greater risk of arriving too late for care," MSF's UK humanitarian representative Liz Harding said.
At the same time as the health system was struggling with funding, attacks on healthcare workers were continuing, MSF said.
In 2025, Sudan saw 1,620 people killed in attacks on medical facilities - which the charity said accounted for 82% of all global deaths from attacks on healthcare worldwide.
According to the UN, more than 19.5 million people are also experiencing "crisis levels" of food insecurity and more than five million are facing "emergency levels of hunger".
The fighting shows no sign of easing - despite the expected arrival of international diplomats in the Sudanese capital, Khartoum, for consultations aimed at ending the civil war.

Reports from North Kordofan state on Tuesday say at least 11 people have been killed in a drone attack on the army-controlled town of Umm Ruwaba. According to medical sources, the projectile struck a crowded courtyard in a court complex.

articles.title: In West Bank, date farmers weigh impact of UK sanctions on Israeli settlers
articles.summary: Palestinians strongly back a ban on settlement goods, but Israel's government says it is a "big mistake".

blocks.text: Dates are among the agricultural products commonly exported from Israeli settlements in the West Bank
ByYolande Knell
Middle East correspondent
Juicy brown and ripening yellow dates dangle down from the branches of each palm tree at Israeli settler farms in the Jordan Valley, in the occupied West Bank.
This year, as Israeli growers get ready for a good harvest, they are also preparing for the impact of new Western sanctions against settlements, which are illegal under international law.

The UK government has announced an import ban on settlement goods and said it planned to take action against companies and individuals who provide services for settlement expansion, as part of what it calls a "comprehensive reset" of policy towards Israel following similar moves by several other European countries.

Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden have also confirmed their intention to introduce national restrictions, or support European restrictions, on trade in goods with settlements.
Palestinians strongly back such a move, but Israel's president says it is a "grave miscalculation".
Israeli date farmer Avigdor Arbel, from the settlement of Mesua, calls such boycotts "really disgusting".
Arbel sells his produce mostly to Europe but also to the US and now, India. However, he says the sector is ready for any new UK ban on settler goods.

"As soon as we have a situation of pressure and boycotts, we always break out and look for other markets," he tells me. "So, I believe that if we get to a situation in which there's no place to sell my fruits in Europe, we'll find other markets."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Settler farmer Avigdor Arbel does not believe Israel will ever give up the Jordan Valley

blocks.text: Settler farmer Avigdor Arbel does not believe Israel will ever give up the Jordan Valley

West Bank settlements have expanded rapidly under the current Israeli government, whose ministers say they want "to bury the idea" of an independent Palestinian state - part of the long-standing international formula for peace in the region known as the two-state solution.
At the same time, settler violence against Palestinians has surged to what the UN says is "an all-time high".

With new settler outposts - which are also illegal under Israeli law - now dotting the barren hilltops of the Jordan Valley, there have been repeated attacks on local Palestinians, particularly Bedouin and herding communities.

In January, the last of some 600 villagers fled their homes in Ras Ein al-Ouja after intense harassment by hardline settlers, often backed by Israeli security forces. It was the largest single displacement of a Palestinian community in the past three years.
Further north, in March, Israeli settlers brutally beat and sexually assaulted a Palestinian shepherd during a night raid on Khirbet Humsa.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Parliament on Tuesday that a set of facts on the ground had been created "to make the two-state solution unviable," while "settler terrorism is rampant".

Quoting a former Israeli minister of health and retired brigadier general, Ephraim Sneh, he said the UK government "agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank perpetrated by settler terrorists", to which the Israeli government had "turned a blind eye" or actually supported.
In a significant change of UK policy, he said the government now agreed with the 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that Israel's continued occupation "is unlawful".
As a consequence, Miliband said this should be reflected "in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories".
"I do not believe that the British people want us supporting the occupation by accepting products from settlements in our shops and supermarkets."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Jordan Valley is a fertile strip of land that comprises nearly 30% of the West Bank

blocks.text: The Jordan Valley is a fertile strip of land that comprises nearly 30% of the West Bank
Medjool dates are the main export crop from both Israeli settler farms and Palestinian farms in the Jordan Valley.

"These are rubbish," says Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim Abu Omar, dramatically reaching up and throwing away a handful of shrivelled, yellow dates from a tree in the grove where he works in al-Ouja, north of Jericho.

Around half of the date palms here have no fruit at all. "It's because we lack water," Abu Omar says. His is an extreme case: this year, the trees he cares for have received less than a third of the water they need to thrive.
Access to water has long been a pressing issue in the West Bank.
Interim peace agreements from the 1990s have left a water disparity between Israelis and Palestinians, and Israeli authorities typically prioritise water for settlers over Palestinians' needs.
Recently, in rural areas of the Jordan Valley, almost all of which is under Israeli security and civilian control, extremist settlers have also taken over several freshwater springs.
The Israeli Civil Administration told the BBC that it keeps "continuous contact" with the Palestinian Water Authority and assists in carrying out repairs to water infrastructure.

This harvest time, Abu Omar has few dates that are fit to show local Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot. His firm, Palestine Gardens, works with 55 date growers in the Jordan Valley to sell to several European countries, including the UK.
Sinokrot believes that if more states ban settlement trade this could curb settlement growth.
"Settlers are very active in the Jordan Valley... and they are not obeying any laws or rules or anything even from the Israeli army itself," he says.
"They are going to the fields of the growers, they are stealing from them, and they are controlling more and more land."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim says half his date farms have no fruit because of a water shortage

blocks.text: Palestinian farmer Abdul Halim says half his date farms have no fruit because of a water shortage

Israeli-state support for settlements, as well as their relatively easy access to global markets, means that Palestinian farmers struggle to compete. Palestinian businesses face greater restrictions and costs to export across Israeli-controlled borders.

Palestinians want the wide swathe of fertile land in the Jordan Valley - along the West Bank's border with Jordan - as part of their own hoped-for future state, along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
However, Avigdor Arbel, the settler date farmer, does not believe that his country will ever give up the Jordan Valley. He has lived there since the 1970s.

Within years of Israel's capture of the West Bank from Jordan in the 1967 Middle East War, the Israeli government began encouraging its citizens to move to this area to counter what it saw as the security risk along the border.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank, not including Israeli-annexed East Jerusalem, alongside three million Palestinians.
There are 340 settler outposts in the Palestinian territory along with 146 settlements, formally recognised by the Israeli government, according to the Israeli anti-settlement group Peace Now.
Current UK and EU laws require labels for settlement goods. Agricultural produce commonly exported includes mangoes, avocados, herbs and grapes.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Israeli settlers diverted a Palestinian village's water to fill a pool in the Jordan Valley this summer

blocks.text: Israeli settlers diverted a Palestinian village's water to fill a pool in the Jordan Valley this summer
There have been questions raised about how a ban on settlement goods would be enforced.

A recent report by the legal advocacy group Global Echo found that some settlement fruits and vegetables sold in Europe were inaccurately identified as coming from Israel - or mingled with produce from inside Israel's internationally-recognised borders.

However, the report's author, Jessica Stober, suggests that a UK ban on settler goods would greatly increase the financial costs associated with any such fraudulent practices. Instead of a seller being fined for misrepresenting their goods, the shipment would be returned.
"A ban is more self-enforcing because you have involved the private sector and it becomes commercially unviable for them to deal in settlement goods," Stober says.

"I would also say that a whole new set of measures become available to the UK government under a sanctions regime, under a ban, including civil and criminal penalties that make compliance much more likely."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot believes sanctions could help curb settlement growth

blocks.text: Palestinian exporter Momen Sinokrot believes sanctions could help curb settlement growth
Speaking just before the UK move was announced, Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it would amount to "gross interference" in Israel's upcoming elections, due in late October.
"I believe it will prove to be a grave miscalculation, a decision that will fall on the wrong side of history," he warned.
Israel's government is threatening retaliation for any UK ban on settlement goods.

"If Britain acts against the State of Israel, the State of Israel will act against Britain," the Israeli Foreign Secretary, Gideon Saar, told an Israeli podcast last week. When I approached him at a diplomatic event on Monday to ask for more details about which steps could be taken, he declined to answer.
Israel recently expelled two Dutch diplomats from a US-led centre in charge of co-ordinating the shaky Gaza ceasefire, after the Netherlands banned trade from settlements.
Other European countries that have already imposed a ban on settlement goods or trade restrictions - arguing it is a legal obligation - include Ireland, Spain and Belgium.
Now, the new action by the UK looks set to put a new, heavy strain on its relations with Israel.

articles.title: Fifty years after Mao’s death, China has transformed. DW looks at why his political legacy still matters.
articles.summary: Mao Zedong was perhaps the most influential, and certainly one of the most controversial, figures in 20th-century China. Even five decades after his death, the legacy of his era continues to…

image.caption: Mao's teachings remain part of China's official ideology, and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen SquareImage: Noel Celis/AFP

blocks.text: On September 9, 1976, Mao Zedong died. The revolutionary leader who led the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to power and founded the People's Republic of China left behind a profoundly contradictory historical legacy.
He shaped the narratives of revolution, nation-building and national independence, but also left behind immense social trauma as a result of successive political campaigns and persecutions.
50 years of transformation: How far has China moved away from Mao?
Over the past five decades, China has undergone radical changes.

When Mao died, China was still a poor and relatively isolated communist state. Today, it is the world's second-largest economy, deeply embedded in the supply and value chains of global capitalism, with a vast private sector, a large urban middle class and a highly digitalized society.

Zhang Lun, a professor at Cergy-Paris University, said Mao left behind four major political legacies: the authoritarian and highly centralized political system; a model of governance that relies on revolution and political campaigns to solve social problems; populist tendencies marked by anti-elitism and anti-rationalism; and utopian visions of egalitarianism and moralism.

From the perspective of political legacies, Zhang told DW, the most fundamental change in China over the past five decades has been "de-Maoization" — while its greatest challenge has been that this process was never fully completed.

blocks.caption: Mao's insistence on the CCP's supremacy is still a fundamental principle in China todayImage: akg-images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The legacy that never left: the party's supremacy
Mao's name remains written into the CCP's constitution, while his thought remains part of China's official ideology and his portrait still hangs in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

Mao helped forge the Chinese Communist Party, and his insistence on the party's supremacy over the state and society has remained a fundamental principle throughout the decades, said Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt, professor at the University of Zurich.

Veteran journalist and political commentator Chang Ping agrees, adding that what has truly endured is the institutional core of the principle that "the party leads everything," serving a state vision of being able to "concentrate resources to accomplish major tasks."
The CCP, he said, can pursue such objectives "at all costs" — meaning the interests of ordinary people can be sacrificed to the maximum extent necessary to preserve the regime.
A return to the 'Mao era?'

Under current leader Xi Jinping, a number of political concepts and methods of governance associated with the Mao era — such as ideological unity and the spirit of "struggle" — have again attracted attention.

Xi's actions such as abolishing the presidential term limits, strengthening his personal authority and the incorporation of his political thought into the party and state constitutions have invited comparisons between him and Mao.
Chang argues that the very term "return" is misleading, since elements of the Mao era have never fully disappeared.
Zhang holds a similar view.

Authoritarian rule, political rigidity, weak rule of law and the lack of effective guarantees for citizens' rights, he argues, are not only important elements of Mao's political legacy but also among the most significant continuities between the Mao era and China's current political system, he underscored.
And Xi, who personally suffered during the Cultural Revolution, seems even move closer to Mao-era policies.
"What Xi learned from the Cultural Revolution was not the lesson of a victim, but the lesson of power," Chang told DW.
The lesson was not that "such a system must never exist again," but rather that "whoever loses power is at the mercy of others," he added.
Felix Wemheuer, professor of modern China studies at the University of Cologne, echoed this view.

"The conclusion Xi appears to have drawn from his own experience of the Cultural Revolution was clearly not that Mao should be completely abandoned," he told DW, "but rather that, for political reasons, Mao's historical status as the founder of the state, the military and the party must be upheld."
Wemheuer views the current CCP leadership's approach to Mao as "fundamentally Machiavellian and pragmatic."

In economic policy, for instance, there is no sign of a return to the Mao era, he said. Today's China operates a highly dynamic model of state capitalism, with a mix of ownership forms coexisting and maintaining a strong private sector. Nor is there any indication that China intends to return to the Mao-era model of a communist welfare state.
The same applies to the idea of "self-reliance." Today's China could hardly afford to withdraw from the global economy and international supply chains.
Trump, Putin or Xi: Who really runs the world?
Xi remains a product of the system Mao created

Experts say similarities between Mao and Xi can be seen in areas such as the emphasis on the CCP's supremacy, the elevation of a core leader, and populist elements that stress a close connection between the people and the leadership.
Wemheuer argues that Xi possesses neither Mao's historical authority nor his personal charisma.

The two also exercise power in fundamentally different ways. Mao could bypass party institutions, go for years without convening a party congress and mobilize the masses against the party and state apparatus.
Mao himself was a populist with certain anarchic tendencies, Wemheuer said, and even tolerated the temporary collapse of the party-state system at the grassroots level in 1966-67.

Xi, by contrast, would never allow such a situation to occur, the expert stressed. Xi places greater emphasis than Mao on control and top-down governance, consolidating power by strengthening institutions and the party apparatus.
Mittelstaedt likewise cautions against equating Xi with Mao.

First, Mao was a revolutionary who destroyed existing institutions during the Cultural Revolution and was fundamentally anti-bureaucratic in his political orientation. Xi, Mittelstaedt argues, does the opposite.
Second, Mao stood above the party. His power came from "being Mao himself" rather than from the party's institutional structures.
Xi, by contrast, is "a party man through and through." His authority derives from party institutions, and he governs through those institutions, Mittelstaedt pointed out.
"At the end of the day," he told DW, "Xi Jinping remains a product of the system Mao created."
Mao nostalgia among younger generations?

China has also seen recurring waves of Mao nostalgia, with some Chinese citizens invoking Mao online and expressing longing for what they describe as an era without social inequality, when everyone supposedly had enough to eat.
Chang argues that what they are longing for is neither Mao himself nor the real Mao era.

The actual Mao era, Mittelstaedt said, was marked by rigid hierarchies, pointing to the urban-rural household registration divide, different levels of privileges and supplies for officials, and a system in which one's family background could determine one's fate. It was, in many respects, more unequal than China today — and voicing grievances could be fatal.

The imagined vision of a more equal world, he underlined, is therefore actually an indictment of the present situation, with widening inequality, soaring housing prices and persistently limited social mobility.
Still, many express the dissatisfaction with contemporary reality through Mao's image and language.

In Chang's view, this is connected to the continuing contraction of space for public criticism in China. When forms of political expression such as independent trade unions, street protests, free media and opposition parties are tightly restricted, Mao remains a historical symbol that official ideology cannot entirely exclude.

The result is a striking irony, he said, pointing to some people invoking Mao's language of anti-bureaucracy, resistance to oppression and even "rebellion" to criticize what they see as corruption, inequality and abuses of power in Xi's China today.

Mittelstaedt said this makes Mao a double-edged sword. He remains an important symbol of the CCP's political legitimacy — but parts of the revolutionary language he left behind can also be turned into standards by which contemporary reality is measured and criticized.
What is China's NPC and why does it matter?

articles.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as relations worsen
articles.summary: For years, Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the EU, but the new government has dropped the pro-Kremlin stance.

blocks.text: Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán says 10 Russian diplomats have been ordered to leave Budapest for taking part in "unacceptable" activities.
"This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote on social media, without giving details.
Hungary was viewed as Russia's closest ally in the European Union under Viktor Orbán for years, but since his election defeat in April the new government has pivoted away from his pro-Kremlin stance.

The Hungarian foreign minister said the decision to expel the diplomats "does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia", but the foreign ministry spokeswoman in Moscow said "the response to the Russophobic lobby will be harsh and painful".

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow from the moment his Tisza party was elected in April. He and the foreign minister have both called on Russia to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.

In May Anita Orbán summoned the Russian ambassador to protest against a big drone attack on the Transcarpathia region of Ukraine that is home to a large Hungarian minority. Commentators have pointed out that her predecessor had not summoned the ambassador since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion in 2022.

Then last month Magyar formally broke with the previous Fidesz government's policies, with new guidelines spelling out that Russia's conduct in Ukraine "poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also puts the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger".
Russia's Ambassador to Budapest, Evgeny Stanislavov, reacted bitterly to Anita Orbán's intention to continue "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules".
Budapest's promise of pragmatic co-operation was worth absolutely nothing, he complained, adding that Hungary's "extremely unfriendly step constitutes an unprecedented and ungrounded escalation".

Before Magyar was voted into office, Hungary had for years insisted on maintaining close relations with Moscow, partly citing cheap Russian oil imports. Viktor Orbán objected to the EU's supply of aid to Ukraine and repeatedly delayed packages of sanctions on Russia.

Ahead of the April elections, independent Russian investigative website Agentsvo reported that 15 of the 47 Russian embassy staff in Budapest were linked to Russian intelligence agencies and six more might be linked.

Former Hungarian counter-intelligence chief András Telkes told the BBC that even though "Russian spying activity" had been investigated before the election, the Fidesz government had prevented any action being taken.
The Russian embassy in Budapest had also rejected as false a report alleging that three Russian military intelligence officers had travelled to Budapest to influence the Hungarian vote.
Russia has routinely denied its embassies are used for espionage. However, hundreds of Russian diplomats have been expelled across Europe since 2022, and Russia has responded in kind.

Telkes told the BBC that the big question now was how Moscow would respond: "If 10 Hungarian diplomats were to be expelled from Moscow, in a tit-for-tat move, that would effectively close the Hungarian embassy there."

articles.title: Air traffic control issue causes flight delays and disruption across UK
articles.summary:
Departures from London airports worst hit with most flights since 2pm affected as National Air Traffic Services investigates technical problem

Flights around the UK are facing delays and…

blocks.text: Flights around the UK are facing delays and disruption due to an air traffic control issue which has affected a string of airports including Heathrow and Gatwick and is expected to take “some time” to resolve.
Departures from London airports are most severely affected, with few take-offs since a fault was reported early on Tuesday afternoon.
Most flights due to depart Heathrow, Gatwick, Stansted and London City airports since 2pm appeared to have been delayed or are yet to take off. Manchester airport has also been affected.
The air traffic control service Nats said at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”.

Nats later added that it had identified the problem, which was in its flight processing system. It said: “Our engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible. We recognise the ongoing disruption to travel, for which we sincerely apologise.
It continued: “Flights are still departing and airspace is open, but recovery will take some time. We will provide further updates as soon as possible.”

The UK’s biggest airport, Heathrow, said planes were continuing to arrive, although Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely to continue until the evening.
In a statement, Heathrow added: “We are supporting our local Nats team in their efforts to resolve the issue as quickly as possible. We will provide updated information when we have it.
“We apologise to those disrupted and advise passengers to check with their airline for latest flight information.”
Heathrow’s website showed several flights due to depart this afternoon have been cancelled. British Airways said it was experiencing some disruption and was in touch with its customers.
Belfast City airport warned of “some disruption” to flights after the technical issue affecting Nats.
“Due to the technical issue referenced below, there may be some disruption to flights due to arrive in and depart from Belfast City airport,” they said in a statement.”

A Birmingham airport spokesperson apologised to customers and advised them to “arrive at Birmingham airport (BHX) in line with their airline’s check-in requirements and to contact their airline directly for the latest flight information and updates.”
Edinburgh airport said it was aware of the issue which “may impact operations”.

articles.title: Ratko Mladic’s funeral casts shadow over Bosnia and Herzegovina vote
articles.summary: Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade, attended by Serbian and Bosnian Serb leaders, has deepened regional tensions and could affect the upcoming election in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

image.caption: Mladic, who was dubbed the 'Butcher of Bosnia' for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, was buried with military honors in Serbia on MondayImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: Belgrade has made a point of insisting that it did not organize a state funeral for former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide in Srebrenica and crimes against humanity in 2017.

But when the body of a war criminal is flown home accompanied by the country's justice minister, when ceremonies unfold with military honors in state-controlled venues in the presence of senior political leaders and when clear condemnation of glorification of the deceased is absent, the message is unambiguous.
The impact of this message is being felt beyond Serbia's borders.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina — the state created by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, which comprises two entities linked by a weak central government — reactions were as deeply divided as the country itself.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: Two entities, two narratives
Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity covering about 49% of the country's territory, sent its officials to the funeral.

blocks.caption: Ratko Mladic was mourned by many in Republika Srpska, the majority Serb entity in Bosnia and HerzegovinaImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Public discourse there was dominated by narratives of "defending the people" and "the injustice of international courts."
"Without Ratko Mladic, there would be no Republika Srpska," was the refrain among thousands of mourners at the funeral in Belgrade.
Sarajevo, the seat of the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sees this approach as a continued policy of relativizing war crimes and a threat to stability.
Bosnia and Herzegovina cools diplomatic ties with Serbia
In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entity where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, the response was very different and the tone sharp.
Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic described Serbia's official response as a conscious choice by Belgrade, not something imposed on it.

He announced measures to cool diplomatic ties with Serbia, withdrawing almost all staff from the country's embassy in Belgrade, leaving only the ambassador, explaining that he lacks the authority to close the embassy but can reduce its presence to a minimum. The move effectively froze day-to-day diplomatic communication on the ground.

blocks.caption: Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic announced that he would be withdrawing almost all staff from the country's embassy in BelgradeImage: Denis Zuberi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: "We will pull out everyone we can; consular services will be relocated to Zagreb and Podgorica," he said.
Denis Becirovic, chair of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, called the funeral with military honors an "anti-civilizational act" and warned of far-reaching consequences for the entire region.
For representatives of Mladic's victims, any public glorification of the former general is a direct insult to the families of those killed.
Political point-scoring
Mladic's death and funeral are not just about the past.
At a time when both Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are facing general elections — Bosnia on October 4 and Serbia likely just a few weeks later — emotions become a resource.
In both countries, parts of the electorate still see Mladic as a symbol of resistance, which means that every gesture in support of him scores political points with these voters.

As the general election in Bosnia and Herzegovina approaches, sharp condemnations from Sarajevo are seen as evidence that the central government is "defending the state" and "the dignity of victims." This, too, is being turned into political capital.

blocks.caption: Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Denis Becirovic called Mladic's funeral with military honors an 'anti-civilizational act'Image: NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Republika Srpska, the presence of officials at the funeral and the narrative of "injustice" strengthen the position of those building their identity in opposition to international rulings.
Yet there are no "winners." The more political points anyone scores on this issue, the worse relations become and the further accession to the EU recedes into the distance — for both countries.

Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka, is clear about who is responsible for these political narratives: "The main culprits are the political elites, because in 30 years we have not moved forward. There has been no critical confrontation with the dark side of history," she says. "This is a darkening of civilizational consciousness."
Topic went on to say that Mladic's funeral "is a welcome gift to the protagonists of ethno-nationalist policies" and noted that these people still hold power in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"Such an institutional stance towards crimes provokes a reaction on the other side, and then everyone exploits the situation, trapping us in a vicious circle where each tries to extract political profit," Topic says.
A divided society and frozen relations

After Mladic's funeral, the Office of the High Representative (OHR) in Bosnia, which was created after the war to oversee the implementation of the US-brokered Dayton Peace Agreement, stressed that Bosnia's future cannot be built on glorifying those responsible for the worst crimes of the past.

blocks.caption: Mladic was convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1990s Bosnian War. Pictured here: headstones of victims of the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre Image: Elvis Barukcic/AFP

blocks.text: "Glorifying convicted war criminals, as well as denying genocide and other war crimes, creates divisions, inflicts additional pain on victims and their families, and undermines the reconciliation process," said the OHR.
Bosnia remains a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 31 years since the war ended.

The fact that the ideology that helped spark that war still lives on, means that Mladic's funeral did not close a chapter in the region's history, it tore open a new one, measuring the Balkans' willingness to step out of the shadow of the 1990s.
While politicians seek to score political points, citizens pay the price of frozen relations.

articles.title: U.A.E. warned Netanyahu of major Hamas operation days before Oct. 7 attack: Israeli newspaper
articles.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was directly warned by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before the militant group led an attack on Oct.…

image.caption: Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks. On Tuesday, Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that he was directly warned by the U.A.E. that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before

blocks.text: World·New

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was directly warned by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before the militant group led an attack on Oct. 7, 2023, according to an Israeli newspaper.
Haaretz says Netanyahu's office called report 'absolute lie'

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was directly warned by the president of the United Arab Emirates that Hamas was planning a major offensive just days before the militant group led an attack on Oct. 7, 2023 , according to an Israeli newspaper.
U.A.E. President Mohammed bin Zayed spoke with Netanyahu 10 days before the attack and said Yahya Sinwar, the leader of Hamas in Gaza at the time, was planning an operation, the Haaretz daily said.

Bin Zayed said it would lead to bloodshed and could destabilize the region and undermine the Abraham Accords, the normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab and Muslim-majority nations, the newspaper reported.

But Netanyahu "reacted with relative calm," according to Haaretz, which said he assured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario and a possible attack was more likely to come from the occupied West Bank.
The attack led by Hamas militants on Oct. 7 killed some 1,200 people and took another 251 hostage, according to Israeli officials.
Haaretz reported Netanyahu's office called the report an "absolute lie" and said Netanyahu did not speak with the U.A.E. president "during the period in question and received no warning from him."

items: Israeli clearance of Gaza rubble could destroy evidence of 'atrocity crimes,' says UN expert
Israel prepared to remove Palestinians from Gaza if U.S. approves, defence minister says

blocks.text: Netanyahu has rejected calls for an official government inquiry into the events surrounding the Oct. 7 attack. His office did not respond to a request for comment.
The U.A.E.'s Foreign Ministry also did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel is holding national elections next month and Netanyahu's actions around the time of the Oct. 7 attack are a key issue in the campaign.
Gadi Eisenkot, a former top general seen as Netanyahu's main opponent in the election, accused the prime minister of ignoring dozens of warnings ahead of the attack.
"He is unfit," Eisenkot wrote on social media.
Another Netanyahu rival, Naftali Bennett, said, "Netanyahu bears personal and direct responsibility for the failure that led to the deaths of thousands of Israelis on his watch."
Israel's offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,650 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia vows to respond after Houthis attack cities and energy facilities
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Yemeni group's attacks have injured 73 people and caused fires at oil facilities, Saudi authorities say.

blocks.text: The spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the Houthi drone and missile attacks targeted civilian and economic sites in the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, and that women and children were among the injured.
An energy ministry statement cited an official source as saying that injuries were also reported after "several energy sector facilities and installations" were targeted.
The attacks "caused fires at several locations, leading to a temporary halt in some operations," they added.

Maliki described Houthi attacks as a "dangerous escalation that confirms the hostile and irresponsible approach of this terrorist militia" and said the Saudi-led coalition would "take all necessary operational measures to deter" the group.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea accused the Saudi military of carrying out more than 120 air strikes on the Yemeni provinces of Marib, al-Bayda, Hudaydah, Taiz and Jawf over the past three days, and of committing "grave crimes".
He said the Houthis had responded to this "brutal aggression" with "dozens of ballistic missiles and drones", which he claimed caused "significant damage".
A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

There has been heavy fighting on Yemen's south-western coast since Thursday, when the Houthis launched an offensive against Yemeni pro-government forces in a bid to take control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The fighting has reportedly left more than 300 people dead and displaced 18,500.
The Red Sea has become crucial for oil shipments from Saudi Arabia during the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: New York City releases documents about air quality after 9/11
articles.summary: Officials assured the public the air was safe after the attacks, but the new documents suggest there were concerns.

blocks.text: New York City has released previously unseen documents raising concerns about air quality in Manhattan in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced on Tuesday.

The documents from 25 years ago suggest that officials had concerns about toxic air after the World Trade Center towers collapsed, while the public was being reassured the environment at the site, known as Ground Zero, was safe.
"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," Mamdani said at a news conference, surrounded by survivors.
The release resolves a lawsuit brought by advocacy group 9/11 Health Watch, which sued the city for the documents.
City officials found 68 boxes of the documents last year. Officials had previously said they did not have them.
"Administration after administration has ignored those calling for answers and clarity," he added, standing next to television host and 9/11 survivor advocate Jon Stewart. "We will do no such thing."
Thousands of people have experienced health effects like cancer from the terrorist attacks, including many who have died, after breathing in hazardous contaminants from the building collapses.
Mamdani said on Tuesday that he planned to release hundreds of thousands of pages of air quality reports through an online portal, timed with the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
He said City Hall will spend more than $34m (£25m) on the effort.
Mamdani said the documents show what the city "knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability".
The mayor said the documents show asbestos was found "nearly everywhere" they tested. He said more documents will be released over the course of the next year.
The release comes after years of survivors advocating for more transparency from city officials.
Speaking at the news conference on Tuesday, Stewart said the documents show the city didn't recognize that the air that everyone was breathing in downtown Manhattan was toxic until October of 2001.
"So to be fair to them, they only buried that information for 25 years," he said sarcastically.

The documents include an October 2001 file known as the "Harding Memo", in which an aide warned former Deputy Mayor Robert Harding - serving under Mayor Rudy Giuliani - that the city could face as many as 35,000 legal claims for its response to the attacks.
The document states that the city could be sued because health advisories caused individuals "to return to the area too soon (causing toxic exposure or emotional harm)".

Days after the attack, city and federal officials - including the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) - declared that the air near the Twin Towers was safe, though research suggests people were breathing in toxic chemicals.
Christine Todd Whitman, the head of the EPA at the time, later apologised for this declaration, saying the agency "did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had".
Illnesses related to the dust and smoke from the collapse of the Twin Towers have claimed twice as many lives than the attacks themselves.
Elizabeth Cascio, a former New York Fire Department (FDNY) emergency medical technician, previously told the BBC that she suffered sinus issues and headaches after responding to the attacks.

"We all knew the air quality was not safe – it was very toxic in terms of how it felt," she said. "Initially, when I came off the bus and arrived at the Trade Center, you felt like you had to hold your breath. But there's only so long you can hold your breath. I could feel the particles coming into my nose and mouth and thought: 'This can't be good'."

articles.title: Four Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist
articles.summary: It is the latest in a string of high-profile art thefts in Europe that has again put the security of museums and galleries in the spotlight.

blocks.text: What we know about the Renoir museum heist
ByMichael Sheils McNamee and Tiffany Wertheimer
Four paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.
Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on Tuesday morning but dropped two of the paintings in the institution's garden as they made their escape, local Mayor Bryan Masson said.
"Attacking the Renoir Museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer," he said.

The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen this year following a string of heists in Europe - which have included four Renaissance paintings being stolen from a museum in Sicily just last month.
CCTV footage has captured the thieves entering the museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said.
He added that two painting were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered.
The two paintings that are still missing are:
And the two pieces that were recovered are:
"It's Renoir's, it is priceless, you cannot sell it like that," the mayor told reporters at the museum.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Jeune fille au puits and Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano are still missing

blocks.text: Image source, Musée Renoir
Jeune fille au puits and Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano are still missing

blocks.caption: Image caption, The thieves dropped Coco Lisant and Portrait of Madame Pichon when they fled - one was found hours later in the museum's garden

blocks.text: The thieves dropped Coco Lisant and Portrait of Madame Pichon when they fled - one was found hours later in the museum's garden
The museum's alarm went off at 05:48 local time (06:48 BST), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms.
Masson later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed".
They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," Masson said.
Masson also confirmed that investigators had found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police arrived at the scene within five minutes of the museum's alarm going off

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Police arrived at the scene within five minutes of the museum's alarm going off
The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.

Opened in 1960, it was Renoir's last home before his death in 1919, and also features many things that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.
The robbery has once again thrust the security of art in some of Europe's leading galleries and museums into the spotlight.
One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen.
"Beyond Cagnes-sur-Mer, this incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums, which now face a new form of organised crime targeting works of art," Masson warned.
The mayor called on the French government to provide more financial support to local areas and museums to protect artwork from "increasingly organised and determined criminals".

articles.title: BSW and AfD – a political love-hate relationship in Germany
articles.summary: The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could help the Alternative for Germany (AfD) into power in Saxony-Anhalt. It is riddled with infighting

image.caption: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund (top) could become head of government in Saxony-Anhalt with the support of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW)Image: Karina Hessland-Wissel/Jan Huebner/IMAGO

blocks.text: Following the election in Saxony-Anhalt, there is no clear governing coalition because the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) with its 44% share of the vote has fallen just short of securing an absolute majority. That means the formation of a new government in one of Germany's 16 federal states is more difficult than ever. This is also partly due to the success that the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which was founded only in 2024, has managed to achieve. Wagenknecht, a trained economist, was a longtime member of the socialist Left Party, formerly a communist who over time has distanced herself further from her political roots. Her party does not conform to traditional labels. Many people can no longer relate much to labels like "left" or "right," she says.
From the very beginning, Wagenknecht also showed no reluctance to engage with the AfD. Her long-held credo has been that the party includes people who are treated unfairly if labeled as Nazis.
What next after far-right AfD win in regional election?

Now, Sahra Wagenknecht and her followers are working towards seeking common ground with the AfD and can even imagine helping the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund into the role of state premier by abstaining from the vote. Wagenknecht mentioned this scenario before the September 6 election.
Both AfD and BSW oppose 'uncontrolled migration'

A few days before the vote, Sahra Wagenknecht spoke on TV broadcaster ntv about overlapping policy preferences of BSW and AfD voters: "These are people who have similar concerns: They want controlled migration, they do not want this uncontrolled migration and they want above all that politics is again conducted in their interests, that their lives are the focus."

However, there is also a significant degree of agreement on issues other than German immigration policy: both parties call for an end to German arms deliveries to Ukraine, which has been attacked by Russia in violation of international law. Or they claim that freedom of speech no longer exists in Germany.

Whether the BSW will actually team up with the AfD remains completely open. AfD lead candidate Siegmund emphasized even before the election that he intended to govern only with an absolute majority of his own.

blocks.caption: Sahra Wagenknecht is no longer the chairwoman of the BSW party, but still its most prominent representativeImage: dts Nachrichtenagentur/IMAGO

blocks.text: When the BSW was founded in January 2024, it had a spectacular start: Formed as a splinter party from the socialist Left, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) was swiftly elected to the European Parliament and in the same year received double-digit results in three state parliament elections. In the eastern German states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party entered straight into government coalitions. That would also have been possible in Saxony, but coalition negotiations with the CDU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) failed.

The BSW favors a tough approach to refugees. It opposes any form of military support, whether for Ukraine or for Israel. The BSW advocates for an end to German weapons deliveries to Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia in breach of international law.

The party's leader, economist Sahra Wagenknecht, who grew up in communist East Germany, aligned her new political home beyond traditional classifications. She repeatedly states that many people can no longer relate to labels like "left" or "right" wing.
Wagenknecht has also had no reservations about contact with the AfD from the beginning. As early as 2023, she stated that some people within the party were being labeled Nazis unfairly.
Far left? Far right? What is Germany's BSW?
From rising star to struggling party

However, the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt has ruled out a classic coalition. Following elections in Brandenburg and Thuringia in 2024, the branches in those states went against the stated will of their founder and joined governments alongside established parties. The permanent conflict between the federal leadership of the party and its state branches led to the breakdown of the coalition with the Social Democrats in Brandenburg, starting in 2025.

In Thuringia, led by a coalition of the CDU, SPD and BSW, most of the BSW lawmakers declared that they were leaving the party two days before the election in Saxony-Anhalt. However, they wanted to remain a part of the CDU-led state government. "We have not been elected to tolerate flirts with right-wing radicals," is how Finance Minister Katja Wolf explained this decision, referring to the rapprochement with the AfD initiated by Wagenknecht.

The BSW's success in Saxony-Anhalt and accompanying key role in the formation of the government has given the party, at least for the moment, a largely unexpected significance. This is because during the Bundestag federal election of 2025 the BSW narrowly failed to reach the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament and, also due to its many internal conflicts, it seemed to have little credibility among the population.

Furthermore, its figurehead Sahra Wagenknecht has stepped back from the leadership of her party and is no longer running for its chairmanship. She continues to exert her influence in the background, though, and is a drawcard at BSW rallies, especially during election campaigns.
Boost for upcoming state elections?

Following their successful entry into Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which according to pre-election polls was by no means guaranteed, Wagenknecht responded confidently: "The BSW's comeback has begun," she told German news agency dpa. How sustainable this upswing is will be revealed on September 20, when parliamentary elections will be held in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state of Berlin.
This article was translated from German.
