articles.title: EU court rules against Belgian far-right party in IKEA case
articles.summary: A European court has backed Ikea's challenge against a Belgian far-right party, saying the use of Ikea-style visuals could harm the company's reputation.

image.caption: Vlaams Belang used graphics resembling the retailer's iconic assembly instructions in a political campaign.Image: Walter Cicchetti/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: A top European Union court ruled in favor of Ikea in a challenge brought by the company against Belgian far-right and Flemish separatist party Vlaams Belang.

The popular Swedish brand may prevent the Belgian party from using its signature illustrations. Vlaams Belang launched the "Ikea Plan" in 2022, a proposal to reform the country's migration and asylum laws.
The plan included images similar to Ikea's furniture assembly instructions. Ikea filed a legal complaint in 2023, accusing the far-right party of unlawfully using its branding.
What did the court rule?

"A proprietor of a trademark with a reputation may prevent that mark from being used by a political party where the latter has not demonstrated that its freedom of expression takes precedence over the rights and interests of that proprietor," the ECJ court said in a statement.

Vlaams Belang argued that the campaign was protected under freedom of expression. However, the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice found this argument insufficient, ruling that the use of Ikea's branding could harm the company's name and reputation.
The Luxembourg judges urged the Belgian court to issue a ruling on the matter in light of the decision by the European Court of Justice.
What did Vlaams Belang and IKEA say about the ruling?
In a statement, Vlaams Belang said it had taken note of the judgement, adding that it "will thoroughly study its scope in the context of the further legal proceedings."
Meanwhile, IKEA representatives welcomed the judgement.

"Inter IKEA strongly believes in and has great respect for freedom of expression. At the same time, the company cannot accept the use of IKEA’s trademarks in a way that harms their reputation or distinctiveness", Inter IKEA, a Netherlands-based holding company that handles the Swedish firm's intellectual property, was cited by Reuters news agency as saying.
Besides its anti-immigration stances, Vlaams Belang also advocates for the independence of Flanders — the northern, Dutch-speaking part of Belgium.
While it made considerable gains in 2024 elections, other parties refuse to cooperate with it.

articles.title: UK announces trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in occupied West Bank
articles.summary: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the measures were in response to what he called "settler terrorism" in the occupied territories. The measures are part of the UK's efforts to support a two-state…

image.caption: Foreign Secrety Ed Miliband announced the measures in the House of Commons [File: July 29, 2026]Image: Leon Neal/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: The United Kingdom on Tuesday announced trade restrictions on goods made in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The center-left Labour Party government has previously sanctioned some Israeli settlers and illegal outposts over violence against Palestinians and illegal development in the West Bank.
What did Miliband say?
"I can announce today that we will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced in the House of Commons.
"We will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate for settlement expansion," Miliband said.
The foreign secretary said those financing or facilitating illegal settlement would "face the full force of UK sanctions."
Before announcing the sanctions, Miliband said that "settler terrorism was rampant" and referenced various instances of violence in the West Bank.
Miliband accused the Israeli government of turning a "blind eye" to what he called "ethnic cleansing" by settlers in the West Bank.
Why is the UK restricting trade
The measures appear to be setting the tone for relations between Britain's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Israel.

According to a Downing Street readout of a phone call between the British leader and US President Donald Trump on the phone on Monday, Burnham laid out "the UK's commitment to working towards peace and security in the region," and stressed the importance of the two-state solution two-state solution in Israel and the Palestinian territories.
The United Kingdom recognized Palestinian statehood last year in an attempt to revive efforts to achieve a two-state solution.

It also comes Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government forges ahead with settlement construction in the West Bank, raising fears among some Western governments that it threatens any possible two-state solution.
The measures also come amd flaring tensions in the West Bank that have involved violent attacks on Palestinians by Israeli settlers.
The UK has previously condemned the violence while calling for civilians to be protected and for those responsible to be held accountable.
Israel warns it will 'act against Britain'
Ahead of the announcement, Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar already indicated that Israel would respond.
"If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain," Saar warned.

Israel's hard-line public security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, urged Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly recognize the Falkland Islands as "Argentine territory under occupation, which the British violently steal from the Argentine people."
This is a developing story. Check back here for updates.

articles.title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing
articles.summary: In strongest condemnation ever by UK government, Ed Miliband announces sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements

blocks.text: Israeli “terrorists” are conducting ethnic cleansing in the West Bank with the tacit backing of the government, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has said as he announced sweeping sanctions, alongside France and Canada, on trade with Israeli settlements.

In the strongest condemnation ever issued by the UK government, Miliband said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, saying such acknowledgment was “the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”
Miliband said that the government would now enact:

items: An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.
A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements.
A ban on the advertising in the UK of illegal settlement properties.
Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.
A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

blocks.text: Miliband said the action would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.

The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.

Miliband said those who financed or facilitated illegal settlements would “face the full force of UK sanctions” and that he expected the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months.
He stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts.
Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians. I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”
He said the British government had previously described settlements as illegal but had not described the occupation itself as unlawful, and that would now change.

France and Canada were also announcing bans on settlement goods on Tuesday, joining the Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway, which have either banned goods or were in the process of doing so.
Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust.
“I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.

“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”

He said to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.

Miliband said he felt a “deep sense of shame about what has unfolded in Palestine under the eyes of the international community” and said there had been “the most unimaginable trauma and suffering in the last three years – death, destruction and dehumanisation on an appalling scale”.
The foreign secretary said the action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine; one that not only condemned but took action.
“Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”
Miliband said the actions of the Israeli government in the West Bank meant more settlements had been approved in the last four years than in the last 20 years combined.
He said he believed the majority of the British people would support the ban on trade with illegal settlements. “Settlements are illegal. They should not be promoted in our country,” he said.
The UK government knew there were also concerns about arm sales to Israel, he said. The UK had already suspended more than 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza, but would now go further.

“We will now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation, in effect a double lock against arms sales. This means the ban on such exports will now remain as long as the occupation persists.”
He said the UK would support “full, robust and fair judicial processes” to determine if Israel had committed genocide and said the government would not pre-judge that process.

“This has been the case for all of the genocides since the 1948 genocide convention: Rwanda, Srebrenica, Cambodia, and acts against the Yazidi people. This will remain our policy. It is right that this issue has been brought before the ICJ [international court of justice] and I want to make it clear that we support the court in coming to its determination.”

However, he said that the most recent reports by international bodies found there was “increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed and we support legal processes to determine this”.
The UK would use the UN general assembly next week to “shine the clearest and harshest spotlight on what is happening and what must change”.

The steps set out by Miliband fall short of the full demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but are a sign the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies, such as Qatar, on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.

Both the US and Israel have threatened retaliation against Britain for the sanctions. The US ambassador to Israel, Mick Huckabee, said the US was considering what action to take, warning it may prohibit the UK from trade with several US states that have anti-BDS (boycott, divestment, sanctions) laws.
Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was “a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation” before the country’s elections in October.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, said: “If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain,” and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, called for the expulsion of the British ambassador.

articles.title: Japan's empty temples seek new ways to survive
articles.summary: With a declining population, shrinking congregations and growing economic pressures, temples are struggling to stay relevant. As more temples are sold or closed, is religion in decline in modern…

image.caption: Centuries-old temples like Odawara are struggling to stay relevant in modern Japan [FILE: October 2026]Image: Alexander Pöschel/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 370-year-old structure has all the attributes of a classically designed Japanese temple, from the curved roof to the timber-frame walls, spacious tatami-mat prayer hall and elaborately decorated altar.

Set in manicured gardens on the Chita Peninsula in central Japan, the 350-square-meter (3,767-square-foot) property is on the market for 482 million yen (€2.66 million). The estate agent's pitch says the price includes dismantling by "expert heritage craftsmen" and delivery to anywhere in Japan, where it would be fully restored into a "stunning" two- or three-bedroom home.
The sale and removal of the temple marks the end of its role in the local community in the hills above the Nagasawacho district, but it is a better fate than many places of worship across Japan.

There are around 77,000 temples across the country, but as many as 17,000 no longer have a full-time resident priest as congregations have shrunk — particularly in rural districts experiencing rapid depopulation — and financial pressures have taken their toll.
That means many temples are being sold off or simply shuttered and left to deteriorate quietly.
A temple brought back to life
Tomomi Iwayama took on the abandoned Ganshu-ji temple in Odawara, a coastal town about 80 kilometers (50 miles) southwest of Tokyo, a decade ago. Today, he is the abbot of a growing congregation.
"The temple had no abbot for 70 years before I arrived because it was just so difficult to operate, and it has taken me until now to get it financially back on track," he told DW.
"Even in a relatively large urban area such as Odawara, which has around 200,000 residents, it has been very hard," he said. "In the countryside, it is much more difficult."

Iwayama's biggest problem is the country's shrinking population: fewer worshippers and falling demand for funerals and other traditional rites make it harder to finance the temple's upkeep. He has worked hard to reach out to the local community and has had success in selling plots in the temple graveyard.

blocks.caption: Odawara Castle was built in the mid-15th century [FILE: March 2018]Image: Koji Sasahara/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: One innovation that has attracted attention is the temple's "smart graveyard," where families scan a card, and a robotic system recovers a relative's ashes from the columbarium.
Temples in rural areas of Japan face far greater challenges, he said.

"Young people in villages usually leave to go to university, and then they find a job in one of the big cities, so they rarely go back," he said. "Maybe they will go back once a year to pay their respects to their ancestors at the village temple, but that is not enough for the temple to get by on."

Equally, when the head priest of a rural temple retires, his children are unlikely to want to take the role on because of these challenges. All too often, Iwayama said, the result is the temple closing.
But he denies the suggestion that religion in Japan is following the same path as in the West, where Christian congregation numbers have plummeted over the decades.
Faith in the Digital Age
Demand for Buddhism remains
"I sense there is still a lot of demand in Japan for Buddhism," he said, contrasting the fast-paced, technology-focused lives that people typically lead with the serenity that they are often seeking.

"Buddhism is a style of living, of an enlightened person," he said. "A lot of people are looking for that. And while the traditional rituals of funerals and anniversaries are declining and that revenue is shrinking, we are finding that more people want to take part in traditional temple cuisine cooking classes, meditation and other things that we can offer."
Temples that are not able to shift to offer experiences more in tune with modern Japan are at risk of closing, said Joey Stockerman, one of the founders of the Mokomoko online real estate service.
"We have had a temple on our site in the past, and we were approached by a foreign potential buyer, so there is certainly interest when these properties become available," he said.

Other foreigners who are long-term residents are doing their best to protect Japan's religious heritage for future generations. American journalist and author Jake Adelstein is currently a Zen priest at Zenshoin Temple in Tokyo's Toshima Ward and is training to become an abbot.

"I do not think that Japanese are becoming less religious; I believe they are becoming fewer because of population decline and they are becoming less wealthy because of the economic situation," he said.
Meet Japan’s AI Buddhist Robot

"Families want to keep the grave plot that they have had for generations, but for many of them it is just too expensive to maintain, and they often live a long way away, so they are unable to regularly visit to pay their respects," he said.
The annual fee for a grave can be up to 100,000 yen, while memorials and other rites can be an additional financial burden, Adesltein explained.
Young people shun religious careers

"Young people are not interested in a career as a priest because temples earn so little money, so there are positions that cannot be filled, and that is especially a problem in the countryside," he said.
Some temples have amalgamated their operations and share a priest, but that will become more difficult in the future, Adelstein said.
As elsewhere, Zenshoin Temple has started vegetarian cooking classes and Zen meditation sessions to appeal to the local community, and Adelstein hopes that will be enough to keep the temple open.
"The training to become an abbot is very tough, and the economics of a temple today often just do not add up, but I see it as a critical part of this society and this nation," he said.
Young people in Japan are leaving large cities

articles.title: Alberta man retraces his steps after traumatic brain injury, waking from coma
articles.summary: When Stan Dworkowski awoke from an eight-day coma with 24 broken ribs and a fractured skull, he could not recall his own age or the faces of his closest friends. He is now retracing his steps, hoping…

image.caption: Business owner Stan Dworkowski was found injured in a ditch not far from his truck-polishing shop in Nisku, Alta., on July 14, 2026. (Stan Dworkowski/Facebook)

blocks.text: Edmonton

When Stan Dworkowski awoke from an eight-day coma with 24 broken ribs and a fractured skull, he could not recall his own age or the faces of his closest friends. He is now retracing his steps, hoping to piece together the hours before he was injured.
Living with amnesia, Stan Dworkowski has turned detective on his own case
Stan Dworkowski is missing time.
When he awoke in an Edmonton hospital room from an eight-day coma with 24 broken ribs and a fractured skull, he could not recall his own age or the faces of his closest friends.
More than a month later, Dworkowski says he still has no memory of the day he was found on July 14 injured, lying in a ditch in an industrial park south of the city.

The 41-year-old man has been conducting his own investigation ever since, attempting to reconstruct the hours before he was found unresponsive along the side of the road near his business in Leduc County, on the western outskirts of Nisku, Alta.
Dworkowski said he was found near an electric dirt bike in the ditch and taken from the scene by paramedics. Weeks after his release from hospital, RCMP are now investigating how he was injured.
“What happened that day and what transpired, from the morning to the night, I don't know, as far as my memory of it.”
Social media search
Dworkowski said he suffered a brain bleed and a cranial fracture that left him with a traumatic brain injury and memory loss.
Along with head trauma and fractured ribs, he said his clavicle, orbital bone and pinky were broken and his shoulder was dislocated.
Dworkowski said he spent a week in the intensive care unit of the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton before transferring to the Glenrose Rehabilitation Hospital, returning home on Aug. 14.
In his search for information, he has published a series of social media posts — sharing photos and videos — in his search for witnesses and tips.

To track his movements on that day, Dworkowski analyzed GPS data from his phone, pored over surveillance footage sourced from surrounding businesses, acquired his medical records and tracked down the man who found him.
He said he wants to “solve the mystery” of what happened to him, hoping that by retracing his steps, something will jog his memory.
He said part of why he’s investigating is that he wonders how he could have been so seriously hurt. He’s gone back to the scene and still doesn’t understand how he ended up in the ditch.

Dworkowski said his colleagues have told him that he was working late inside his truck-polishing shop the night he was injured, and left his business on an electric dirt bike he borrowed from one of his employees.
He said surveillance footage shows him on the bike around 6:30 p.m., entering a property about two kilometres south of his shop, just across the road from where he was found.
He said, at this point, his GPS co-ordinates stop moving until his transfer to hospital.
If I was walking on the other side of the road, I probably would not have found him.- Brock Anderson
Brock Anderson found Dworkowski that evening and called paramedics to the scene.

In an interview with CBC News, the Fort McMurray man said he was staying in a hotel nearby before flying to B.C. for a family vacation. After his wife and kids went to bed around 8:30 p.m., he decided to go on a walk.
First he spotted a sandal. Then he came across Dworkowski, motionless in the tall grass, a few steps away from a dirt bike laying on its side.
“I could tell he was breathing, but he wasn't responsive,” Anderson said.
“It was quiet. The bike wasn't making any sounds. He wasn't making any sounds, so if I was walking on the other side of the road, I probably would not have found him.”
Anderson said he called an ambulance to the scene and left shortly after paramedics arrived.
He thought he would likely never get an update on the man he found but ended up connecting with Dworkowski after his colleague found one of his posts on social media.
Anderson said the pair spoke last week and he told Dworkowski where exactly he had been found and provided him with a video he had taken of the scene.
“He mentioned to me that he might have been laying in the ditch there for hours before I came,” Anderson said. “Obviously he didn't know what happened. There's a big gap.
“To be honest with you, I don't really know what happened.”
RCMP open investigation

In a statement to CBC News, officials with Emergency Health Services Alberta said paramedics responded to the area of 4th Street and 13th Avenue in Nisku at 8:50 p.m. on July 14, where a patient was found in serious, potentially life-threatening condition.
In response to questions about Dworkowski’s case, RCMP said a formal police investigation did not begin until Sept. 5.
RCMP said officers did not initially attend the scene when Dworkowski was found and the incident was not formally reported to them until last week.
Police said the investigation remains in its early stages but they have received no report of a collision or a hit and run at the time and location where Dworkowski was found.

Dworkowski said he met with RCMP after a missing person’s file, created when his family reported him missing that night, was closed. He said he felt his injuries were traumatic enough to warrant further investigation.

He said he called the detachment more than a dozen times to ask for an investigation before the file was formally opened last week. He hopes his own research will help speed along the police investigation.
Long recovery ahead

Dworkowski said doctors have told him it could be months or longer before his memory might improve. He's decided to shut down both his truck-polishing operation and the Hot Wheels collectibles shop he owns, to focus on the long recovery ahead.
He said the ordeal has been most traumatic for his wife and four children, who wrote about his experience on a community fundraising campaign page.
But Dworkowski admitted he has been struggling with the lasting effects of his traumatic brain injury as well as anxiety about the memories he’s missing.
“I need to know what happened so I can heal.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Wallis Snowdon is a journalist with CBC Edmonton focused on bringing stories to the website and the airwaves. Originally from New Brunswick, Wallis has reported in communities across Canada, from Halifax to Fort McMurray. She previously worked as a digital and current affairs producer with CBC Radio in Edmonton. Share your stories with Wallis at wallis.snowdon@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Argentina targets oil company operating in Falklands
articles.summary: The move comes days after President Javier Milei stepped up Argentina's claims of sovereignty over the Falklands.

blocks.text: The Argentine government has said that it would file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands.
The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean.
Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.
The simmering dispute heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the Falklands.
Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.
In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that."
The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty.
He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory.
Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination".
The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering".

Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives.
Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities.
"The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted.

Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development".
Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement.
Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands.

articles.title: Afghanistan's women: A national soccer team without a home
articles.summary: The Afghan women's national football team has finally been officially recognized by FIFA. Now the players want to make history both on and off the field.

image.caption: The Girl Power Summer Camps are a game changer for Afghanistan's women's teamImage: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: On the football pitches of Bundesliga club Wolfsburg, the Afghanistan women's national team is training and doing exactly what is strictly forbidden in their home country: playing football.

In the first session of the day, the coaches' main focus is helping the players get to know each other better and have fun. That's because, as of April of this year, these young women are now officially allowed to play football as the Afghan national team.
FIFA, the world's football federation, has amended its regulations, allowing Afghan women to once again represent their country in official international matches and FIFA competitions.

"This was a huge victory for us, a wonderful moment, and one of the moments we're most proud of. Because once again, the women of our country have made history and brought about change," Khalida Popal told DW. The former captain and founder of the organization Girl Power has been a pioneer for women's football in her country.
Karimi: 'I'm incredibly proud'
Since the Taliban took power in 2021, the players and Popal have fought for the recognition that has now become a reality.
"I'm incredibly proud that we can now officially play as a national team," said midfielder Maryam Karimi.
For Karimi, who has been living in Portugal since fleeing Afghanistan, FIFA's decision is more than just a formality.
"I hope that one day we'll be able to play in Afghanistan again with this team."

blocks.caption: Almut Schult (fourth from the left) coaching the Afghanistan women's teamImage: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Until then, however, Afghanistan remains a national team without a home.
"We'll probably be one of the first national teams in history that has no home and no country in which to play," said Popal. "We'll compete from exile and represent our country."
Today, the players are scattered across the world. Many have traveled from England, Italy, Portugal or Germany, but some have also found refuge in Australia.
"We come from different countries and can't play together regularly. But when I see the players, they're incredibly united. They keep going and push each other forward,” said Karimi.
Gaining More Visibility Through Football

The 39-year-old Popal wants to use her experience to help the players and advance their athletic development. She wants the national team to be known not only for what was taken from them, but also for what it achieves on the field.

"The first goal, of course, is to build a strong team that performs well on the field," said Popal. "Because the better we play, the better we can represent our country, and the more visible we'll become."

But that is precisely where the biggest challenge currently lies. In Afghanistan itself, a regular system for women's football cannot be established at this time. As long as the Taliban are in power, women are not allowed to play sports.

So there is nowhere for young talent to be nurtured; there is no funding and no support from the country the players represent. This is because the Afghan Football Federation — unlike FIFA — does not recognize the women's team. For the time being, therefore, the team's future must be built outside the country.

"We have no federation and no country where talent can develop," said Popal. That is why the team relies heavily on the Afghan diaspora. There, the team is looking for players who may never have played for a club in Afghanistan, but who could represent their parents' country in the future.
Popal: 'The Taliban are erasing women from society'

To organize football camps like these, the women rely on outside support. The summer 2026 camp was made possible by an invitation from Volkswagen and Wolfsburg, but Popal and her organization still have a lot of work ahead of them.

Giving players who have fled Afghanistan a place back in international football is one part of the challenge, but so is creating structures and a foundation on which Afghan women's football can be built.
"It will be a team that stands up to the Taliban. Because the Taliban are erasing women from society,” said Popal.
"We will play football to stand up for the women of our country. When the players take the field, they're also playing for those women in Afghanistan who aren't allowed to."

blocks.caption: Almuth Schult & Khalida Popal talking at Girl Power Summer CampImage: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Just like the former captain, the other young women on the team feel the same way. Midfielder Karimi wants to use football to draw more attention to her friends and all the women in her homeland.
"I can make my voice heard through the way I play football," Karimi said. "I can make my voice heard from the field."
Popal: "These girls are our future”

Despite a long battle for the human rights taken away from women by the Taliban, Popal keeps pushing because she wants to make sure that the women wearing the national team's jersey today are not the last generation to do so.

"I believe that Afghanistan won't stay this way forever. These dark days will pass. These girls will be the next coaches of the Afghan women's national team, the next directors of football academies, the next president, or the next ministers of our country," said Popal.
"And that is exactly why we are investing in these girls: because they are the future.”
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: German police arrest suspect in power grid sabotage case
articles.summary: Investigators say the suspect used homemade rockets and conductive wire to target high-voltage lines in three German states, apparently as part of a campaign against fossil fuels.

image.caption: Police mounted a search after two short circuits in one of the incidents in BrandenburgImage: Frank Hammerschmidt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German police on Tuesday said they had arrested a 48-year-old man suspected of carrying out a series of sabotage attacks on the country's electricity network.
The suspect was reportedly spotted near the Weisweiler power station, close to Aachen in western Germany, after being sought by authorities for several days.
How were the attacks carried out?

Investigators suspect the man of trying to cause short circuits at several locations in the states of North Rhine-Westphalia, Brandenburg and Saxony over the past week, using homemade rockets to fire thin conductive wire across high-voltage power lines.
The method appears to have worked in at least two cases.
In Bergheim, west of Cologne, several units at a power station were put out of operation for several days.
At a substation near the Jänschwalde power station in Brandenburg, more than 20 homemade rockets were allegedly used to fire conductive material onto power lines, causing two short circuits.
However, neither incident resulted in a power outage.
Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid
Last week, armed police located and raided a truck thought to have been used in the attacks.
What was the suspected motive?
Investigators have linked a series of letters claiming responsibility for the attacks to the 48-year-old suspect from Gevelsberg, in the southern Ruhr region.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the letters contained information that could only have been known to the perpetrator.
"The knowledge revealed in these letters is clearly knowledge belonging to the perpetrator," Dobrindt said.
He described the attacks as apparent "climate terrorism" carried out by a lone offender.
In the letters, the suspected attacker reportedly justified targeting the electricity network as part of a campaign against fossil fuels.
"Generating electricity from fossil fuels is a crime," one of the letters said.

Lignite is still mined and used for electricity generation in all three states where the suspected attacks took place. The burning of lignite releases massive amounts of carbon dioxide into the air, a major factor in climate breakdown.

articles.title: Hungary orders 10 Russian diplomats to leave
articles.summary: Budapest says the expulsions are necessary to protect security and sovereignty after years of comparatively close ties between Hungary and Russia.

image.caption: Hungary said the embassy staff's activities were incompatible with their diplomatic statusImage: Aled Betts/cc-by/Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text: Hungary has ordered 10 members of Russia's diplomatic mission to leave the country over activities it said were incompatible with their diplomatic status, Foreign Minister Anita Orban said on Tuesday.
The move marks a significant step by Budapest against Moscow, with Orban saying it was intended to protect Hungary's "security and sovereignty."
Why is Hungary expelling the diplomats?
Orban said a Hungarian Foreign Ministry official had informed the Russian ambassador that the 10 individuals had engaged in activities deemed "unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention."
She did not specify what the individuals were accused of doing.
Hungary's authorities had made the assessment before the government called on them to leave, Orban said.
"This decision protects Hungary's security and sovereignty," she wrote.
Does this mean a break with Russia?
Orban stressed that Hungary was not severing diplomatic relations with Moscow.
"It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia," she said, adding that Budapest intended to maintain "the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules."
Orban has served as Hungary's foreign minister and deputy prime minister since May, following the change of government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar.
The expulsion is nevertheless a notable deterioration in relations with Moscow, particularly given Hungary's previously close relationship with Russia under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

articles.title: Marcos welcomes Norway, South Korea ambassadors
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has welcomed the new ambassadors of Norway and the Republic of Korea to the Philippines during separate ceremonies at Malacañan Palace. Marcos on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has welcomed the new ambassadors of Norway and the Republic of Korea to the Philippines during separate ceremonies at Malacañan Palace.

Marcos on Tuesday first received the credentials of His Excellency Kristian Netland, ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary of the Kingdom of Norway. He underscored the “warm and very productive” relations between the two countries and expressed optimism about exploring new areas of cooperation.
“I think that there are many, many areas that we can continue to pursue and new areas that we can explore and develop,” Marcos told Netland.

“We are happy to count Norway as a friend of the Philippines, and we look forward to all that we will do to strengthen that relationship and to make deeper the engagements between our two countries,” he added.
Netland said the Philippines and Norway have enjoyed many decades of friendship “founded on trust, mutual respect, and a shared commitment to peace, democracy, and international cooperation.”
“Norwegian companies have been present in the Philippines for decades, contributing with expertise, technology, and jobs,” Netland said.

“As both our countries pursue sustainable growth and the green transition, I believe there are substantial opportunities to expand cooperation and create new partnerships that benefit our peoples,” he added.

Marcos also received His Excellency Lee Dong-gy as the new ambassador extraordinary and plenipotentiary of the Republic of Korea. He presented his letters of credence to Marcos in a separate ceremony.
In his brief remarks, Marcos expressed confidence that the Strategic Partnership between the two countries would be further enhanced during Lee’s tenure.

“As we know, the relations between our two countries have been very, very strong and very, very close for many, many years… I look forward to the work that we will do here together in the time you have here in Manila and in the Philippines as Ambassador,” Marcos said.
Lee said the Philippines and South Korea share a longstanding friendship built on “mutual respect, shared values, and close people-to-people ties.”
He added that the partnership between the two nations has continued to expand across the areas of politics, economy, defense and security, law enforcement, and culture.
Moreover, Lee conveyed South Korea’s full support for the Asean Chairmanship of the Philippines and reaffirmed South Korea’s continued engagement with the regional bloc.

“As ambassador, I will devote my utmost efforts to further strengthening this important relationship and to expanding our cooperation in ways that will bring tangible benefits to both our peoples,” he said.
Marcos held separate closed-door meetings with Netland and Lee at the Study Room. /mcm

articles.title: At least two people dead after Russian strikes on Kyiv
articles.summary: Air raid alerts and sounds of explosions rang out in Ukraine's capital as Russian forces launched drone strikes early on Tuesday.

blocks.text: At least two people have been killed after Russia resumed airstrikes on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv early on Tuesday, officials said.
The attack came after both countries agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while US Donald Trump's top envoys visited Moscow and Kyiv.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday he expected the war to continue into the winter, following talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - their first visit to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion.
Air raid alerts warned civilians to seek shelter as Russian forces launched drone strikes on Kyiv early on Tuesday, authorities said.
A series of explosions across Ukraine's capital overnight killed two people and injured ten others, the city's state emergency service said on Telegram.
Residential buildings were hit, according to authorities, including a five-storey apartment block in the Solomianskyi district, while vehicles caught fire in the Podilskyi district.
People sought shelter inside a metro station in Kyiv during the overnight missile attack, something that is routine for residents protecting themselves during the ongoing war.
In Russia, buildings were struck in the city of Saratov during a Ukrainian drone attack, its regional governor Roman Busargin said on Telegram early Tuesday.
The talks with Trump's top envoys on Sunday in Ukraine, which lasted several hours behind closed doors, finished without any major breakthroughs.

Zelensky told reporters they had agreed that officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US.
According to a BBC Verify analysis, Kyiv is suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's invasion in 2022.

articles.title: US-Canada tariff dispute weighs on cross-border ties
articles.summary: As Canada's retaliatory tariffs take effect, Canadian and US car industries fear the trade war will hit them hard, while Canadians are cutting back on travel.

image.caption: The Gordie Howe International Bridge links Windsor, Canada, with Detroit, Michigan. After US President Trump threatened to block its inauguration, it has become symbolic for fraying US-Canadian tiesImage: Dax Melmer/REUTERS

blocks.text: A new suspension bridge connecting the United States to Canada recently opened after more than two decades of planning, but only the Canadians showed up to celebrate.
The Gordie Howe International Bridge spans the Detroit River, connecting Detroit, Michigan with Windsor, Ontario. It is named after a Canadian hockey player who starred for a US team.
"In normal times, that would be a very, very big celebration, a grand event, with leaders of both countries present," Michigan auto industry spokesperson Glenn Stevens Junior told DW.
But these are hardly normal times in US-Canada relations.
'Escalating tariffs will harm workers'

In July, US President Donald Trump announced a 50% tariff on a wide range of goods from Canada. A second Trump announcement days later of the doubling of tariffs on Canadian automobiles and auto parts to 50%triggered even more concern for businesses on both sides of the new bridge.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney countered with tariffs between 15% and 50% on $20 billion (€17.2 billion) worth of goods imported from the US.
US-Canada trade war: The cost of fighting back

The retaliatory measures took effect at 12.01 Eastern Standard Time (05:01 GMT/UST) on Tuesday September 8. Polls by the Canadian non-profit Angus Reid suggested that the majority of Canadians were in favor of a tougher stance in tariffs.
At the same time, Canadian workers feared for their jobs, the polls found.
Business leaders, too, have warned of the harmful effects of the tariffs on the economies of both countries.

"An escalating cycle of tariffs and retaliation will ultimately harm businesses, workers, and consumers on both sides of the border," the Detroit-based Canada and US Business Association (CUSBA) said in a statement in response to the tit-for-tat tariff hikes. "Each new tariff compounds costs, disrupts production, delays investment, and weakens the competitiveness of US and Canadian businesses."
Jobs at stake on both sides of the border
Further north, the Financial Accountability Office of Ontario estimated the new tariff regime will cost 119,000 local jobs in 2026.
Many of these are predicted to be in the auto industry, with Ontario's auto manufacturing output estimated to shrink by 8% in 2026 compared with a no-tariff scenario.

This contraction is expected to be felt on the US side too, especially in Michigan, where more than a fifth of all vehicles produced in the US in 2022 were built, including several well-known household brand names.
The economies of Michigan and Ontario are deeply interconnected, the Detroit Regional Chamber stressed in August.

"Engines that are built in Michigan go into trucks that are built in Ontario, engines that are built in Ontario go into trucks that are built into Michigan," said Glenn Stevens Jr, who is also the chamber's Chief Automotive and Innovation Officer.
Figures show that by 2023, Detroit automakers supported 815,000 indirect jobs through supply chains, as well as 147,000 direct workers across the US.
Detroit's chamber has called for a restoration of "normalcy," defined as a focus on the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, (USMCA, or CUSMA in Canada), due for an annual review.
Tariffs, EV attacks and AI blamed for job cuts
Even before the announcement of Trump's tariffs and Canada's counter-tariffs, Detroit's famous car industry had stalled.
The volume of production for companies was relatively stable as were jobs on and around auto factory lines, Stevens Jr said.
Although this meant there wasn't a significant loss in employment, new job opportunities weren't being created.
Analyzing the number of US car dealership franchise listings for new vehicles is a standard way of tracking auto production.
These listings show vehicle production has generally increased in the past 12 months, but the past 30 days show a significant slowdown.
Data from industry weekly Automotive News has around 33,000 more listed vehicles compared to this time last year, but 70,000 fewer vehicles were listed in the past month.
Can North America launch its own EV revolution?
Beyond the car showrooms, the US auto industry's cautionary approach is apparent.
US auto companies were adjusting business plans even before the latest round of tariff announcements, with business leaders warning of increased US manufacturing costs.
These costs have now been handed down to the consumers, with US shoppers seeing record sales prices of more than $52,000 for new cars in September.

Companies had resisted hiring people or expanding over the past 18 months since tariff talks between Canada and the US had started to intensify, Stevens Jr said, adding to a lack of investment in new designs owing to withdrawn US federal support for electric vehicles.
Is cross-border friendship fraying?
Apart from the auto industry, the tariffs are impacting other sectors.
Across the US, real estate market media in June described a "cooling relationship between the two countries," affecting property transactions, tourism revenue and the local economy.
"Most Canadians think it's unpatriotic ... to visit the United States," Claude Molineri, CEO of Visit Detroit said of the cooling friendship and downturn in tourism.
Earlier this year, Detroit's official visitor site reported that the city had seen an 11% decrease in Canadian guests compared to 2025.
Meanwhile, several "buy Canadian first" online campaigns have been referring users to local businesses and Canadian ingredients in everyday grocery items in response to the tariff enouncements.

The cities of Detroit and Ontario's Windsor/Essex normally facilitate trade worth more than $100 billion each year, which is almost a third of all annual trade between the US and Canada, according to Downtown Detroit Partnership, a group of business and community leaders.
The cooling ties between the two countries could come at a heavy price.
Why Canada rejected Trump's terms despite economic risks

articles.title: New Hampshire and Rhode Island electorate to vote in state primaries - US politics live
articles.summary:
Voters will choose candidates across full slate of federal, state and local offices over next two days

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

New Hampshire and Rhode…

blocks.text: Key events

items: nowTrump says Canada's Bombardier must build jets in US or lose market access
17m agoNew Hampshire and Rhode Island electorate to vote in state primaries

blocks.text: Trump says Canada's Bombardier must build jets in US or lose market access
President Donald Trump said that ⁠Canadian private jet maker Bombardier would ⁠no longer be allowed ​to sell its planes in the United States unless it started manufacturing in the country.
“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
“If ⁠they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank’,” he said.

Trump made the post as a trade dispute between Washington and Ottawa esclates, part of the near-global tariff wall in his second term ⁠that has drawn complaints from many US trading partners. Canada is set to introduce a wave of counter-tariffs against the US on Tuesday.

Bombardier, the Montreal-based rival of US business jet manufacturer Gulfstream Aerospace, has an American workforce of 3,500, and a US footprint of 2,800 suppliers, along with factories and service centers in the country.
The company is now adding its sixth US service center and produces wings for its flagship Global 8000 jet in Texas.
New Hampshire and Rhode Island electorate to vote in state primaries
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
New Hampshire and Rhode Island primary voters will choose candidates across a full slate of federal, state and local offices over the next two days.

In New Hampshire, US senator Jeanne Shaheen’s decision to not seek reelection created a cascade of competitive races, AP reported. Two of the eight Republicans hoping to replace the three-term Democrat are former US senators she previously defeated: John E. Sununu and Scott Brown.
The five-way race for the Democratic nomination includes US representative Chris Pappas, whose departure from his 1st congressional district seat in turn attracted a crowd of candidates.

Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen, is among those seeking the Democratic nomination for Pappas’ seat, along with former candidate Maura Sullivan. Several other candidates in top races also are making repeat appearances.

Meanwhile, in Rhode Island, governor Dan McKee faces a tough Democratic primary challenge tomorrow in his bid for a second full term. Voters will also choose nominees for a full slate of federal, state and local offices.

McKee was elected governor by a wide margin in 2022 after first assuming the role in March 2021 when then-governor Gina Raimondo stepped down to become US commerce secretary. He now is at risk of becoming the nation’s first elected governor since 2014 to lose renomination and the first in Rhode Island since 1994.

His challenger is Helena Buonanno Foulkes, a former longtime executive with Rhode Island-based CVS. She placed a close second behind McKee in the five-way 2022 Democratic primary. She is the niece of former Democratic senator Chris Dodd of Connecticut.
In other developments:

items: President Donald Trump said on Monday that ⁠Canadian private jet maker Bombardier would ⁠no longer be allowed ​to sell its planes in the United States unless it started manufacturing in the country. “NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “If ⁠they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ’piggybank’.”

New York mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to come face-to-face with Rudy Giuliani at the main September 11 memorial service, just days after the former mayor – who led the city at the time of the 2001 terrorist attacks – disparaged his Muslim religion and said he should skip the ceremony. In an interview with right-leaning Newsmax at the weekend, Giuliani said: “Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming.”

A cluster of advocacy groups that boast veteran lawyers, voting experts and ex-judges have expanded legal challenges to Donald Trump’s authoritarian executive orders on voting and other presidential actions they see as a “war” on the rule of law in the US. Heavy legal opposition to Trump’s two executive orders on elections to curb voting rights and supplant the authority of states on election matters has come from the Democracy Defenders Fund, the Campaign Legal Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and kindred groups.

The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently released a report linking “gender ideology” to leftwing authoritarianism and political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted and “nakedly political”, likely leading to greater politicization of science and health. It follows attempts by the administration to limit access to gender-affirming care – including, on Friday, an agreement reached between the Department of Justice and a New York hospital to no longer offer pediatric gender-affirming care.

articles.title: Kenya: Crackdown on foreign traders prompts xenophobia fears
articles.summary: Fears of xenophobia are rising in Kenya after President William Ruto ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as hawkers. The government insists however that legally documented foreign traders…

image.caption: Kenya's government says it wants to crack down on small-business traders from other countries who do not have licenses to operate in the countryImage: picture-alliance/AP Photo/S. Wandera

blocks.text: Kenyan authorities are moving in on some foreign nationals working in the country's informal economy after President William Ruto called for small-scale businesses focused on hawking and petty retail to be primarily reserved for Kenyan citizens.

"We have a bill in parliament [requiring] that there are some trading activities that foreigners can't do in Kenya," he explained, adding that foreign nationals should not come to Kenya to compete with citizens in business settings which need little capital.
The government had announced that the enforcement of this law would begin on Monday, September 7 — and appears to have made good on its pledge.

Ruto framed the latest move as a protection measure for Kenya's economy, highlighting that the focus in the country's economic development should shift to foreign investors who bring capital, create jobs and contribute to local production.

"The investor confidence we have built is for investors, not traders and hawkers. From next week, all traders doing those small businesses should close them," Ruto emphasized, highlighting also that there has been a step increase in informal traders from China in the country.

blocks.caption: For many young Africans, running a small, informal business remains one of the few options to make a livingImage: AP

blocks.text: Mixed reactions to a complex situation
Reactions among Kenyans to these developments have been mixed; some welcomed the crackdown, arguing that foreign traders have been taking away job opportunities in a struggling economy.

"We have been suffering for long. Our jobs are taken," said Nairobi resident James Mwaurah, adding that many Kenyans are unemployed, competing with foreign workers who often are willing to work for lower wages.
"We say thanks to the president for what he has done," Mwaurah added.
Others meanwhile have expressed support for the government's initiative to enforce immigration laws and business regulations, but reject the idea of simply sending foreigners home.
"We accept to have foreigners in our country. Legally, we live with them very peacefully," another local resident, Babu Claudius, told DW on the streets of Nairobi.
In his view, Kenya continues to need foreign workers as well as international business, warning that "chasing them away might scare investors."
Many Kenyans — including Claudius — however seem to agree on one thing: Foreign nationals "have to be here legally."
China, US and EU all want to do business in Africa
There are some 17.4 million people who work in Kenya's informal sector, according to official numbers published in 2024; eight in ten of those workers engage in registered business dealings.
For many people, hawking or running a small shop in the informal economy — with or without papers — remains one of the few accessible ways to make a living — including foreigners in the country.
Kenya's mood ahead of elections

Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang says that there is little evidence suggesting "that if you were to kick out the traders, that would immediately result in Kenyan nationals having more opportunities."
According to Olang, there may be other motivations at play, as the new policy appears to come at a "convenient" moment ahead of elections.

In her view, "a lot of it is also just populist," describing the current crackdown on foreign traders as a "feel good policy" ahead of the polls; she highlights that the policy could also serve as a message to external players at this moment: "Foreign investors coil back or they freeze or they wait until the election is finished."

Olang argues that since Kenya wants to keep making itself more attractive to serious foreign investment, it should rather concentrate on tackling broader structural problems instead of focusing on smalltime foreign traders.
"We need to work on corruption. We need to work on our Ease of Doing Business Index so that it's easy to invest within Kenya," she told DW.
The East African country meanwhile attracted a record $3.2 billion (€2.75 billion) in foreign direct investment in 2025 — an increase of almost 38% compared the previous year, according to UNCTAD.
Ruto remains keen to expand on this success story.

blocks.caption: Youth unemployment remains a major issue across the African continent; in South Africa, these disparities have led to repeated attacks on foreignersImage: Nic Bothma/EPA-EFE

blocks.text: A wider push for local opportunities

One approach in Ruto's arsenal is the proposed Local Content Bill 2025, which is currently before parliament. The draft law would require foreign companies covered by the legislation to source at least 60% of certain goods and services locally.
Among other things, it would require at least 80% of their workforce to be Kenyan citizens.
But according to Olang, the measure would not address the roots of Kenya's unemployment crisis, in particular among the country's discontent youth:

The World Bank estimates the unemployment rate among Kenyans aged between 15 and 24 to stand at 15.25%, though local and regional organizations like the Federation of Kenya Employers often cite a much higher figure of roughly two-thirds of all young Kenyans being affected by unemployed and underemployment.

blocks.caption: There are an estimated 7.41 million micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) operating in KenyaImage: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Who is actually affected by the policy?
The government has not published a comprehensive list of businesses that will be affected by the crackdown, as it remains unclear how many foreign nationals could be impacted by the move.

Meanwhile, Kenya's Foreign Affairs Principal Secretary Abraham Korir Sing'oei emphasized that foreign nationals who meet all existing legal requirements, including holding the necessary work permits and licences, will remain legally protected to operate their businesses in the country.
He said that Ruto's current initiative was direcly linked to the introduction of the Local Content Bill, and should not be regarded as a push to get rid of foreigners in the country.

Questions remain over the broader legality of the developments: Under the East African Community's Common Market rules, citizens of member states have the right to move and provide services across the region — though they have to comply with national licensing and other legal requirements.

The debate has also resulted in comparisons being drawn to recent developments in South Africa, where widespread frustration over a sluggish economy has led to foreign-owned businesses and migrants repeatedly being targeted by anti-immigration campaigns this year.
Kenya has not experienced anti-migrant violence on the scale seen in South Africa — yet.
Immigrants in South Africa pushed out of their own shops

articles.title: Australia targets big tech with algorithm opt-out bill
articles.summary: The "My Feed, My Way," legislation would require the likes of Facebook, TikTok and Instagram to let users opt out of algorithms or risk heavy fines.

image.caption: Platforms that fail to comply could face hefty fines.Image: Jeremy Piper/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Australian government announced planned new rules for social media platforms on Tuesday that would give users greater control over their social media algorithms.
Under the "My Feed, My Way" initiative, social media platforms would have to allow users to opt out of content recommended by an algorithm in their feeds.
What is in Australia's social media algorithm bill?
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese unveiled draft legislation that would impose a "duty of care" on major social media platforms, including Facebook, TikTok, and Instagram.
Users would only see content from accounts they choose to follow.
"It's not about giving government control. It's about giving people control," Albanese said.
The bill is expected to be approved by the Australian Parliament and introduced later this year.
Companies that do not comply could be fined up to AU$100 million ($72 million, €62 million).
Social media bans: What it means for you
Social media bans for children

Anika Wells, Australia's Minister for Communications, said the measure would help ensure children's safety on social media. Australia became the first country to restrict social media access for under-16s in 2025.
Several countries, including Germany, Spain, France, Denmark, and New Zealand, followed Australia's lead and drafted plans to introduce similar age restrictions.
Some big tech companies have opposed such new regulations. They argue it could encourage young users to move to unregulated online spaces.

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv, ending three-day halt for US talks
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine – Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv overnight, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes…

blocks.text: KYIV, Ukraine – Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv overnight, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes on the city.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the pause in attacks as US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals at the weekend.
AFP reporters in the city heard fresh explosions ringing out in the early hours of Tuesday, triggering fires and sending locals down into basements and metro stations for shelter.

“The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on social media.
“His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.”

Witkoff and Kushner’s trips provided no immediate breakthrough in ending the four-and-a-half-year war, but represented Washington’s reengagement with trying to broker a deal between the two sides, which had been on hold for months.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said people were trapped in a residential building after the strikes.
Russia’s army said it had a carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial sites, logistics hubs and storage centres in Kyiv and its suburbs.
Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia’s invasion, according to statistics verified by the United Nations.
In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people.
US proposals

The strikes came hours after Witkoff touted “substantive progress” in the discussions with Ukraine and Russia, raising the prospect of reviving three-way peace talks to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
“President Trump is working hard to stop the killing and work towards a lasting and durable peace,” he said on X.
Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday, before holding separate talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in their first official trip to Kyiv.

The Kremlin announced Monday that it did not rule out three-way talks, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling reporters “it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage”.
Zelensky told US news outlet Axios that the United States was pushing to de-escalate the conflict ahead of the long winter.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since invading in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20C.
Zelensky has said the weekend talks included US proposals around energy facilities, grain shipments and oil and gas exports, but declined to give further details.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Tuesday appeared to rule out a Turkish proposal for a truce on strikes in the Black Sea, saying it was “unrealistic” and “impossible to monitor”.
The two sides appear no close to agreeing on how the war should end.
Moscow is demanding Ukraine cede territory in its eastern Donetsk region that it still controls and renounce Western military support.
Kyiv has said such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a fresh attack in its bid to install a Moscow-friendly puppet government.

articles.title: 3 years on, Morocco earthquake victims still wait for help
articles.summary: On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco, killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction. In the village of…

blocks.text: On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco, killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction.

In the village of Ighermane in the High Atlas Mountains, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Marrakech, Mohamed Ait Belaid, 72, feels like things are actually going pretty well for him three years later.
He had been living in a tent after the earthquake but now resides in a newly built house, even though it’s smaller than the one destroyed in the earthquake.

“I benefited from partial [state] support and received 80,000 dirhams [around €7,300] for rebuilding,” he told DW. “I added about 100,000 [€9,110] dirhams from my own pocket. And thanks to God, I like my new house and I’m comfortable in it. I’m at peace because my wife, my children and I are all healthy and I haven’t lost any of them.”
Around 40 kilometers away, in the town of Azgour, it’s a different story. Larbi Ait Jelloulat, also 72, is sitting in front of a pile of rubble that was once his house.

“I want to know where my rights have gone,” he said angrily. “Who took what’s rightfully mine? For three years, I’ve been going from one department to another, from one complaint to another, from one petition to another, just looking for an answer. Why have I been excluded? Am I not a Moroccan citizen?”

Ait Jelloulat was formerly a council employee and saved for years in order to build the large home that was destroyed in the 2023 earthquake. As far as he can tell, bureaucratic issues mean he must prove he was a resident in the area.
“My only dream was to spend the rest of my life in my own home, a rest after years of service,” he explained. “Now they say I’m not a resident … Where’s the logic in that?”

blocks.caption: Larbi Ait Jelloulat sits on the rubble of his home in Azgour; he’s been fighting to get state help but has been unsuccessful so far Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: Why such different experiences?

Reconstruction seems to be happening faster in Ighermane, the village where Ait Belaid lives. About 90% of the village is rebuilt and most residents’ lives are back to normal, said Omar Saeed from the Ighermane Association for Development and Solidarity.
Of the village’s around 150 families, 114 received state support of some kind, although most also had to contribute some of their own money to rebuild.
Meanwhile, in Azgour, where Ait Jelloulat lives, there’s been more to do. Azgour was the village most impacted by the earthquake in the area.

There, about 76 families have had help with reconstruction, Ait Jelloulat said, while 56 others are still waiting for help. “What’s more, the 76 families who rebuilt their homes in a different location are also having problems connecting to water and electricity,” he added.

blocks.caption: Azgour village was among those hit hardest by the 2023 earthquake, and reconstruction is still ongoing Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: Rebuilding difficult in remote mountain villages

According to a March statement from the High Atlas Development Agency, or ADHA, which was established in October 2023 to bring help to affected areas, 54,425 homes have been built or rehabilitated and more than 3,000 homes are still under construction. The government has given out more than 7.2 billion dirhams (€656 million/$770 million) to affected families. The sum includes funds to help rebuild as well as monthly emergency aid payments.

In terms of the pace of construction, Marrakech-based architect Mohamed Belmejjad believes the state is actually doing fairly well. “I believe the progress so far, relative to the timeframe, to be positive,” he told DW.
Given the circumstances, it would be hard for things to have gone much faster, he suggested.
Immediately after the earthquake, it was difficult to reach affected locations, especially remote mountain villages and towns. Then rubble had to be cleared before building could begin.

After that, other factors complicated reconstruction, including the distance of some villages from paved roads, the difficulty of transporting building materials in and debris out, problems with connecting water and power, and the need to relocate whole villages and construction sites to avoid dangers like landslides. There’s also a need to respect local building traditions, ensuring that construction materials are solid and will last.

“We also lack the necessary expertise here, whether that’s in terms of architects, design offices, contractors or even the labor required for construction,” Belmejjad pointed out. Given all that has happened reconstruction could actually be considered ahead of schedule, he suggested.
‘No one has remembered us’
Despite that, the National Coordination for Al Haouz Earthquake Victims reports receiving complaints from more than 3,000 families who haven’t had any state help.

Montasser Itri, a member of the organization, explains that some of these families were excluded because they had moved to other parts of the country to work and their national identity cards then show them as residents of places unaffected by the 2023 earthquake.

“The government is trying to make us, the victims of the Al Haouz earthquake, into mere statistics linked to the progress of construction and the removal of tents,” Itri told DW, “rather than treating us as human beings and with dignity.”

blocks.caption: In Amizmiz, local woman Fawzia Aliban is worried her house might collapse before she gets any help Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: That’s why the coordinating committee is already demanding an independent and transparent investigation into how local authorities have handled the payouts. In the past they’ve organized demonstrations outside parliament buildings in the capital, Rabat, to demand compensation and rehousing solutions and to accuse local authorities of failing to honor commitments.
Other impacted locals are hoping the upcoming general election, slated for September 23, might make a difference.

“[Prime Minister Aziz] Akhannouch promised us a solution to the issue and God knows we are waiting,” said Fawzia Aliban, whose home in Amizmiz was damaged in the earthquake. “We hope the problems will be resolved because I was denied benefits even though my house is on the verge of collapse.”

“Three years have passed, and no one has remembered us […] but recently some political figures turned up and promised to solve the problem,” added Mohamed Belkaid, who is still living in a tent in the Amizmiz area with his four children.
He hasn’t received any aid to rebuild because he is listed as a tenant, not an owner, and is not optimistic things will change.

blocks.caption: Mohamed Belkaid has lived in this tent with his family since the 2023 earthquake Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: “They promised to review our files, asking us to trust them and to vote for them,” he complained. “But this is exploitation. If they truly wanted to solve the problem, they would have done so before the elections. Where have they been all these years?” /dl

articles.title: Why thousands are paying to watch people play Dungeons & Dragons live
articles.summary: The growing world of "actual play" is taking tabletop role-playing games from living rooms and online streaming to sold-out theatres. Performers and scholars say its appeal lies in the…

image.caption: Brennan Lee Mulligan is set to bring his Endless Dungeon actual-play show to Vancouver's Queen Elizabeth Theatre for a sold-out performance on Sept. 10. (Leo Montero/@truffleimages)

blocks.text: There is no script, no fixed ending and no guarantee the heroes will make it out alive.
Onstage, performers build a fantasy world together while dice rolls and split-second choices can send the story to places nobody planned.

On Sept. 10, nearly 2,800 people will fill Vancouver's Queen Elizabeth Theatre for a sold-out performance of Endless Dungeon, led by comedian and game master Brennan Lee Mulligan. The Vancouver date follows a sold-out May performance at Toronto's Coca-Cola Coliseum.

Endless Dungeon is part of the growing world of "actual play" — tabletop role-playing games performed for an audience — a genre combining improvisational theatre, collaborative storytelling and game mechanics, with dice helping determine whether characters succeed or fail.
For performers and scholars, the appeal lies in uncertainty, intimacy and collaboration — and in knowing that no two performances will be exactly alike.
Mulligan told CBC News that part of the attraction is simply "the joy of live theatre."
"It's happening in front of your face," he said, adding that the audience reactions become part of the draw. "You are there, your gasps, your laughs, your groans at a bad D&D pun."
Why live D&D is drawing thousands — and changing who gets seen
A roller coaster with no track
The term "actual play" is recent, but the practice is a longstanding one according to Emily Friedman, a professor of English at Alabama's Auburn University who studies the format.

Online shows such as Critical Role, Mulligan's Dimension 20 and The Adventure Zone helped bring actual play into the mainstream. Live performances are often self-contained, with clearer character goals and story beats designed to reach an ending in a few hours. That makes the action "heightened and brightened and made sharper and quicker and faster," Friedman said.
She compared its appeal to being on a roller coaster where "the track is being laid in front of you at high speed."
Vancouver comedian Jess Lupini, who is joining Endless Dungeon for this stop, compared it to another form of unscripted entertainment.
"Watching actual plays is exciting in many of the same ways that watching hockey is exciting," she said. "You don't know what's going to happen."
'The feeling of being in the room'
But that unpredictable nature only partly explains why people pay to see a format they can watch online.
Abdul Aziz, a Vancouver comedian joining Mulligan for this Endless Dungeon performance, says the attraction is "probably the feeling of being in the room."
