Aziz also performs on the actual-play podcast Spout Lore, which has tried to preserve the atmosphere of friends playing together even as those conversations became entertainment for strangers.
"We sort of are more focused on each other while playing than we are focused on the audience," Aziz said.

items: Level up your next Dungeons and Dragons adventure with these creative makers
Tabletop role-playing games can be intimidating. Here's one anyone can jump into

blocks.text: Friedman says audiences are watching two things at once: fictional characters and the real people creating them reacting genuinely when another player's choice surprises them.
Mulligan says performers have to make the audience feel included without sacrificing their connection to one another.

"The best part of live theatre is the preservation of authentic connection between performers and feeling totally invisible as an audience member, even as everything has been arranged to include you," he said.
"Whatever you do to delight your players will delight the audience."
A place to imagine differently
For Aziz, fantasy also offers room to question rules that can seem fixed in the real world.
Aziz, whose parents are from Egypt and who immigrated to Canada as a child, says growing up in a mainly white community gave him an outsider's perspective on cultural conventions.

items: How a Dungeons and Dragons club became a 'lifesaver' for a group of neurodivergent Ontario youth
From 'satanic panic' to church-approved, Dungeons & Dragons thriving after 50-plus years

blocks.text: That carried into Spout Lore. While building his barbarian character's homeland, Aziz drew heavily on Middle Eastern cultures.
"In a very literal sense, the outsider's perspective was immediately useful in our show," he said.
For Lupini, who is also a recurring cast member on BlackwaterDnD, an actual-play show streamed on YouTube and Twitch, taking on different characters became a way to explore herself.
Lupini, who is transgender, says tabletop role-playing games give people a chance to try on different identities, pronouns and personalities.
Before transitioning, she played characters who used she/her pronouns.
"That was really liberating and felt like a safe way of exploring a piece of myself that I had been conditioned to be really afraid of exploring," she said.

items: These girls are learning to master Dungeons and Dragons
The rise of Critical Role: How a crew of 'nerdy-ass voice actors' became Dungeons & Dragons rock stars

blocks.text: Friedman says women, gender-nonconforming people, 2SLGBTQ+ people and disabled people have always been part of tabletop gaming as players and creators, but were not always visible in traditional gaming spaces.
"It's just the shift of the spotlight in a lot of ways," she said.
Mulligan agrees, saying actual play didn't create those experiences, but made them easier to see.
"Actual play provided visibility for a reality that was always there," he said.
A safe place to play
That kind of exploration depends on trust, says Em Carlson, CEO and creative director of BlackwaterDnD and another performer joining Vancouver's Endless Dungeon.
Carlson, whose professional background is in mental-health therapy, says the group does extensive preparation around safety and collaboration and notes that "play can't happen if you're not safe."

Tabletop role-playing culture still hasn't fully achieved its ideals of inclusion, Carlson says, but the stories reaching audiences have broadened as people want stories that help them feel included in the narrative.
"They can be a part of that joy that the players experience at the table."
For Carlson, Endless Dungeon offers something increasingly uncommon in an era of endlessly replayable media: a story created once, for the people present.
"It's a one-night experience where a fantastic, amazing audience gets to come in and laugh with us and cry with us and feel big feelings and cheer."

articles.title: Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
articles.summary: A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people. Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and…

blocks.text: A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people.

Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and development, recently called for a national political debate on administrative reform. He proposed creating 12 to 15 new provinces or setting up 160 empowered district governments to improve governance and the delivery of public services.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who first raised the idea of an administrative “reset” in July, said on Saturday that any new administrative units should be created with public support.
Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, meanwhile, has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots.
Despite the growing calls to create new provinces, no formal decision has been taken.
Even within the ruling coalition, there is disagreement over how and when such reforms should be pursued.
There are also questions about whether creating smaller provinces improves governance, or whether devolving power directly to local governments would be more effective.
More provinces, better governance?
Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether creating more provinces is the solution.

“Smaller provinces are not a substitute for empowered local governments. Even with smaller provinces, you will still need empowered local governments to make the system effective and improve service delivery to the people,” Miftah Ismail, a former finance minister and economist, told DW.
Supporters of creating more provinces argue that Pakistan’s four existing provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan — have become too large and overly centralized.
Iqbal, the planning minister, has argued that the existing system has not delivered adequate improvements in health, education, and other social services.
Interior Minister Naqvi, on the other hand, has called for an administrative structure that is better suited to Pakistan’s growing population.
But there is disagreement over the solution.

“Without effective local governments, whether there is one province or 25, decision-making will remain centralized at the provincial level,” Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank, told DW.

He said any proposal for new provinces or administrative units should be assessed against potential improvements in local tax collection and the costs of creating new provincial institutions, including secretariats, assemblies, and bureaucracies.
Suleri stressed that it should also be examined whether such changes would deliver justice and public services more effectively.
Altering the political balance

“Pakistan’s history suggests that empowering local governments is a better choice in terms of governance and provision of services,” Muhammad Shoaib, a political scientist and assistant professor at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, told DW.
The debate, therefore, is not simply about how many provinces Pakistan should have, but whether creating smaller units would actually make the government more responsive to citizens.
Creating new provinces could also affect the political balance in the country.
New provinces would mean new governments and assemblies, while potentially changing political representation and the distribution of federal resources.
Any attempt to redraw boundaries could also reopen disputes over water, taxation, and natural resources.

The political resistance has already begun, with Sindh’s provincial assembly has opposed creating new provinces or administrative units in the province, while political groups have warned against dividing existing territories.
A risky strategy?
Shoaib said dividing resources would present a major challenge, even if all provinces were reorganized at the same time.
“Even if all provinces are divided simultaneously, the division of resources like finances, water, and jobs, and special privileges for territories within provinces will be a challenge,” he said.
“Challenges like these require lengthy negotiations and compromises for political consensus,” he added.
The issue is therefore not only about administrative efficiency, as redrawing provincial boundaries could also redistribute political and economic power.
Ismail believes redrawing provincial boundaries would be risky, particularly in Sindh.
He said empowering existing local governments within current provincial boundaries would be a safer option.

“We can learn from the US and the southern states of India, where empowered small administrative units, while competing with each other, are more responsive to citizens and deliver better services,” Ismail said.

Shoaib said Pakistan could also learn from other countries, particularly democratic systems that have empowered local governments and taken time to work through the division of large states into smaller units.
“In Pakistan’s case, the risk of resistance and perpetual resentment is real. A partially finished division will aggravate existing ethnic tensions,” he said.
For Pakistan, the debate is therefore about more than whether the country should have four provinces or 12 or 15.

It is about whether changing the administrative map can actually bring power, resources, and accountability closer to its people, and whether such a transformation can be achieved without creating new political and ethnic tensions. /dl

articles.title: PISA test reveals alarming drop in reading and math skills
articles.summary: The 2025 results from the influential global study show a downward trend in students' performance. Germany's 15-year-olds are faring worse than ever.

image.caption: 760,000 students in 91 countries and economies worldwide took the testImage: Armin Weigel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The results of the 2025 PISA study, published on September 8, show a dramatic drop in performance in reading and mathematics around the world.

The Program for International Student Assessment, better known as PISA, is a global study that measures how well 15-year-old students can apply their knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations. The test is designed to measure problem-solving skills rather than evaluate students on memorized school facts, which means they cannot revise in preparation for it.
First administered in 2000, it is considered the world's most influential measure of educational performance.
In 2025, more than 760,000 students in 91 countries and economies took the test.

The study always includes in its ranking the average of the international group of 38 advanced, high-income countries that are part of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD.
Downward trend in students' performances
Between 2015 and 2025, reading skills have seen the most significant decline, decreasing by 28 points in OECD countries, and by 16 points in the other participating countries and economies.
Scores in math have dropped by 22 points across the OECD on average, compared to a decline of 8 points in the rest of the world.
In science, the focus of the 2025 PISA assessment, a seven-point decline was measured in OECD countries, while the performances in other countries and economies remained broadly stable.
Nearly a third of OECD students considered 'low performers'
The latest PISA study reveals that around 29% of 15-year-olds in OECD countries are now estimated to be "low performers" across all three subjects.
What does this mean?

In science, they struggle to interpret simple data or decipher a graph. In reading, they find it hard to find information in simple texts. In mathematics, they might be unable to understand, for example, the relationship between units and price — basic skills needed for grocery shopping.
Drop in global reading scores most concerning
Across the OECD, reading scores fell by 25 score points on average.
The study points out that 20 score points are about equivalent to a year of learning. This implies that most 15-year-old students were performing at the level typically expected of 14-year-olds.
Among the OECD countries, the drops were most extreme in Iceland and Slovenia, with scores going down by more than 50 points.

Reading scores improved in five countries only: Qatar (up 11 points), Brunei Darussalam (18), Cambodia (26), the Philippines (27) and Zambia (50). Even though these education systems are still below the OECD average, they "deserve recognition for achieving measurable gains despite the broader global decline," notes the study.

blocks.caption: Zambia has made remarkable progress in its education systemImage: Emica Elvedji/PIXSELL/picture alliance

blocks.text: Not all schools are equal in Germany
In some countries, such as Iceland, Cambodia and Finland, for example, there is very little variation in performance among schools, showing less than 10% overall variation in student achievement.
But in 10 countries, including Germany, differences among schools account for at least 50% of the total variation in performance.

The study notes that these countries' systems presumably have schools reserved for higher-achieving students, leaving disproportionately large numbers of lower-achieving students enrolled in the other institutions.

For the authors of the PISA study presentation, this is a problem that needs to be taken seriously: "Where such academic segmentation compounds with social background, it can amplify inequalities, producing pockets of excellence while failing to ensure consistent learning outcomes across the education system as a whole."
Germany's PISA shocks
The very first PISA study was held in the year 2000. As one of the 31 participating countries, Germany was shocked to discover that its 15-year-olds scored below the international average.
In the last PISA test, held in 2022 and published in 2023, the scores of German students had dropped to a new low.
In the latest study, scores have plunged even deeper.
Between 2022 and 2025, reading scores plummeted by 15 points and math scores by 11 points, while science scores have gone down by seven.

The top six rankings in reading skills are held by Asian countries. Germany barely remains above the OECD average, coming in 24th. The United States comes in 13th position, Poland ranks 14th and Turkey 18th.
In math, Germany is below the OECD average, coming in 26th, just a rank above the United States. All top seven positions are held by Asian countries, followed by Estonia in the 8th spot.

In science, Germany is only two score points above the OECD average, ranking 23rd. Turkey made important progress in this field, now ranking 19th, with an increase of 18 score points since the 2022 study.

blocks.caption: The PISA study also asked about students' boredom in class and their use of AI in schoolworkImage: Armin Weigel/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why is educational performance falling globally overall?

The data itself cannot explain the decline in reading skills, but the authors of the study note that while school closures due to COVID-19 may be one factor, there is no direct relationship between how long schools closed during the pandemic and the students' performances in reading.
There was already a downward trend in many countries long before the pandemic struck, the study notes.

These long-term declines in skills "suggest deeper structural issues within education systems, with challenges at the school and system level," according to the study. These challenges include the impact of digital distractions on students and growing disinterest towards reading books.

blocks.caption: Cell phones and social media have an impact on the popularity of reading booksImage: Disobeyartphotograph/Dreamstime/IMAGO

blocks.text: AI has had an immediate impact on learning. The 2025 PISA study asked students about their use of AI in schoolwork; more than 40% said they used it to draft texts for writing assignments once or twice a week, or even every day. Students who reported using AI chatbots got lower scores in science, on average, than those who didn't use AI.

"Overall, the data suggests weaknesses in how education systems are adapting to social, technological and economic change," states the study's summary. "Looking ahead, the challenge for policymakers is not simply recovering lost ground, but to ensure schools meet the rapidly changing demands of the world. As PISA shows, it is not an easy task."

While waiting for policymakers to react, the study suggests that parents can contribute to children's potential by being supportive and curious about their studies and helping them develop positive attitudes towards school. "Even something as simple as asking children what they learned or did at school, about once a week or more, is associated with an average 26-point increase in science performance, after accounting for socio-economic status."

articles.title: Avalanche kills 11 climbers in southern Russia – rescuers
articles.summary: MOSCOW — An avalanche on one of Russia’s highest mountains has killed 11 climbers and left six others missing, rescue services said Monday. Rescuers received reports of the avalanche on…

blocks.text: MOSCOW — An avalanche on one of Russia’s highest mountains has killed 11 climbers and left six others missing, rescue services said Monday.
Rescuers received reports of the avalanche on Mount Mizhirgi, around 5,000 meters (16,400 ft) tall, at around 5 pm (1400 GMT) on Sunday.
Unverified video on social media showed what appeared to be a mound of snow and ice crashing down a mountainside in the area, as people in the background could be heard swearing.
“Tragically, 11 people were killed. The fate of six climbers remains unknown,” the local branch of Russia’s emergency ministry said in a statement.
“Search and rescue operations are being complicated by difficult terrain and the risk of avalanches,” it added.
A group of 33 climbers were in the area at the time.
Ten managed to evacuate on their own, while six had to be transported out by rescue services, according to the local branch of Russia’s emergency ministry.
Prosecutors have opened a case into criminal negligence.
Mount Mizhirgi, near the Georgian border, is Russia’s eighth-tallest mountain.
Surrounded by pristine forest and glaciers, the area is popular with hikers. /dl

articles.title: Threatening letters revive fears among Kashmiri Pandits
articles.summary: A new wave of threatening letters targeting Kashmiri Pandits has deepened fears among those who have returned to the region as civil servants under an Indian government federal rehabilitation scheme.…

blocks.text: A new wave of threatening letters targeting Kashmiri Pandits has deepened fears among those who have returned to the region as civil servants under an Indian government federal rehabilitation scheme. Kashmiri Pandits are members of the Hindu minority community who fled the Muslim-majority Kashmir Valley during a militant uprising in the 1990s.
The latest letters, which surfaced in the last week of August, named several employees. The letters also included their addresses, vehicle registration numbers and phone numbers.
Personal details exposed

“Similar threat letters surfaced in early August, but the latest contains our Jammu residential address, vehicle and phone numbers, which have also been shared on social media,” Anil Koul, a government employee, told DW, urging authorities to investigate the source of the leak.

The letters have been attributed to a little-known group calling itself the United Liberation Council, which security officials suspect could be a front for the Pakistan-based Islamist militant outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba.

The group reportedly first surfaced in July, when it released a poster marking the death anniversary of a former militant commander. Authorities have yet to confirm the letters’ authenticity or the existence of the group behind them.

The latest letters also distinguish between Pandits who never left the Valley — and are therefore “safe” — and those recruited under New Delhi’s rehabilitation program, who are accused of working for “masters” outside Kashmir.
The fresh threats have also triggered a political row.

Jammu and Kashmir National Conference (JKNC) president and former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, called them a “conspiracy” aimed at delaying the restoration of statehood, which the region lost in 2019.
Abdullah also questioned why Hindu officers from outside the region were not facing similar threats.
His remarks drew sharp criticism from Kashmiri Pandit groups and the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused him of being insensitive to the community’s fears.
Familiar fears
Government records show 44,167 Kashmiri migrant families registered as having left since 1990 citing security concerns, of which 39,782 were Hindu.
For Pandit community representatives, however, the latest threats are part of a much longer security problem.

Sanjay Tickoo, president of the Kashmiri Pandit Struggle Committee (KPSS), said the threats should be viewed against the backdrop of targeted killings and repeated security concerns faced by Pandit government employees in the Valley. He blames security lapses and says repeated meetings with officials since a wave of killings in 2022 have failed to resolve their concerns.
“Since 2022, meetings have resulted in nothing,” Tickoo told DW.
He also wondered how those making the threats have access to employees’ personal details.
“How are these details being posted on social media?” Tickoo asked.
Targeted killings have occurred sporadically in the years since. At least seven Kashmiri Pandits were killed by militants during a spike in violence between 2020 and 2022.
One of the starkest cases was that of Rahul Bhat, a Pandit revenue official who was shot dead inside his government office in Budgam in May 2022.
The last confirmed targeted killing of a Kashmiri Pandit was in October 2022, when Puran Krishan Bhat, an orchard farmer, was shot dead in Shopian district.
Former Jammu and Kashmir police chief S P Vaid described the latest threats as part of a familiar militant playbook.
“There is nothing new in this,” Vaid told DW, calling it “a ploy by Pakistan to Islamize society.”
He said similar tactics had been used against migrant workers in the Valley.

The difference, this time, is the precision of the threats. Personal data that should not have been easily accessible has been made public, and no clear explanation of how it was leaked has been provided.
The return dilemma

The KPSS estimates roughly 6,500 Pandits who never left the Valley, along with another 4,000 who have returned as government employees under a federal rehabilitation scheme, live in India-administered Kashmir.
But the reintegration of those who fled decades ago has proved challenging.
Rahul Pandita, a journalist and author of “Our Moon Has Blood Clots: A Memoir of a Lost Home in Kashmir,” said the government’s record on rehabilitation was inadequate.

“The BJP has had no rehabilitation policy for Kashmiri Hindus,” Pandita told DW, arguing that the government employees in the Valley had returned under a policy introduced during the previous government of former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh.
Some land has been returned and cases of killings have been investigated, he said, but “it is too little and too late.”
Pandita said the bigger problem was that no government could guarantee a completely secure environment for a mass return.

“No matter what the government does, the situation will never be conducive enough for the Pandits to return,” he said, arguing that as long as Islamist militancy exists in the region, Kashmiri Hindus would still be targeted.
“It’s for them then to decide if they are willing to take such a risk,” he said.
Beyond government employees, some Pandits who have returned and established businesses in the Valley are already living there quietly, Pandita said.
“That is the best-case scenario for Kashmiri Pandits in Kashmir Valley,” he said.

blocks.caption: Pandits accuse the government in New Delhi of not doing enough to protect them from alleged Islamist threats Image: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Security beyond protection
Sushobha Barve, executive secretary of the Center for Dialogue and Reconciliation, said the latest threats expose a wider security paradox.
“Despite claims of normalcy, a tiny group of active militants has successfully disrupted the lives of migrant families. Breaking the cycle of panic is essential,” Barve told DW.
She said there was also growing political frustration over the delay in restoring Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood, arguing that this grievance cut across the region.

Amitabh Mattoo, an academic and professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University who has written extensively on Kashmir, said any return of Kashmiri Pandits had to be both secure and dignified.

“The state has an essential role in ensuring their physical security and in protecting their property, cultural and other legitimate rights. But security measures alone will not suffice,” Mattoo told DW.
“A sustainable return will also require patient reconciliation, engagement with local civil society, and the gradual rebuilding of inter-community trust and social and economic ties.” /dl

articles.title: Pupils return to West Bank school behind barbed wire to protect against settlers
articles.summary: Six people, including three pupils at the Palestinian school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of Israeli settler-related violence.

blocks.text: A school in the occupied West Bank has been surrounded by barbed-wire fencing as Palestinian parents fear for their children's safety due to the rise of Israeli settler attacks in the area.

The isolated village of al-Mughayyir, north-east of Ramallah, has been increasingly surrounded by Jewish settler outposts, and regularly blocked by Israeli forces who frequently operate an ad-hoc checkpoint at the entrance.

Six people, including three pupils at the school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of settler-related violence against Palestinians. One of them, 14-year-old Aws al-Naasan, was shot dead by a settler outside the school gates in April.

All Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. Many of the small ad-hoc settler outposts that have mushroomed around al-Mughayyir are illegal under Israeli law too.

articles.title: Elversberg: Bundesliga newcomers from tiny town make waves
articles.summary: A team from a small southwestern German town of just 7,000 inhabitants made history by sealing promotion to become the 59th club to play in the Bundesliga. Elversberg has got off to a memorable start.

image.caption: Elversberg have got off to a dream Bundesliga start, with two wins from twoImage: Thilo Schmuelgen/REUTERS

blocks.text: How are Elversberg doing in the Bundesliga?

So far, remarkably well. The smallest town ever to be represented in the top flight got off to a dream start on the Bundesliga's opening weekend, racing in to a 3-0 lead against 2024 champions Bayer Leverkusen. In the end, they held off a late surge to claim a 3-2 victory.

A trip to Borussia Mönchegladbach on matchday two looked to have brought them back down to earth, with the hosts leading 3-1 with little over 30 minutes to play. But a sensational comeback was crowned by a Maurice Krattenmacher winner in injury time. The win moved Elversberg above champions Bayern Munich as one of only four sides to have won both their opening two matches, but Krattenmacher was trying to keep some perspective.
"We know every opponent is good in the Bundesliga, but Bayern is on another level entirely. We’ll have to play as a team, and then we’ll see how it goes," he said.
Where is Elversberg?
Elversberg is a small town northeast of Saarbrücken in the small state of Saarland, in southwestern Germany.
As part of Spiesen-Elversberg, the town has a population of around 13,000 but Elversberg alone has just 7,000 people living in it. There is no train station and just three bakeries.
What is Elversberg's back story?
The club was formed in 1907, although folded during World War I before reforming in 1918.

In 2013, the club reached the third division alongside RB Leipzig, but they were promptly relegated. After two playoff defeats in 2016 and 2017, the club finally returned to the third division in 2022 and slowly began to gain a greater reputation.
The club's surge coincided with the appointment of Nils-Ole Book in 2017 and head coach Horst Steffen, a former Bundesliga player, a year later.

Book first joined as a scout before becoming sporting director, where he played a key role in recruitment. Steffen secured back-to-back promotions for the club as they reached the second division in 2023 as a newly-promoted side in the third division.

Germany and Newcastle striker Nick Woltemade played a key role in the club's promotion that year before moving on, and Bayern Munich's Paul Wanner enjoyed a successful loan spell at the club a year later.

In just their second season in the second division (2024-25), Elversberg were in the promotion playoff. But a 95th minute winner from Heidenheim broke their hearts, as they missed out on the top flight. Steffen left for Werder Bremen, star player Fisnik Asllani returned to Hoffenheim and five other key players departed. Not only did it look like the chance had gone, but the club looked more likely to battle against relegation the following season.
How did Elversberg reach the Bundesliga?

Aided by continuity at leading levels of the club, Elversberg found a way to turn a desperate situation into a remarkable one. What proved particularly helpful was having the father-son duo of Frank Holzer, chairman of the supervisory board, and Dominik, the president, leading the way and also calling the shots at main sponsor Ursapharm.

The appointment of head coach Vincent Wagner from Hoffenheim's reserve team was understated, but Wagner did not change much from Steffen's approach. Aided by former Bundesliga legend Mike Frantz, the assistant coach, and team manager Selina Wagner, who won a Champions League with Wolfsburg, the unit off the field appeared as united as the one forming on it.

The departure of star striker Younes Ebnoutalib to Frankfurt during the transfer window and sporting director Book to Borussia Dortmund in March didn't derail the club's promotion ambitions. After losing to relegation battlers Fortuna Düsseldorf in the penultimate game of the season, promotion hopes were wobbling once again. But a win on the final day was enough to keep their spot in second thanks to a superior goal difference. The Bundesliga had been reached.
"A friend of mine told me this week: 'If Elversberg get promoted, then it's like flying to the moon.' Well, today we made it to the moon," Wagner said afterwards.

blocks.caption: Two of the key figures in Elversberg's rise are former head coach Horst Steffen (left) and former sporting director Nils-Ole Book (right)Image: Steven Mohr/Jan Huebner/IMAGO

blocks.text: Where do Elversberg play?

At the Waldstadion an der Kaiserlinde, which has a capacity of 10,000 — more than the population of the town. Construction to reach Bundesliga requirements —15,000 capacity — is reportedly not expected to be finished until 2027, though Elversberg have already been granted an exemption to that rule.
Who are the key figures at Elversberg?
The strength of this team appears to be the collective, and the continuity in leadership positions, rather than one or two individuals.

On the field though, Bambase Conte was signed on loan from Hoffenheim and the attacking midfielder was integral to the club's promotion push. Long-standing goalkeeper Nicolas Kristof enjoyed a strong campaign, as did winger Lukas Petkov who pitched in with 13 goals and seven assists. Striker David Mokwa was bought in January for just €1.5 million, but aided the team down the stretch last term before scoring in the club's first two Bundesliga games.

The squad's average age is 25.3, making it one of the younger squads in the second division. Having reportedly made €10 million from transfers and spent just €3 million on new arrivals, it's clear what this team's approach is. But this summer, it will be intriguing to see how the club approaches the transfer market as it looks to build a squad capable of staying in the Bundesliga.
This article was updated on September 9, 2026 to reflect Elversberg's strong start to the new Bundesliga season.

articles.title: Female footballers offered egg freezing but doubts remain
articles.summary: Spain's football federation are set to join a handful of clubs in paying for female players to freeze their eggs during their careers. While players have pushed for the move, there are welfare…

image.caption: Alexia Putellas was reportedly a key figure in urging the Spanish FA to pay for egg freezingImage: Action Foto Sport/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Balancing motherhood and work is a challenge in any profession. But for footballers, whose peak sporting years coincide with their peak fertility, the choice can feel stark.

"For a woman whose sports career might last, say, 10 years at a high level, she starts thinking that getting pregnant really isn't an option," former Real Sociedad player, Larraitz Lucas, told DW. "When you are competing at a high level, all you are focusing on is the present."

Until the last few years, only about 2% of footballers got pregnant during their careers, with many leaving the sport to pursue motherhood. But with increasing professionalization, organizations are starting to wrestle with the question of how to deal with players who want to have children.

Binding maternity regulations were introduced to the sport only in 2021 and strengthened in 2024. But for those who wish to postpone their pregnancy while playing, the issue of freezing eggs as a fertility treatment has come to the fore.

US club, Racing Louisville, were the first club side to offer to pay for such treatments in 2021, while English club Chelsea have announced this month that egg freezing will be funded for any player that wants it.

But, perhaps more significantly, the Spanish football federation, RFEF, are expected to become the first national federation to announce a similar policy soon after reported lobbying from star player Alexia Putellas and others.
Playing during egg extraction a tough ask

Such options weren't available to Spaniard Lucas in her playing career, which ended more than a decade ago. While she went through egg retrieval, in her case it was so her partner could have an embryo implanted to carry the baby.

"You keep competing as best you can but no matter how much you try to align it with a weekend break from matches it's tough. Really, before, during, and after the egg extraction, well... it wasn't ideal," said Lucas.

Though it depends somewhat on circumstances, egg freezing can take around three weeks. Women inject themselves every day before their eggs are harvested and frozen under sedation. To use the eggs at a later date, they must be thawed and injected with sperm to create embryos.
IVF explained: Process, costs & risks

But, as athlete gynaecologist, Lamia Zafrani, told DW, egg freezing is far from straightforward. "Egg freezing is not an insurance policy that is guaranteed to pay out. It's always better if you freeze your eggs whilst you're young because you've got younger eggs to then use for future IVF.

"But actually there's no guarantee that when you defrost or thaw those eggs, turn them into embryos, that they'll actually be successful and result in a successful live birth. And I think it's these conversations that the athletes need to be made aware of because, at the end of the day, it's all about informed consent."
Egg freezing 'shouldn't be tool to pressure players'

Zafrani added that the number of athletes in her London clinic asking about the procedure has risen sharply in recent times. "It is definitely something that athletes are very much asking for," she said.

"But there's always nuance to all of these conversations. While it's great because the federations are listening to the players, ethically, it always does bring up the question of whether by offering egg freezing and fertility preservation, the underlying message is that you're telling your players 'don't get pregnant whilst you're working for us.' And that can be problematic."

It's a concern that is shared by Alexandra Gómez Bruinewoud. The legal director of global players' union, FIFPRO, was a co-author of the maternity policies adopted by football's global governing body, FIFA. She said FIFPRO have been working on policies for assisted reproduction, including the freezing of eggs, but that ensuring players were educated about their choices was paramount.

"We don't want it [egg freezing] to be used as a tool to pressure players not to become pregnant while they are playing because they are and they should always be fully entitled to decide when and how to become pregnant," Bruinewoud told DW.

blocks.caption: Former Germany goalkeeper Almuth Schult is one of relatively few players to give birth mid-careerImage: Memmler/Eibner-Pressefoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: There are, she said, several other considerations with regards to fertility and football, including doping concerns.

"When players go through assistive reproduction in general and if they are going to freeze eggs, in some situations they have to take hormones. And these substances can be prohibited in the WADA (World Anti Doping Agency) code.
"So we want to be sure to prevent a player being sanctioned when they are actually only trying to become pregnant or prepare things to be able to become pregnant in the future," said Bruinewoud.
Universal solution difficult to find

She added that with costs, recovery and procedures varying, mandating one blanket global rule would be near impossible, and should be guided by medical practitioners. It is also tough to apply any universal standard to a sport where professionalization and finance varies significantly between countries.

"In my view, the best solution for that is collective negotiation at national level,” Bruinewoud said. "These are very expensive procedures and most of the players worldwide will probably not have access to this because of the cost."

For all three women, the most important factors are choice, education and empowerment to get pregnant at a time that suits them. The hope is that, if managed well, egg freezing provides another option, rather than the default path.

articles.title: Flights resume gradually in Indonesia after volcanic eruption
articles.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesia had planes flying again on Tuesday after a volcanic eruption forced the country’s major airports to close for days, with authorities saying that flights would resume…

blocks.text: JAKARTA — Indonesia had planes flying again on Tuesday after a volcanic eruption forced the country’s major airports to close for days, with authorities saying that flights would resume gradually.
The disruption, caused by the eruption of Anak Krakatau, halted nearly 3,000 flights and stranded more than 340,000 passengers.
The country’s main airport serving the capital Jakarta and four other airports reopened early Tuesday after authorities cleared volcanic ash from critical infrastructure.
Transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi told reporters it would take time for flight schedules to return to normal.
Dudy said there were around 178 aircraft at Soekarno–Hatta International Airport, Jakarta’s main air travel hub.
“We will be operating these aircraft, but before we do so, we want to ensure their airworthiness. So, it may take a bit of extra time,” he said.
“We ask for a little patience from passengers and the public, as we will be carrying out inspections to ensure that these aircraft are fit to fly,” he added.
The transport minister said three flights departed shortly after the airport reopened, including two commercial flights to eastern Indonesia.
Airport operator Angkasa Pura Indonesia said in a statement that volcanic ash had been cleared from the runway and other areas to ensure the facilities were safe for flights.
Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatau, sits in a strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.
The volcano erupted at least three times on Tuesday morning alone, according to the head of the Geology Agency, Lana Saria.
It has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea nearly a century ago in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatau.
A 2018 tsunami triggered by a collapse of parts of Anak Krakatau killed more than 400 people and displaced thousands. /dl

articles.title: Eiffel Tower to reopen after row over removing women staff
articles.summary: PARIS — The Eiffel Tower was set to reopen Tuesday after staff walked out over the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group which later apologized. The operating…

blocks.text: PARIS — The Eiffel Tower was set to reopen Tuesday after staff walked out over the removal of women colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group which later apologized.

The operating company that runs the Paris landmark, SETE, acknowledged that the Hindu delegation had requested the visit be organised so as to limit “interactions with women” and said that “these conditions should not have been accepted”.
It said the landmark was due to reopen on Tuesday following a meeting the previous day between staff and management.
The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) spiritual movement apologized for “any pain or inconvenience caused” by the incident.
“To the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower,” the organization wrote on X.
“Due to the size of our delegation, the visit was arranged in conjunction with the Eiffel Tower team at the start of normal operating hours to avoid disrupting or inconveniencing others.”

Eiffel Tower staff said in a statement that it condemned “professional instructions that led to female employees being sidelined, replaced and made invisible because of their sex” during the visit by the delegation.

“Instructions were given to female employees of the Eiffel Tower and to female employees of contractors to make themselves invisible in order to welcome this delegation,” the staff said in their statement, adding they were shocked to have been put in such a situation.

“Some were asked to leave their posts and withdraw to other areas. In some posts they were replaced by men. And all female employees were instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present.” /dl

articles.title: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore
articles.summary:
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded

There isn’t much that we Indians agree…

blocks.text: There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.

Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.

The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?

Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.

In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.

blocks.caption: Critics say the government has hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.

“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”

In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.

Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)

Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.

But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.

The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.

Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.

blocks.caption: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke at a protest against leaked exam papers, as young people in India face soaring rates of unemployment. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.

That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.

The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Mumbai bound … British singer Olivia Dean is headed to Lollapalooza. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

blocks.text: Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.

The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.

Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
after newsletter promotion
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Bean-to-bar movement … artisanal chocolate is having a moment. Photograph: Manam

blocks.text: Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: A controversial revision … one-third of the electorate in Delhi have been deleted from voter lists. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: First of many mashups … Ismail Langa Group pose with a larger-than-life image of Shakira. Photograph: Ismail Langa

blocks.text: Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).

It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.

It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

articles.title: 'Good to have choice': Australians on opting out of social media algorithms
articles.summary: The BBC spoke to people in Sydney about Australia's plans to force social media companies to allow users to easily opt in or out of personalised algorithms.

blocks.text: Australia is set to force social media companies to allow users to easily opt in or out of content recommended by algorithms when they log in.
The BBC spoke to people in Sydney about how they feel about social media algorithms, and the Australian government's planned legislation.

articles.title: Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints
articles.summary:
Shinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisy

A neighbourhood in Tokyo…

blocks.text: A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.

In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.

The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan.

While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.

Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.

Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.

Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”
Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb. The Guardian has contacted Airbnb’s Japan office for comment.

The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.

Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.

“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.

A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.

Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.
The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

articles.title: Kauai on tornado watch as Hurricane Lowell nears Hawaiian islands
articles.summary: HONOLULU, United States — Residents of Kauai were warned to watch for tornadoes late Monday as Hurricane Lowell edged toward the westernmost Hawaiian islands in the US Pacific island chain, the…

blocks.text: HONOLULU, United States — Residents of Kauai were warned to watch for tornadoes late Monday as Hurricane Lowell edged toward the westernmost Hawaiian islands in the US Pacific island chain, the National Weather Service said.
“Conditions are favorable for tornadoes in and close to the watch area” of Kauai, including the city of Lihue, NWS officials said.
The core of Lowell was expected to pass near or just west of Niihau late Monday or early Tuesday, the National Hurricane Center said in a bulletin at 5:00 pm (0300 GMT).
“Dangerous conditions are expected for Niihau, Kauai and Oahu, with flash flooding, damaging waves and high winds expected from Lowell,” NHC said.
The center warned that the combination of a storm surge and tide would flood normally dry areas near the coast in Kauai and Niihau.
A tropical storm warning was also issued for the island of Oahu, where Honolulu is located.
The storm was expected to dump 4-8 inches of rain on Kauai, with 3-8 inches of rain forecast for the Big Island.
The storm was about 230 miles (370 kilometers) southwest of Honolulu and moving north-northeast, the center said.
Lowell, which was packing maximum sustained winds of 110 miles per hour (175 kilometers per hour), was expected to gradually weaken over the next several days.
The storm briefly reached Category 5 strength earlier this week.
Hawaii is still recovering from the impacts of Hurricane Lala, which grazed the southern part of the Big Island last month, bringing destructive winds and flash floods.

Lowell is one of two storms in the Pacific Ocean right now, where a near-record-strength El Nino climate episode warms the waters. Tropical Storm Marie, about 745 miles southwest of San Diego, was moving west away from land.
El Nino is the warming phase of a natural cycle in the tropical Pacific known as the El Nino-Southern Oscillation. It comes along every two to seven years.
The oscillating climate pattern promotes hurricane formation in the tropical Pacific while decreasing their likelihood in the Atlantic.
Climate change increases El Nino’s global weather impacts. /dl

articles.title: Asia News Network releases new e-book, Asia’s Hidden Heritage Treasures
articles.summary: SINGAPORE – The Asia News Network (ANN), a premier alliance of 20 leading news titles across the continent, has released a comprehensive new e-book dedicated to celebrating the cultural heritage,…

blocks.text: SINGAPORE – The Asia News Network (ANN), a premier alliance of 20 leading news titles across the continent, has released a comprehensive new e-book dedicated to celebrating the cultural heritage, modern innovation, and enduring spirit of Asia.

Launched under the banner of “Bringing Asia Closer,” the digital publication, titled ‘Inside Asia’s Hidden Heritage Treasures,’ aims to offer global and regional readers an authentic glimpse into the continent’s shared identity. (You can download the e-book here.)
Designed as a definitive peek into the soul of Asia, the publication deliberately moves past the geopolitical headlines that frequently dominate international news cycles.
Instead, it explores the deeper spiritual, cultural, and historical threads that bind the world’s largest and most populous continent together.
Readers diving into the digital volume will discover a rich tapestry of content, ranging from time-worn civilisations to bustling cultural hubs steeped in history.

Expect an exploration of amazing Unesco heritage sites, tourism attractions both ancient and modern, Asia’s best-kept secrets and unique cultural treasures that would tempt any traveller looking for their next adventure.

Current ANN Chairperson and Malaysia’s Star Media Group Chief Content Officer, Datin Paduka Esther Ng, says the e-book celebrates Asia’s unique ability to rapidly modernise, while deeply honouring its roots.

“Asia is living proof of heritage and legacy living on and evolving,” Ng states, noting that the region seamlessly blends ancient legacies with ultra-modern facets and the fastest technology adoption in the world.

Ng highlights the e-book’s focus on Asia’s “winning factors” that foster global togetherness, and adds that the region has inherited a priceless form of heritage defined by endurance and survival — two traits that she views as the most accurate descriptions of the Asian experience.
The project also directly addresses a long-standing challenge in regional media: the historical reliance on Western perspectives to tell Asian stories.

Former ANN Chairman Mahfuz Anam, Editor-in-Chief and Publisher of Bangladesh’s The Daily Star, recalls that the network was founded 27 years ago precisely to correct this imbalance, calling the new e-book an integral part of a “journey of rediscovery.”

“Our mutual understanding mostly depended on how foreign news agencies and globally reputed newspapers covered us,” Mahfuz explains, stating that said coverage tended to lend a problematic perspective.

“This awareness led 20 leading English-language dailies and a select number of national news agencies of Asia from Japan to Pakistan, covering most of the countries of Asia, to form a network to exchange news, views and features about ourselves for the reading and viewing of the general public of our respective countries,” he says.
To him: “The more we know about ourselves, the more we are at ease in dealing with others. It helps us appreciate our differences and, in turn, respect them.”

As regional cooperation transitions from a luxury to an absolute necessity in a globalised world, ANN is proud to share that a second e-book is already in development to continue uncovering the vast plethora of Asian culture.

The ANN e-books are produced in partnership with Lion Rock Group, a global leader in book printing and print management, trusted by the world’s top book publishers, education innovators, and creators across Asia, Australia, Europe, and North America. For more information, visit https://www.lionrock.hk/.
Visit the official ANN portal at https://asianews.network/ for more information. /dl

articles.title: Zelensky says Russia ‘ready to negotiate’ – Axios
articles.summary: KYIV — Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that Russia showed readiness to negotiate towards a conflict settlement at talks with US envoys, Axios reported. The weekend…

blocks.text: KYIV — Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that Russia showed readiness to negotiate towards a conflict settlement at talks with US envoys, Axios reported.

The weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner marks Washington’s latest bid to break a diplomatic stalemate in Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four years ago.
Witkoff touted progress in the meetings and raised the prospect of reviving three-way peace talks to end the war.
Zelensky told US news outlet Axios that the United States was pushing to de-escalate the conflict ahead of the long winter.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since invading in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20C.
Zelensky said the US envoys — who held separate talks with the Ukrainian and Russian leaders — told him that “the Russians are ready to negotiate”.
“Russia really thinks that this winter can help them to break us,” he told Axios.
But the administration of US President Donald Trump could pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to de-escalate, he added, and Putin “doesn’t want” to “upset” his US counterpart.
Zelensky said the weekend talks included US proposals around energy facilities, grain shipments and oil and gas exports, but declined to give further details.
The Ukrainian leader said the US approach aimed to resume negotiations between the warring countries and ensure the coming winter was different from previous ones.
The goal was to make progress before or during winter in order to “bring (the) sides closer to the peace,” Zelensky said. /dl

articles.title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia
articles.summary:
US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa

The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off…
articles.byline: Mohamed Gabobe in Mogadishu and Peter Beaumont

blocks.text: The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.

Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.

Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.

blocks.caption: Armed Somali pirates guard the beach in Hobyo district, 540km north-east of Mogadishu, in 2008.  Photograph: Badri Media/epa/Corbis

blocks.text: The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.

However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.

blocks.caption: Members of Somalia Puntland maritime police force on duty in 2023.  Photograph: Daniel Irungu/EPA

blocks.text: In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.

He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”
According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”
Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.

Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.

blocks.caption: Yemenis protest against Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping. Experts warn that these attacks in response to the US-Israel war on Iran are allowing piracy to thrive. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty

blocks.text: Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.
Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.

According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.

blocks.caption: The MV Sward, a cement carrier hijacked in April, was repurposed as a pirate mothership. Photograph: EU Naval Force Operation Atalanta

blocks.text: Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.

That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.

In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.

blocks.caption: Residents of Galkayo, Somalia, said money has begun to circulate in the local economy since the hijacking of the Lutuf. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Observer

blocks.text: During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.

Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.
The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.

Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.

blocks.caption: Somali pirates apprehended by French soldiers in the Gulf of Aden in 2009. Photograph: Sipa Press/Rex Features

blocks.text: “What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.

“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.
“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”

articles.title: Gen Z uprising reshaped Nepal’s politics. A year on, questions linger
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Rakesh Mahato lies in a hospital bed in Kathmandu with a simple wish—to get up, take a few steps and make it home. The 25-year-old from Sarlahi district has spent the entirety of…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Rakesh Mahato lies in a hospital bed in Kathmandu with a simple wish—to get up, take a few steps and make it home.
The 25-year-old from Sarlahi district has spent the entirety of the past year in hospital after being shot by police while protesting against corruption on September 8, 2025.

Mahato is among the thousands injured during the youth-led uprising, which has come to be known as the Gen Z protests. Although the immediate trigger was the KP Sharma Oli government’s ban on social media, the youth were protesting systemic corruption and decades of power-sharing among a small group of ageing politicians.

The protests began as a peaceful demonstration but soon spiralled out of control, leading to massive casualties and the loss of private and public property. As many as 76 people were killed and 2,638 were injured during the demonstrations on September 8 and the violence that followed the next day. The spontaneous protests became a historic political event—triggering a major upheaval in the young democracy and turning the lives of thousands, including Mahato’s, upside down.
People, however, have yet to see the promises of the monumental movement translate into their daily lives, activists who took part in the protests say.

The faces in Singha Durbar, the country’s administrative centre, have changed. For the injured and families of those killed, however, life remains frozen on the two days of the uprising. Kantipur spoke to nearly a dozen people affected by the protests. Their demands were strikingly consistent—an end to corruption, better governance and a state that answers to its citizens. The movement transformed Nepal’s political leadership. Shah, once mayor of Kathmandu, became prime minister after the election. The party secured a near two-thirds majority. But for those who bled on the streets, little has changed, Mahato says.

blocks.caption: Prakash Bohora, 29, from Dailekh, became a symbol of the Gen Z uprising after an image of his blood-stained white shoes went viral. Dipesh Darshandhari/TKP

blocks.text: Mahato was one of thousands of ambitious young men who travel to Kathmandu every year from across Nepal, seeking opportunities beyond their rural villages and small towns. He was studying for a bachelor’s degree at a commerce college and preparing for Loksewa, Nepal’s civil service examinations. He hoped to support his struggling family, get his younger brother a good education and make it big himself. Even in the capital city, jobs were scarce and the economy was in freefall. Like thousands of others, the Mahato brothers grew disillusioned by what they saw. Attributing these systemic issues to entrenched corruption, nepotism, and favouritism, they joined the protests together.

The demonstration was peaceful until shortly after noon, when gunfire suddenly erupted. One protester, Dipendra Basnet, was shot in the head in front of Parliament. Mahato and others rushed to help him. “That’s when police opened fire from behind,” Mahato recalled to Kantipur from his hospital bed. “I was shot in the belly and then I collapsed on the spot.”

The bullet entered through the right side of his abdomen and lodged on the left. Mahato regained consciousness three days later. By then, the protests had already set in motion a dramatic political transition. Gen Z representatives had proposed former chief justice Sushila Karki as interim prime minister during talks with army chief Ashok Raj Sigdel, while discussions were under way at the president’s office over forming a new government.

Mahato, meanwhile, was struggling to move his legs in the intensive care unit at the National Trauma Centre. He could not. A doctor eventually told him that he would never walk again and would probably depend on a wheelchair for the rest of his life. The nerves below his waist had been severed.
Mahato was devastated.

On September 12, four days after Oli resigned, an interim government was formed under Karki, following the violent uprising. Six months later, parliamentary elections brought the Rastriya Swatantra Party to a near two-thirds majority, and Balendra Shah, the rapper, structural engineer and former mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, became the prime minister. That a 35-year-old political novice had become the prime minister was a tectonic shift for the country’s politics dominated by a handful of geriatric men.
Mahato watched from his hospital bed as Shah took office. He was hopeful.

A year later, that hope has receded. “They haven’t even investigated who shot us and why,” Mahato said. “No one has been punished. Sometimes it feels like this government is no different from the previous ones.”

An inquiry led by former chief justice Gauri Bahadur Karki concluded that police had used excessive and indiscriminate force during the protests. The panel said security forces fired continuously for about four hours before a curfew was imposed and that the police and the political leadership failed to intervene.

The report prompted police to arrest former prime minister Oli and former home minister Ramesh Lekhak on charges linked to the deaths during the crackdown. Shah’s first Cabinet meeting had decided to implement the inquiry’s recommendations. The two were later released after the Supreme Court considered a habeas corpus petition.
